# Modifications to TOMB5

## 1. What this is

This is a modified version of **TOMB5**, the PC Tomb Raider Chronicles decompilation
project by Troye/Trxyebeep and contributors, <https://github.com/Trxyebeep/TOMB5>. It
was modified between **2026-07-30 and 2026-10-30** (ongoing) for the *TR5 Randomizer*
project.

The upstream code as received is preserved as the first commit of this repository (no
hash is named here on purpose: it changes whenever the history is rewritten for privacy
scrubbing, the content does not), so every change made here is visible as a diff against
it. That baseline differs from current upstream in exactly three files: one upstream
commit made after this copy was taken (`setup.cpp`: Two Gun gains `undead = 1`) and two
small local fixes that predate this repository and are documented in the files themselves
(`dxsound.cpp` LOCSOFTWARE, `function_stubs.cpp` DO_LOG).

Measured on **2026-10-30** by comparing every file under `TOMB5/` against that first
commit: **130 files changed, 189 entirely new - 319 in all**, none deleted,
**269** of them carrying the modification notice at the top, which `grep -rl
"Modified 2026 by ChrisChanSan" TOMB5/` lists. The project file `tomb5.vcxproj` carries
the same notice as an XML comment.

50 of the 319 do not carry the notice, and none of them should:

- the 40 `specific/hd/hd_shader/*.inc` (9 vertex and 31 pixel shaders) are compiler
  output (`fxc` bytecode as a C array), regenerated from the eleven `.hlsl` files beside
  them and carrying no source of this project at all;
- `tomb5/libs/stb/stb_vorbis.c` and `tomb5/libs/discordRPC/LICENSE` are other people's
  files that are not modified here in any way - stb_vorbis carries its own licence at the
  end of the file, and the second one *is* a licence. A notice on them would claim an
  authorship this project does not have;
- the other eight are under `vendor/trforge/`: five source files copied from TRForge
  (MIT), its `LICENSE`, its `NOTICE.md` and a `VERSION.txt` recording where they came
  from. The five sources carry a hidden signature in their first three lines; writing
  anything into them, a notice included, would destroy it. Four are byte for byte
  TRForge's; `trf_remaster/Trg.h` differs only in three comment passages left out, which
  `VERSION.txt` names with the file's new hash, so there is nothing else to notice.

`game/trex.h`, `game/raptor.h` and `game/compy.h` carry the notice and additionally name
tomb3 as their origin further down (section 2.3).

The engine builds from a clean clone of the tracked files alone; the four test suites
(`Preparation/Tools/README.md` gives their counts) run with 0 failed. InterpTest reads
Lara's key frames from the player's own `ANDREA1.TRC` and LipsTest the player's `.OBJ`
folder; without those files the checks that need them fail and say so.

This modified version remains licensed under the **GNU General Public License version
3**, the same licence as the original. See `LICENSE`. The complete corresponding source
is distributed alongside any binary released. Every file changed under `TOMB5/` carries
a modification notice at the top, as required by GPLv3 section 5(a).

Original credits are unchanged and remain with the upstream project: Troye (main
programmer, project leader), ChocolateFan, thatguyfrombb, Raildex. The work recorded
below is layered on top of theirs.

How this record is laid out: section 2 holds the engine's modifications in ten areas
(2.1 the native Windows port, 2.2 the engine's support for the randomizer, 2.3 the Tomb
Raider III enemies, 2.4 the HD art read from the player's own Remaster files, 2.5 sixty
frames a second, 2.6 modern controls and the options menu, 2.7 the first person view,
the cheats and the `-log` seams, 2.8 and 2.9 the corrections and the cleanup before the
first public push, 2.10 the rounds after it); section 3 lists the randomizer's own
changes since Beta 1.0 as short rows; section 4 says how to build; the appendix maps the
task numbers that the commit subjects carry to the entries. Every entry has one form:
What was changed, Why, How, the Decisions where a choice was made, and the Commits that
made it - and nothing else. Where a number in the code carries a rule, the entry gives
the number and its reason; the measurements behind it are not part of this record.

## 2.1 Native Windows 11 port

TOMB5 as received draws through DirectDraw and Direct3D 3 and plays its effects through
DirectSound. On Windows 11 that stack no longer creates a rendering device at all, so the
port replaces it with Direct3D 9 and XAudio2 and the game runs without a wrapper such as
dgVoodoo2. The rendering work follows the approach TR2Main used for Tomb Raider II.
Everything that touches the player's own files is optional and read at run time: the
remaster's `MAIN.SFX`, the player's own OGG soundtracks. No audio and no game data of any
kind ships with this project, and nothing is taken from another program's binaries. Paths
below are relative to `TOMB5 Code/TOMB5/`.

### Direct3D 9 renderer in place of DirectDraw and Direct3D 3
2026-07-30 - 2026-07-31

**What.** The whole rendering path is Direct3D 9: device creation, surface handling,
present, adapter and mode enumeration and the cooperative level. Textures are uploaded
with `CreateTexture`/`LockRect`; room drawing keeps its bump mapping; effects, HUD bars
and the transform state constants follow. The adapter selection defaults to the adapter
that drives the Windows primary monitor instead of a hard-coded index, and the setup
dialog appends the Windows display number (`\\.\DISPLAYn`) to each Graphics Adapter entry
so that two identical GPUs can be told apart. A window is sized from the adapter's current
desktop resolution (`GetAdapterDisplayMode`) rather than from the enumerated
exclusive-fullscreen mode list, which can be much shorter than what the monitor supports.
Fullscreen is borderless windowed. The device is created with `D3DCREATE_MULTITHREADED`,
and `FullScreen_RefreshRateInHz` is left 0 so the driver keeps the display at its current
rate.

**Why.** On Windows 11 `IDirect3D3::CreateDevice` fails outright, for the hardware device
and for software emulation alike. Real exclusive fullscreen never recovered from device
loss: after alt-tabbing back in, `TestCooperativeLevel` stayed at `D3DERR_DEVICELOST`
permanently and froze the game. `LoadTextures` runs on the background level-loading thread
and calls `CreateTexture`/`LockRect` on the same device the main thread presents with,
which is undefined behaviour per the D3D9 documentation and hung level loads
intermittently. Forcing an exact refresh rate from the enumerated mode list was rejected
by `CreateDevice` at higher resolutions, for example 2560x1440. `setupdlg.cpp` hard-coded
`nD3DDevice = 1`, the "hardware" index of the old two-device D3D3 enumeration, while D3D9
enumeration produces one device per adapter at index 0.

**How.** `specific/dxshell.cpp`, `.h` hold device, surfaces, present, enumeration,
cooperative level and the adapter choice (`DXGetInfo` matches the enumerated adapter
against the primary monitor via `GetAdapterMonitor` and `MonitorFromPoint`).
`specific/output.cpp`, `.h` the render and present path; `specific/function_table.cpp`,
`.h` the one-time render state setup in `HWInitialise` plus an `HWDrawPrimitive` helper
wrapping `DrawPrimitiveUP`; `specific/texture.cpp`, `.h` the upload;
`specific/drawroom.cpp` the bump-mapped rooms; `specific/polyinsert.cpp` the
`HWR_DrawSortList` submission only, the clip and subdivide maths untouched;
`specific/specificfx.cpp` and `specific/drawbars.cpp` effects and HUD bars;
`specific/3dmath.cpp` and `specific/d3dmatrix.cpp` the transform state constants;
`specific/file.cpp` one stray texture call; `specific/winmain.cpp` and
`specific/setupdlg.cpp` back buffer access, `Clear`, render states and the adapter
dropdown, whose text is built in `InitDDDevice` from `DDIdentifier.Description`/`.Driver`;
`global/types.h` and `tomb5/pch.h` the `DXPTR` struct and the includes. Two sampler
differences the port had to absorb: `SetSamplerState` instead of `SetTextureStageState`
for the filters, and explicit CLAMP addressing, since D3D9 defaults to WRAP.
`HWInitialise` had `D3DTSS_ALPHAARG1` on `D3DTA_TFACTOR` while `D3DRS_TEXTUREFACTOR` is
never set anywhere, so alpha test and blend never saw real per-pixel texture alpha; it is
`D3DTA_TEXTURE`, which is what removed the menu text ghosting and the black boxes around
foliage and vines.

**Commits.** `05e3b2c`, `d943e07`, `fcf8664`, `dded076`, `74e0123`, `7774945`, `09f9816`,
`103eb75`, `a659e96`, `3c9e395`, `2e22d92`, `92c8bc5`, `e5bb808`, `3f7cd6a`, `e7c0363`,
`8fc6f7f`, `cb7b941`, `b6d2f70`, `2cb5434`, `6e41063`, `a819765`

### Bink video drawn through a Direct3D 9 texture
2026-07-30

**What.** FMV frames are uploaded into a D3D9 texture and drawn as a full-screen quad
instead of being blitted with the GDI `StretchBlt` the original used. `fmv.cpp` keeps a
small standalone DirectDraw object and surface as the Bink decode target only; nothing of
the rendering path goes through it.

**Why.** GDI blitting does not reach the screen while a D3D9 device holds the display,
because the display scans out directly from the D3D back buffer, so every FMV played as a
black screen. This is also why `Ddraw.lib` has to remain on the linker line.

**How.** `specific/fmv.cpp`.

**Commits.** `7774945`, `0db6681`, `3c9e395`

### Savegames: the screen grab, the folder, and the check on read
2026-07-30 - 2026-08-22

**What.** The frame grab behind the save thumbnail and the Escape-menu backdrop is copied
with `GetRenderTargetData` into a `D3DPOOL_SYSTEMMEM` surface and locked there. Savegames
live in a `savegame\` subfolder, and any `savegame.N` still lying loose in the game folder
is moved there once at startup, never overwriting. The number of bytes the read actually
returned is kept, and the checksum is computed the moment the file is read rather than
after the fade and the level reload.

**Why.** D3D9 back buffers are not directly lockable; locking one crashed the game
whenever a save screen or the Escape menu was opened. Keeping the read length means a save
written before the struct grew is recognised before it is applied. The game loop keeps
running behind the menu and increments the level timer, so a load during Lara's death
animation failed with "corrupted savegame" on a file that was provably read in full, and
worked after a restart when no frames lay in between.

**How.** `specific/LoadSave.cpp`, `.h` (`CreateMonoScreen`) and the screenshot key path in
`specific/dxshell.cpp` (`DXShowFrame`) for the grab; `specific/gamemain.cpp`, `.h` for the
folder and the migration; `game/savegame.h` and `specific/LoadSave.h` for the read length
and the checksum point.

**Commits.** `a819765`, `89d0d36`, `4b34a7d`, `2ef9a4d`

### Sound effects on XAudio2
2026-07-30

**What.** The sound effect pipeline runs on XAudio2. Pooled, reusable
`IXAudio2SourceVoice` channels submit shared decoded PCM with `SubmitSourceBuffer` instead
of creating and destroying a duplicated DirectSound buffer per play.

**Why.** The effect path was the other half of the legacy DirectX stack being replaced,
and one decoded buffer can serve every voice that plays the sample, so the
duplicate-buffer-per-play model had nothing worth keeping.

**How.** `specific/dxsound.cpp`, `.h`. Volume and pan keep DirectSound's
hundredths-of-a-decibel convention at the call sites and are converted to XAudio2's linear
gain inside this file.

**Commits.** `8291574`

### Music and FMV sound off DirectSound
2026-08-17 - 2026-08-21

**What.** The CD-track music stream plays through one XAudio2 source voice fed by a refill
thread instead of a DirectSound ring buffer with position notifications; Bink FMV audio
goes through WaveOut instead of a raw `IDirectSound` object. Only the device layer
changed: the MS-ADPCM to PCM decoding, the looping seek, the end-of-file run-out and the
return to the level ambience are as they were. Volume keeps DirectSound's
hundredths-of-a-decibel convention at the call sites and is converted to XAudio2's linear
factor at the API boundary.

**Why.** Music and film sound were the last two playback paths still on DirectSound; one
audio path instead of two is the more robust delivery, and after them nothing in the game
itself used DirectSound any more.

**How.** `specific/audio.cpp`, `.h` hold `MusicVoice`, the `MusicVoiceCallback` that only
wakes the refill thread, and the queue that serves both the original tracks and the OGG
path; `specific/dxsound.cpp`, `.h`, `specific/gamemain.cpp` and `specific/winmain.cpp`
lose the DirectSound set-up and `App.dx.lpDS`; `specific/fmv.cpp` calls
`BinkSetSoundSystem(BinkOpenWaveOut, WAVE_MAPPER)`, which needs a device id rather than a
COM object and picks the same default device as the XAudio2 mastering voice.

**Commits.** `82ad2fd`, `a5b4dfd`

### Optional high quality sound bank from the player's remaster
2026-09-02 - 2026-09-21

**What.** Chronicles has no `MAIN.SFX` - that was TR4. From TR5 on the samples live in the
level files, so every `.TRC` carries its own bank of MS-ADPCM at 22050 Hz. The TR4-6
Remaster went back to one global `MAIN.SFX` of plain PCM at 44100 Hz. If the player copies
that file out of the installation into `audio\`, the engine takes the sample data from it;
without it nothing changes at all.

**Why.** That `MAIN.SFX` is not the old material resampled: its spectrum runs through
11025 Hz without the cliff a resampled signal always shows, so it is genuinely better
material and worth offering. Only files the player already owns are read, and nothing is
taken from that game's own programs.

**How.** `specific/hqsfx.cpp` and `specific/hqsfx.h`, both new. The bridge between a
level's own sample numbers and the bank's global ones runs over the sound ids, which both
sides index the same way. Only the audio data is swapped; the level's own tables stay in
charge, so the sounds imported from Tomb Raider III keep their original samples and
`MAX_SAMPLES` is untouched. Playback needed three changes in `specific/dxsound.cpp`: a
source sample rate per voice, read from the sample rather than assumed; `DSAdjustPitch`
reduced to the plain 16.16 ratio it had always been computing, clamped to 100/22050 at the
bottom and 4.5 at the top; and `MaxFrequencyRatio` lowered from 8.0 to 4.5 at
`CreateSourceVoice`, because XAudio2 caps `MaxFrequencyRatio * source rate` at
`XAUDIO2_MAX_SAMPLE_RATE` (200000), so at 8.0 a voice could never be switched to 44100 Hz
while 4.5 clears both rates (4.5 * 44100 = 198450) and costs nothing that was ever
reachable. Two unrelated holes were closed on the way: `LoadSamples` read samples into a
fixed buffer with no length check, and `DXCreateSample` did not check its `malloc`. The
bank writes `MODLOG bank ...` lines to the log and tests the log switch before it builds a
line.

**Commits.** `4e89a0d`, `f4b43e4`

### HQ soundtracks in OGG
2026-08-22

**What.** If a file named after the track number lies in `audio\HQ`, it is played instead
of the original track; without those files nothing changes. Language-specific sets follow
the language selection.

**Why.** No music is shipped with this project - the player supplies the files.

**How.** `specific/audio.cpp` looks the file up by track number and decodes it with
stb_vorbis by Sean Barrett, vendored unchanged as `tomb5/libs/stb/stb_vorbis.c` and placed
in the public domain by its own header, so it adds no licence obligation of its own.

**Commits.** `f136cf0`, `7afba2c`, `35a81e8`

### Real controller support
2026-07-31 - 2026-08-25

**What.** `DXUpdateJoystick` polls XInput and falls back to DirectInput8 for controllers
that are not XInput devices, so the remapping screen the game already had finally binds
something. Pause, Quicksave, Quickload and the small and large medipack hotkeys are
bindable and persist to the registry; the four tilt directions of the right stick are
bindable as extra buttons; buttons are named after the DualSense (Cross, Circle, ..., PS
Button); Circle acts as menu back and cancel alongside Escape; binding a button that
another action already holds unbinds that other action; the Joystick controls screen no
longer prints keyboard key hints; the Pause button also closes the pause menu, not only
Escape. Joystick enumeration runs on its own thread instead of on the startup path. The
*Control method* row offers Keyboard, PS5 Controller, Xbox Controller, generic Joystick
and Reset; the three controller settings pick only the button *vocabulary* (registry
`JoyStyle`, `-1` meaning automatic - an XInput pad found picks the Xbox page, otherwise
PS5), while the bit order the engine reads comes from `joystick_is_xinput`, set by each
poll. Back and confirm are asked for by role, not by a fixed bit. Circle also closes the
inventory ring, and the still-held button is no longer read as a roll on the frame after.

**Why.** `DXUpdateJoystick` was a stub returning zeros despite the complete remapping
screen, so no controller worked, and `Key()` shifted joystick button indices by the wrong
amount and was therefore dead code. `IDirectInput8::EnumDevices` can take ten seconds when
a controller is paired over Bluetooth but attached over USB, because DirectInput waits for
the absent paired device; the delay is a DirectInput timeout, reproducible in a standalone
program outside this code, and it left the game on a black screen for that time. The right
stick read the wrong DirectInput axes (Rx/Ry instead of Z/Rz), and the D-pad produced no
diagonals through the DirectInput fallback. A DualSense reaches the engine raw over
DirectInput but as an XInput device behind a wrapper, so one fixed bit order can never
name its buttons right; back sat hard on bit 2, which under XInput is X, and the cutscene
skip on bit 1, which is B. The inventory ring closed on `IN_OPTION` alone, the inventory
toggle, which a gameplay button cannot carry without tearing the ring open on every roll,
so the ring was the one screen without the way back every other menu has.

**How.** `specific/input.cpp` holds the polling, the bindings, `Key()`, the binding
screen, `JoyStyle`, `ActiveJoyStyle()`, `JoyBitConfirm()` and `JoyBitBack()`;
`specific/dxshell.cpp` the enumeration thread; `game/newinv2.cpp` reads a left-over
deselect at the end of the frame, after the modes above the ring have consumed theirs;
`specific/LoadSave.cpp` and `specific/registry.cpp` carry the control-method row and
`JoyStyle`; `game/spotcam.cpp` and `game/control.cpp` ask by role.

**Commits.** `cedb10b`, `c2f745d`, `9a5eaea`, `d70fa26`, `bb50307`, `ddde1eb`, `17e1700`,
`ecf95ab`, `61f1c07`, `2f12872`, `b1bcfc5`, `1e6e2aa`, `b88e982`, `7c78ff4`, `64a48e7`,
`7707d63`, `009fec3`, `d2c2f82`, `b543742`, `eb3c602`, `afa0bab`

### The setup dialog offers only what the engine still honours
2026-08-25

**What.** The 3D device list and the texture format list are gone and the device is a
label naming the renderer; the sound device list is gone. The resolution list holds one
entry per resolution rather than one per mode. The five registry indices (`DD`, `D3D`,
`VMode`, `TFormat`, `DS`) are clamped on read and written back as 0 where the control is
gone. Sound is switched on only by `DXDSCreate`, on success, and the voice creation checks
the engine pointer. `Dsound.lib` leaves the linker line. The dialog corner carries the
build date and time, the same that the log writes on its first line.

**Why.** Three controls had quietly died with the port: D3D9 enumerates exactly one device
per adapter, so the device and format lists offer one thing each, and the sound device
selection was never read at all, since XAudio2 always plays through the system's default
endpoint. Nothing checked the registry indices although they can outlive the machine that
wrote them - a saved `DD=2` reads past the adapter list once a monitor is unplugged, and
any `TFormat` above 0 from an older DirectX 3 build points past a one-element array that
`LoadTextures` walks three of in one expression. `SOUND_Init` used to set `sound_active`
unconditionally, so a machine without an audio device would have turned sound on over a
null XAudio2 and crashed on the first effect; it never showed only because the dialog
forced "Disable" whenever the DirectSound enumeration found nothing. `EnumAdapterModes`
reports each resolution once per refresh rate, so a 165 Hz screen produced seven identical
"2560x1440" lines for one thing, the rate never being used because device creation
deliberately leaves `FullScreen_RefreshRateInHz` at 0. A `VMode` saved before this points
at a different entry, is clamped, and re-picking the resolution once settles it.
`dsound.h` stays for `DSBPLAY_LOOPING`. The build date in the dialog lets a picture of the
dialog and a `log.txt` be matched to one build.

**How.** `specific/setupdlg.cpp`, `specific/registry.cpp`, `specific/dxshell.cpp`,
`game/sound.cpp`, `tomb5.rc`.

**Commits.** `a8d928b`, `2107ce9`

### Bounds checks, a log that survives a crash, a glyph guard, and the build
2026-07-30 - 2026-08-22

**What.** Fixed-size arrays that are filled from counts in the level file are
bounds-checked before they are written: the savegame buffer, the texture page array,
`items[]`, spot cameras, animating-texture ranges, the sound buffer pool (`DS_Buffers`,
raised from 256 to `MAX_SAMPLES`, 450), `BuildOutsideTable`'s stack array and the
per-frame queue. `Log()` writes millisecond timestamps and flushes after every line.
`PrintString` skips a character whose code lies outside the font table instead of reading
past it; what the font can show is shown. Discord Rich Presence is compiled out behind
`TOMB5_DISCORD_RPC` - the code stays in place and one `#define` re-enables it - and the
executable links the static C runtime (`/MT`), no longer links `discord-rpc.lib`, and
writes its output to the top-level release folder.

**Why.** The bounds checks are one bug class: a level file longer than the array silently
overwrote whatever followed it. Upstream TR2's original 1996 code already had a guard in
its equivalent of `WriteSG`; TR5 either never had one or lost it in decompilation, and the
randomizer produces levels denser than the originals. `DS_Buffers` was the narrowest place
in the engine's own sound system: `sample_lut` has always been laid out with `MAX_SAMPLES`
and the level format's sound map holds the same 450 entries, while the memory for the
decoded sounds stayed at 256 - and a randomized level reaches 223 samples where the
original reaches 218. Without the flush the log was routinely empty after a crash, which
made it useless exactly when it was needed. `CharDef` holds 106 entries plus the accent
codes 128 to 173, and the kana indices of the Japanese PSX language file reach to 181. The
Discord application id in that call belongs to the upstream project and is not this
project's to use; the bundled `discord-rpc.lib` is built against the dynamic C runtime,
which prevented linking statically, and with `/MT` the executable runs without the Visual
C++ redistributable. discord-rpc is therefore not part of the shipped binary.

**How.** `game/savegame.cpp`, `.h` (savegame buffer), `game/setup.cpp`
(`BuildOutsideTable`), `game/items.cpp` (per-frame queue), `specific/file.cpp` (the
level-load bounds checks), `specific/polyinsert.cpp` (the diagnostic drawtype logging read
`Textures[texture].bump` unconditionally, including for line-draw calls where `texture` is
outside the 0-63 range), `specific/function_stubs.cpp` (`Log()`), `game/text.cpp`
(`PrintString`), `specific/dxsound.cpp` (`DS_Buffers`), `tomb5/tomb5.cpp` (the guarded
Discord call) and `tomb5.vcxproj` (runtime, output path, removed library).

**Commits.** `89d0d36`, `09f9816`, `b543742`, `4d49e52`, `9c47bb7`, `9abb4f5`, `84b1b48`

## 2.2 Engine support for the randomizer

These are the engine changes a rolled campaign needs. They fall into three kinds: limits
raised where the original sizes were built for hand-made levels, places where the engine
asked the level when it should have asked the item, and defects of the original that
only become visible once items, enemies, outfits and the level order move. One rule runs
through all of them: new behaviour hangs on marks that no vanilla level file carries,
and new object slots sit beyond the range any original level uses, so an unmodified
level plays byte-identically. Paths are relative to `TOMB5 Code/TOMB5/` unless a
randomizer path is given in full.

### Level identity separated from level slot
2026-08-22

**What.** `gfLevelId` is a second number, taken from the level's file name at load time,
and every level-specific branch in the engine asks it. `gfCurrentLevel` keeps its slot
meaning: which entry of `SCRIPT.DAT` is being played, for order, savegame and level names.

**Why.** Upstream uses one number for two different questions, which is correct while the
two are the same, as in vanilla. As soon as the level order is shuffled they are not, and
every place where the engine does something only one particular level needs fired in the
wrong level: the Iris hazard, the gunship, the Area 51 laser, a shatter sound table
indexed per level, footprints, the puzzle-hole special case.

**How.** `game/gameflow.h`, `game/gameflow.cpp` derive and hold the identity;
`game/tower.cpp`, `game/objects.cpp`, `game/switch.cpp`, `game/footprnt.cpp`,
`game/health.cpp` and `game/traps.cpp` ask it.

**Commits.** `e662d3f`

### Twice as many items per level
2026-08-02 - 2026-08-15

**What.** `MAX_ITEMS` is 512 instead of 256. The savegame buffer grows to 28980 bytes
because the per-item section scales with the item count. Buffers that depend on what a
level contains are sized from the level rather than from a fixed guess.

**Why.** The densest vanilla levels already hold 248 (rich2) and 244 (joby3) items, which
left almost no room for the randomizer's extra enemies and scattered weapons. Saves from
older builds are cleanly refused by the existing short-read detection.

**How.** `global/types.h` holds the constant and the savegame buffer; `items[]` is
allocated from the `game_malloc` pool with it and the free list is parametric. Triggers
address items through a 10-bit field (`items[trigger & 0x3FF]`), so 512 stays fully
reachable. The `ItemNewRooms` deferred queue and its kill flag `0x8000`, which tolerates
indices up to `0x7FFF`, derive from `MAX_ITEMS` too, including the extern declaration in
`game/control.h`; `game/control.cpp`, `game/init.cpp` and `game/items.cpp` carry the
headroom and the guards.

**Commits.** `89d0d36`, `7d984d4`

### Sixteen AI enemies active at once
2026-08-15

**What.** `MAX_LOT` is 16 instead of 5, and Lara's target arrays are sized from it through
the new `MAX_TARGETS (MAX_LOT + 1)`. The `game_malloc` pool is raised from 15 to 20 MB
(`MALLOC_SIZE` 20000000). The eviction path remains as the fallback for the seventeenth
enemy.

**Why.** Upstream allowed five AI enemies to be active at once; the sixth triggered enemy
evicted the one farthest from the camera and froze it as `ITEM_INVISIBLE`. With 10 to 20
extra enemies placed per level, frozen bystanders were routine. The pool is raised not for
the slots but because a randomized level carries the imported enemies' meshes, animations
and frames and so runs several times the size of a vanilla one. Lara's target acquisition
collected up to `MAX_LOT` targets plus a terminator into fixed
`TargetList[8]`/`LastTargets[8]` arrays, correct for five slots and a buffer overflow from
eight active enemies up.

**How.** `global/types.h` holds `MAX_LOT`, `MAX_TARGETS` and `MALLOC_SIZE`;
`game/larafire.cpp` derives both arrays and their loop bounds from `MAX_TARGETS`;
`game/lot.cpp` allocates per slot a `CREATURE_INFO` plus `num_boxes x BOX_NODE` from the
`game_malloc` pool, roughly 25 KB per slot in the largest level. Savegames store creature
state per item and re-acquire slots on load, so there is no compatibility impact.

**Commits.** `b13a521`

### Engine-only object slots beyond the original 460
2026-08-15 - 2026-09-04

**What.** `SLOT_FILE_BOUNDARY` is 460 and the loader uses it instead of the enum constant
`NUMBER_OBJECTS` when splitting static-object sprite slots from moveable slots;
`LoadObjects` skips, and logs, a moveable record whose slot this build does not know. On
that footing the enum carries slots no original level uses: `BLUE_GUARD2` (460), the
second guard model, a full member of the soldier family; `ROMAN_GOD2` (461), the hammer
version of the Roman god, so that both of its versions can stand in one level with the
weapon decided by the item's OCB (`trigger_flags` 1 = sword, 0 = hammer) and the model by
the slot; `MESHSWAP_CROSS_SWAT` (462), `_SWATPLUS` (463), `_TWOGUN` (464), `_GUARD` (465),
`_MAFIA` (466), `_GUARD2` (467), `_HITMAN` (468) and `_CRANEGUY` (470) as mesh warehouses,
one per enemy, beside the four that alias `SMASH_OBJECT5..8` (`MESHSWAP_CROSS_GLADIATOR`,
`_IMP`, `_ROMANGOD`, `_ROMANGOD2`). Enemies of the imported pool take their swap meshes
through `MeshSwapSource()`, which prefers the designated fallback slot and otherwise
behaves exactly like upstream.

**Why.** The level file format encodes static-object sprite slots as `460 + static
number`, 460 being the value `NUMBER_OBJECTS` had when the original levels were built;
`LoadSprites` used the enum constant for that split, which silently breaks every existing
level the moment a new moveable slot is appended, and an unknown slot wrote past the end
of `objects[]`. `MESHSWAP1` holds, per level, the swap meshes of that level's own enemies
- the soldier family's gun hands 10/13, the Imp's alternate head 10, Two Gun's source mesh
2, the Gladiator's and the Roman God's full damage sets - so an imported enemy needs the
set of a level that actually carries it, and that cannot go into `MESHSWAP1` without
breaking the target level's native users. Vanilla carries two different guard models in
the same slot 37, rich levels one and joby levels the other, and both Roman gods share
slot 61, so in each case the two can never coexist. With the enum unchanged both loader
changes are no-ops: 460 equals `NUMBER_OBJECTS` there, and no vanilla level carries
unknown slots; the fallback slots are loaded by no vanilla level and are reached by the
engine only through `item->object_number` range checks, so without items of those types
they are inert.

**How.** `game/objects.h` defines `SLOT_FILE_BOUNDARY` and the slots, `specific/file.cpp`
uses the constant in `LoadSprites` and `LoadObjects`, `game/setup.cpp` wires
`BaddyObjects` through `MeshSwapSource()`. Grouping is by swap-set donor, which can differ
from the model donor: rich1, the model source for the Guard and Two Gun, carries no
`MESHSWAP1` at all, because its enemies never set their swap bits in vanilla. The slots
need no `_MIP` twin, since distance models are off for enemies; the cyborg's own slot 469
belongs to its own entry below.

**Commits.** `d05fbaf`, `b16fcd6`, `db9ada4`, `560dc1d`, `be7918a`, `2f0cb8f`

### Distance models switched off for enemies
2026-08-17

**What.** `DrawAnimatingItem` no longer draws an enemy's distance model (MIP/LOD). Doors
and bridges (mip 2048-4096) keep theirs.

**Why.** The routine took the slot after the enemy as soon as anything at all was loaded
there. That is safe in an original level, where level and enemies were built together, but
the randomizer places enemies into levels whose MIP slot holds something unrelated, and
the enemy is then drawn as that foreign model with its own bones and frame; 51 such
combinations are reachable across the thirteen levels. Almost nothing is lost: the game
has exactly seven genuine MIP cases, SWAT, SWAT+, Guard and Two Gun in the three rich
levels, all with the same mesh count as the full model. It also removes the need to
reserve a `_MIP` twin for every new enemy slot.

**How.** `game/draw.cpp`; `intelligent` separates the two groups cleanly, because every
enemy with an `object_mip` sets it and the scenery does not.

**Commits.** `a3e28b1`

### An enemy's animations come from its own slot
2026-08-15 - 2026-09-04

**What.** Four places that picked one globally chosen animation base read
`objects[item->object_number].anim_index` per item instead. `SasControl` takes the soldier
family's vault and special animations from its own object entry; `ResetGuards`, the
body-bag trigger, gives each thinking item its own set; `HitmanControl` reads
`item->object_number` in the twelve places it reached for `objects[HITMAN].anim_index`;
the flipeffect wake-up in `effects.cpp` uses the second guard slot as the last anchor of
the same alias chain.

**Why.** In vanilla no level loads two members of the soldier family at once, so a global
pick is correct there; with a mixed enemy pool they coexist, and the loser of the pick
indexed into the other one's animations. `ResetGuards` wrote SWAT's index if loaded, else
the mini sub's, else the Guard's, into every thinking item - almost harmless in the four
vanilla levels that carry a body bag, where what stands in them is soldier family, but
with a mixed pool it hands a hydra or a dinosaur an absolute animation number out of a
foreign slot, which is the wrong frame data over the wrong bone tree. A family member left
without an anchor falls through to animation 0 and becomes invisible and invulnerable
while its shadow and its damage remain. Two vanilla resets change, both broken before: in
Andy2 no anchor is loaded at all, so the chain gave the skeletons animation 0, which is
Lara's first animation, and in joby3 Mafia 2, which carries 58 animations of its own, got
the Guard's. The stub soldiers resolve to exactly the same number as before, because
`setup.cpp` already aliases their `anim_index` onto that same anchor.

**How.** `game/sas.cpp` (the index from the item's own object entry, the set
`InitialiseObjects` already aliased for that type), `game/control.cpp` (`ResetGuards`; the
forced rest state is left as written, Two Gun keeps its `+6` because its `+0` is a walk,
and the chef, the maze monster and the will-o'-wisp asked for their own set already),
`game/hitman.cpp`, `game/effects.cpp`, `game/setup.cpp` (the alias chain, with the guard
on slot 460 as the family base), `game/romangod.cpp` (`RomangodControl` fetches its
animations via `item->object_number`, which is what lets both Roman gods coexist).

**Commits.** `f4b2461`, `b244df4`, `8618d19`, `b16fcd6`, `d7b9695`, `c7b5f09`, `2f0cb8f`

### Enemies that could not die, and corpses that never left
2026-08-14 - 2026-08-29

**What.** Larson's corpse fades out like every other enemy: when the death animation
reaches its last frame the routine sets `after_death = 1` beside the heavy-trigger probe
it already ran. Pierre's death animation can no longer restart itself - the routine holds
it one frame short of its end and sets `after_death = 1`. Larson's and Pierre's
40-hit-point flee only engages when a matching escape marker actually exists, checked by
the new `PierreCanFlee()`. The chef, the skeletons and the swamp witch can be killed: the
chef borrows the soldier family's gunshot death, the other two shred. The Imp and the Maze
Monster shred as well, through `CreatureDie(item, 1)` into `ExplodingDeath2`.

**Why.** All of these rest on assumptions the randomizer breaks. Larson's death animation
carries no `KillItem` command, because the only place the body is ever removed is Trajan's
Markets, where a cutscene takes over at exactly that frame, and everywhere else Larson
never dies at all, fleeing below 40 hit points; the death animation is a 207-frame set
piece that ends upright, so without the fade the body would stand there dead for good.
Pierre's `+12` death animation jumps back into a living animation when it ends, because
Core never uses Pierre's generic death - in vanilla Pierre dies by cutscene. Core places
the escape marker in every vanilla level that needs it; as pool enemies both can land in a
level without one, and then `FindAITargetObject` never finds a target, they chase Lara
around fleeing forever, and the hit-point clamp makes them immortal. The chef, the
skeletons and the swamp witch have hit points and take damage but their control functions
never read `hit_points`; in vanilla it never shows, because the chef's level takes Lara's
weapons away beforehand, the swamp witch only wakes when the level is as good as over, and
the skeletons' level hands Lara nothing to shoot them with. Trajan's Markets is unaffected
by the Larson fade, because the cutscene hides the body in the same instant.

**How.** `game/pierre.cpp` holds all three Larson/Pierre changes; `PierreCanFlee()` runs
the same type/OCB/zone match as `FindAITargetObject` before the clamp, so with a reachable
marker everything behaves exactly as vanilla and without one they fight to a normal death.
`game/chef.cpp` borrows the soldier family's gunshot death - the chef's skeleton is
bone-identical with theirs and the chef's own death animation is a one-frame stub - and
OCB 1 switches the chef from kitchen work to hunting. `game/skeleton.cpp`,
`game/swampy.cpp`, `game/imp.cpp` and `game/willwisp.cpp` use `CreatureDie(item, 1)` into
`ExplodingDeath2`: the scraps are the enemy's own meshes thrown as `BODY_PART` effects, so
no extra model is needed, and `CreatureDie` also does everything a death animation would -
`KillItem`, dropped loot, AI off, the invisible flag for the savegame. For the Maze
Monster this replaces a stopgap, because Core never finished that death and the lying pose
sinks into the floor. The fade in `game/draw.cpp` is what `after_death` drives.

**Commits.** `e59d89c`, `0d5a78c`, `6204552`, `f4824ba`, `7fab020`, `614805c`, `8b86e3f`,
`ee464f6`, `ca29432`, `df34902`, `c7b5f09`
