### Balance.txt: every weapon, enemy, attack and hazard settable
2026-08-02 - 2026-09-04

**What.** A plain-text settings file, `Balance.txt`, is read once at startup from the
folder the game runs in. It carries an individual value for each of Lara's weapons, the
hit points of each enemy, each separate enemy attack, each of five fixed level hazards,
the audible range of the stationary level ambience (`SceneryRange`, shipped at 65, the
original being 100), and three percentages that scale everything at once: `WeaponDamage`,
`EnemyHealth` and `EnemyDamage`, each 100 by default. If the file is absent the game
writes it out with its defaults and an explanation of every line; a missing or unreadable
line keeps the built-in value; settings a newer version has added are filled in. Every
value is clamped on read, and the weapon percentage is capped at 127 because the engine
holds weapon damage in a `char`. Two hit-point figures are changed in the code itself: the
Maze Monster from 4000 to 120 and Two Gun from 24 to 90. The Roman God's armour stages,
fixed at 225/150/75 out of 300 upstream, are computed as three quarters, one half and one
quarter of the object's own maximum.

**Why.** The randomizer needs one place from which enemy and weapon strength can be
scaled, and a single slider for all of Lara's weapons that does not overwrite per-weapon
values a player set by hand. Upstream built the Maze Monster effectively unkillable,
because in its home level it is a chase set piece and not a combat target, and as a pool
enemy it must die. The Roman God's stages are computed so that they still line up when the
file scales its hit points; with the original hit points the numbers are identical to
vanilla. Falls, fire, poison, drowning and the trap code deliberately bypass all of it and
stay exactly as hard as the original. The five hazards - the autogun, the gunship, the
Iris, the Area 51 laser and the electrical cables in the submarine pen - are settable
individually but are not enemies and are left out of the percentages, because they never
move between levels.

**How.** `game/balance.cpp` and `game/balance.h` are new. One table in `balance.cpp` is
the single source of truth: it holds the shipped default, a second figure that is what
`setup.cpp` writes, the allowed range, the explanatory text and, for hit points, the
object slot; the template file is generated from that same table, so the two cannot drift,
and `BalanceSetEnemies` logs a warning where the code and the table disagree.
`game/setup.cpp` calls `BalanceSetWeapons` at level start, the point where vanilla already
re-set the revolver's damage per level, and `BalanceSetEnemies` once in
`InitialiseObjects` after the three setup routines have written the originals; that
function writes the per-enemy hit points, then applies the percentage to everything
intelligent and damageable, so Lara and the flare keep theirs. `game/lara1gun.cpp` takes
the HK's two values, which vanilla rewrites on every shot, and applies `WeaponDamage()`.
`game/sound.cpp` reads the ambience range that used to be a compile-time constant.
`game/hitman.cpp`, `game/mafia2.cpp`, `game/pierre.cpp`, `game/sniper.cpp` and
`game/sas.cpp` pass their own gunshot damage into `ShotLara` instead of a literal. The
per-attack values are applied through `EnemyDamage()` at the 28 places in 20 enemy files
that subtract from Lara's hit points - `game/dog.cpp`, `game/huskie.cpp`, `game/lion.cpp`,
`game/bat.cpp`, `game/spider.cpp`, `game/people.cpp`, `game/twogun.cpp`,
`game/gladiatr.cpp`, `game/joby.cpp`, `game/hydra.cpp`, `game/minisub.cpp`,
`game/autogun.cpp`, `game/tower.cpp`, `game/chef.cpp`, `game/skeleton.cpp`,
`game/swampy.cpp` and the rest - which is also where the global percentage is applied.
`game/romangod.cpp` computes the armour stages. The wiring sits where the engine really
decides these numbers rather than in one patched-over table, because three of the values
in `weapons[9]` are dead.

**Commits.** `8e0d25c`, `6b459de`, `4a366bc`, `14d7036`, `f192670`, `f073e79`, `ee464f6`,
`162da17`, `c5cded7`

### Lara's meshes follow the outfit, not the level
2026-08-12 - 2026-08-26

**What.** Five places that upstream keys on the level range key on what Lara is actually
wearing. The child-Lara torso swap and the young-Lara left-hand mesh correction
additionally require `GF_YOUNGLARA`. The Russia braid anchoring (torso sphere shifted by
-11/-16/+25, fixed radius 94) and the braid-root welding table engage for the Russia
outfit, marked with `LaraType` 2 (`LARA_BUNHEAD`), or for an unmodified Russia level
(`LARA_NORMAL`). A new draw type `LARA_PONYTAIL`, `LaraType` byte 5, draws exactly like
`LARA_NORMAL` and exists for the standard outfit worn in a Russia level. The catsuit draw
path draws the thigh holsters like the standard one, but only when the holster objects
(slots 13-16) are loaded. A skin joint whose seam pairing found no vertex to sew is left
undrawn.

**Why.** The randomizer moves outfits between levels, and upstream could conflate outfit
and level because in vanilla an outfit never leaves its section. Without these, clearing
`GF_YOUNGLARA` to play the Ireland levels with the adult Lara left her with the child's
chest and a bent hand triangle; the braid pierced the body or collapsed into a spike when
the Russia outfit travelled; and a joint that matched nothing could only put geometry
where it does not belong. No vanilla file carries `LaraType` 2 or 5 and vanilla Russia
levels are `LARA_NORMAL`, so vanilla behaviour is unchanged. The `loaded` guard on the
holsters also prevents drawing a stray mesh through `objects[].mesh_index == 0`.

**How.** `game/laramisc.cpp` (`LaraInitialiseMeshes`, the torso swap),
`specific/drawroom.cpp` (`ProcessMeshData`, triangle 30 of `LARA_SKIN`'s left hand),
`game/hair.cpp` (the anchoring), `game/laraskin.cpp` (`HairSkinVertNums[5]` versus `[0]`,
and `SkinJointUsable`), `global/types.h` and `specific/drawlara.cpp` (`LARA_PONYTAIL`, the
`DrawLara__4` holsters), `game/delstuff.cpp`, `game/delstuff.h` (`SkinJointUsable`, asked
by the three joint loops in `specific/drawlara.cpp`).

**Commits.** `f7f170d`, `e59d89c`, `7b8b33a`

### Cutscene mesh swaps no longer outlive the cutscene
2026-08-15

**What.** `CutseqLaraMeshesBack()` resets all 15 of `lara.mesh_ptrs` from slot 0 at the
single place in `handle_cutseq_triggering` where every cutscene teardown passes, beside
Core's own holster restore. `handle_lara_chatting` skips the speech-head install when the
new `GfForeignSpeechHeads` flag is set.

**Why.** Cutscenes graft vanilla-outfit meshes onto Lara at run time:
`handle_lara_chatting` swaps her head against `LARA_SPEECH_HEAD1-4` during dialog
passages, and the joby5 suit exit swaps hips and legs. The swap-back only happened when
the respective table ran past its terminator, so skipping the cutscene mid-passage, or a
passage reaching the final frame, left the last swap state installed into normal gameplay
until the next weapon draw reset the head. This is an original-game defect that vanilla
masks, because there the grafted meshes match the level outfit. The flag exists because a
donor outfit may have no speech heads of its own - the VCI levels know no dialog cutscenes
- in which case installing them would graft a foreign head.

**How.** `game/deltapak.cpp`, `game/lara.cpp`, `game/lara.h`. Slot 0 is primed with the
current skin by `LaraInitialiseMeshes`, the child torso from `ANIMATING6_MIP` as there.
The flag comes from `data[2]` of the 32-byte block before the main level chunk, read in
`LoadLevel` (`specific/file.cpp`) next to LaraType and WeatherType; all 16 vanilla files
carry 0 there, so unpatched levels behave byte-identically. The randomizer sets it when an
outfit donor has no speech heads and otherwise imports the donor's, so dialog mouths keep
animating. A weapon or torch held in hand across a cutscene is reset to the skin hand too;
the weapon state machine reinstalls it on the next draw.

**Commits.** `60b2502`

### Room for a full inventory reset at every level start
2026-08-22

**What.** `gfPickups` and `gfTakeaways` hold 128 script entries each instead of 16, and a
`GIVEOBJ` that stands in the block behind a `TAKEOBJ` is applied after the takeaways in a
third phase rather than being swallowed by them. Both arrays are bounds-checked on fill;
previously `gfPickups` was written unchecked into sixteen entries.

**Why.** A randomized campaign clears the whole key, puzzle and pickup family at every
level start - about 74 `TAKEOBJ` lines per level - so that no key or puzzle item can
travel into a level that holds a different object in the same generic slot. Sixteen
entries could not hold that. The counters are `uchar`, so 128 costs nothing. The third
phase is needed because the takeaways deliberately run last in `setup.cpp`, where they
also remove the pistols that every level with a loaded pistol model presses back into
Lara's hands; without it a deliberate gift after a clear-out would be taken away again.
Vanilla puts all gifts before all takeaways, so nothing changes there.

**How.** `game/gameflow.cpp`, `game/gameflow.h` (`gfPickups[128]`, `gfTakeaways[128]`,
`gfLateGives`), applied in `game/setup.cpp`.

**Commits.** `66aa619`

### Keys are counted, not flagged
2026-09-04

**What.** `LARA_INFO::keyitems` is an eight-byte counter array, read and written exactly
like `puzzleitems`: a lock consumes one copy, a script `TAKEOBJ` clears the slot, and the
inventory ring shows the number from two copies upwards. Savegames written before this are
refused.

**Why.** The field was a 16-bit bitfield with one bit per `KEY_ITEM1..8`, while puzzle
items had always been counters. Picking up a key ORed the bit in and the pickup was
removed either way, so a second key of the same type was silently destroyed - vanilla
joby2 hands out two Key 7 for two separate locks, and a randomized layout can put both of
them in front of the first door. The change alters `sizeof(SAVEGAME_INFO)`, which is
serialized raw, so old saves are refused by the existing size and checksum check in
`sgRestoreGame()` rather than decoded from a shifted layout. `keyitemscombo`, the halves
of a combinable key, is genuinely unique and stays a flag field.

**How.** `global/types.h` (the field), `game/newinv2.cpp` (pickup, display, consumption),
`game/setup.cpp`.

**Commits.** `5f9ffd0`

### Relocated pickups: a dropped wall pickup and the pushable block
2026-08-20

**What.** When an enemy carrying a wall pickup dies, the low OCB bits (2 and 9) are
cleared on the drop, so it lands as an ordinary floor pickup; the pickup trigger's own
bits are untouched. A pushable block rolls over pickups again: the collision test asks
what is in the way, and pickups let the block through and are there again once it moves
on, while enemies, statues and a second block still stop it. The next entry keeps a wall
pickup out of every carried chain in the first place; the clearing stays for a chain a
savegame restores.

**Why.** OCB 2 and 9 mark the pickups Lara pulls off a wall, and that manner demands a
wall behind the item and her angle onto it; `DropBaddyPickups` puts the item on open
floor, where the condition can never be met again and the item is lost for good. TR5
refuses a push as soon as `GetCollidedObjects` reports anything at all on the target tile,
a medipack included - TR1 to TR4 had no such general test - so with items relocated a
stray medipack could block the only push path to a puzzle.

**How.** `game/box.cpp` (`DropBaddyPickups`), `game/moveblok.cpp`.

**Commits.** `d45962f`

### An enemy never carries a wall grab
2026-09-26

**What.** `GetCarriedItems` hands every enemy and every searchable object the pickups
within half a sector of it at level start and takes them out of their room; a wall grab, a
pickup whose OCB (`trigger_flags & 0x3F`) is 2 or 9, is not among them any more. It stays
on its wall as the level placed it. Every other pickup in reach is carried as before. With
`-log` the level start writes one `CARRYLOG` line for every pickup in a carrier's reach.

**Why.** A wall grab an enemy takes off its wall is lost either way. The drop of the entry
above makes it a floor pickup in the engine's bookkeeping only: the item keeps the model
made for the wall and lies where its carrier fell, and in the game it was then either gone
or on the floor at a wrong place, and could not be picked up. A searchable object hands
its chain to Lara herself when she searches it (`game/pickup.cpp:1128-1143`), so a wall
grab it carried was not lost; it, too, now leaves the grab on its wall. Both manners
measure Lara against the item's origin on the wall (`game/pickup.cpp:52-53`, `:65-66`):
OCB 2 is pried off with the crowbar (X -256..256, Y -100..100, Z 200..512, 30 degrees
either way, Lara put at 0,0,215), OCB 9 is pulled out by hand (X -512..0, Z 0..512, Lara
put at -224,0,240). The item on the wall is no stand-in for another pickup: it is the slot
the inventory receives, and in the original levels it is the only item of its slot in its
level, so no floor pickup of the same type exists there (`ItemCheck` over slots 172, 174
and 220). The six wall grabs of the original levels are Andrea2 item 121, `PUZZLE_ITEM3`
(slot 174), the golden coin; Andrea2 item 128, `PUZZLE_ITEM1` (slot 172), the valve wheel;
Andrea3 item 68, `PICKUP_ITEM1` (slot 220), the philosopher's stone; andy3 item 26,
`PUZZLE_ITEM1`, the chalk - these four with OCB 2 - and andy3 item 6, `PUZZLE_ITEM3`, and
joby3 item 41, `PUZZLE_ITEM1`, both with OCB 9, the two crowbars: `AddDisplayPickup` turns
those two slots into `CROWBAR_ITEM` in Old Mill and Submarine (`game/health.cpp:270`). The
names come from the object commands of the original `SCRIPT.DAT` (`ScriptCheck`) and the
text list in `game/gameflow.h`. Picked up, a puzzle item adds one to `lara.puzzleitems`,
`PICKUP_ITEM1` sets bit 0 of `lara.pickupitems`, and a crowbar sets `lara.crowbar`
(`game/newinv2.cpp:3136`, `:3167`, `:3175`). Items 121 and 68 carry bit 0x40 (raw OCB 66):
the pickup leaves them in place, invisible and triggered, for the pickup trigger
(`game/pickup.cpp:1035`); the other four are removed. In the sixteen original level files
no carrier stands in the room of any of the six, so no original level start changes.

**How.** `game/setup.cpp:2300-2317`, in `GetCarriedItems`, at the place a pickup in reach
is chosen: the OCB is read (`:2300`) and a pickup with OCB 2 or 9 is not linked into the
carrier's chain (`:2311`); its room link, its position and every other field stay as the
level loaded them. The reach is the one `game/setup.cpp:2279-2289` states: a carrier is a
slot with `intelligent` set or `SEARCH_OBJECT1..3`, never `CYBORG`; it looks only at the
items linked into its own room; an item is in reach at |dx| < 512, |dy| < 256 and |dz| <
512 against the carrier when its collision is `PickUpCollision`. The seam (`:2305`) goes
through `Log`, which writes nothing without `-log`, and runs once per level start:

    CARRYLOG baddy=<item>/<slot> item=<item>/<slot> ocb=<ocb> d=<dx>,<dz> <verdict>

`<verdict>` is `carried` or `skipped wall grab`, and `d` is the item's position less the
carrier's. The slot names come from `HDSlotName` (`specific/hd/hd_bind.cpp`, a plain table
that is linked into every build and needs no HD state; `game/setup.cpp:84` includes its
header). A wall grab in reach of two carriers writes a line for each. The comment of
`DropBaddyPickups` (`game/box.cpp:857-865`) names the case its OCB clearing now serves:
`carried_item` is written and read for every carrier (`game/savegame.cpp:447-448`,
`:872-873`), and a load runs `SetupGame`, and with it `GetCarriedItems`, before
`sgRestoreGame` (`game/gameflow.cpp:1015`, `:1028`), so a save written while a wall grab
was carried restores the chain, and the drop's OCB clearing is what the carrier's death
meets.

**Decisions.** Items that are broken out of a wall are never taken along by enemies in the
first place, rather than repaired after the drop; the drop's position and room stay as
they are. The drop keeps its OCB clearing, for a restored chain and for any path that
still fills one. The randomizer's bar on wall grabs within a carrier's reach stays: a spot
under an enemy's feet is a poor place for an item, and the engine's rule is the net under
a placement, not its reason.

**Commits.** `608b699`, `befad7f`, `ca369f4`

### A secret bonus, and the reward read from a file
2026-08-03 - 2026-08-30

**What.** Finding every secret in a level awards items, in the manner of Tomb Raider II.
What it awards is read from `SecretRewards.txt` beside the executable, keyed by the
level's position in the campaign (`gfCurrentLevel`) rather than by its file name, with one
line for each of the fourteen levels that are really played. Only weapons, ammunition and
medipacks are accepted as rewards. If the file is absent it is written out with the
defaults on first start, and a line naming something else is skipped with a message.

**Why.** The level order is itself rolled, so a key by file name would attach the reward
to the wrong level. A key or a puzzle item as a reward would open a door out of order. The
title screen and the three development levels have no secrets and get no line.

**How.** `game/secretreward.cpp`, `game/secretreward.h` read, validate and complete the
file (`SECRET_REWARD_FILE`); `game/newinv2.cpp` hands the reward out in `GrantSecretBonus`
at the point where the secret count becomes complete, `game/savegame.cpp` carries the
per-level state. The randomizer can write the file; a player can edit it.

**Commits.** `81e4630`, `c7b5f09`, `c5cded7`

### The stationary level ambience: a stacking guard and a range brake
2026-08-18 - 2026-08-22

**What.** Ambient scenery sound sources are marked as such while they are created, and the
stacking guard and the range brake in the sound code hang on that mark. The audible range
is the `SceneryRange` value in `Balance.txt` rather than a compile-time constant; enemies
and Lara always keep their full range.

**Why.** Without the mark the engine could not tell a scenery loop from any other sound,
and identical loops stacked on top of one another. The original let machines, fire and
dripping water carry through half the level.

**How.** `game/effects.cpp` sets the mark at creation; `game/sound.cpp`, `game/sound.h`
carry the guard and the range, `game/balance.cpp` supplies the value.

**Commits.** `948c9ce`, `4a366bc`

### Two level-start freezes in dense levels
2026-08-15

**What.** `aInit()` (room vertex buffers) and `aMakeCutsceneResident()` (cutscene
textures) run on the main thread after the loader joins, instead of on the loading thread.
`S_FinishLoadBar()` forces the loading bar complete once the loader has joined, and the
bar's catch-up loop is bounded.

**Why.** Two threads used the one device while the main thread presented the loading bar.
Separately, the bar's completion test (`loadbar_maxpos <= loadbar_steps`, with steps
growing by `100/maxpos` per step and `maxpos` = texture pages + 20) becomes mathematically
unreachable at roughly 75 texture pages and up, leaving the catch-up loop spinning forever
with a full bar. Vanilla levels carry 9 to 17 pages and never reach it; randomized levels
with 79 and 82 pages hit it at once.

**How.** `specific/file.cpp` moves the two calls behind the loader join;
`specific/drawbars.cpp`, `specific/drawbars.h` hold `S_FinishLoadBar()` and the bounded
loop; `game/gameflow.cpp` and `game/control.cpp` carry the level-start milestones. Cheap
seam logs remain around the load hand-off and those milestones.

**Commits.** `084de18`, `cb45288`, `f0c846e`

### A door wrote through the previous level's AI slots
2026-08-25

**What.** `FreeLevel` clears `baddie_slots` where the pool dies, and `ShutThatDoor` runs
its slot loop only while the array belongs to the current level. `LoadItems` validates the
slot and the room number of every item as it reads them and stops with a message box
instead of a wild access, in the same manner as the existing `MAX_ITEMS` check.

**Why.** `FreeLevel` sets the `game_malloc` pool back to its start, which is the moment
every global pointer into it goes stale: the address from the level before now points into
the middle of the level about to be loaded. `baddie_slots` was read again before it was
reallocated, because `InitialiseLOTarray` runs after `S_LoadLevelFile` while
`ShutThatDoor`, called by `InitialiseDoor` during loading, walks all `MAX_LOT` slots and
writes to each. Skipping that loop during loading loses nothing, since it drops the path
target of creatures that are already thinking, and at load time none are. This is an
upstream defect that only became fatal with levels dense enough for the stray writes to
hit live data.

**How.** `specific/file.cpp` (`FreeLevel`, `LoadItems`), `game/door.cpp` (`ShutThatDoor`).
Behind `-log`, `LoadItems` also writes `ITEMLOG`, one line per item before its
`initialise`, so a crash during loading names the item, and `ITEMWATCH`, a scan after each
`initialise` that reports both an item whose room number became impossible and the item
being initialised when it happened; the scan is quadratic, is therefore gated at the call
site, and switches itself off after the first find.

**Commits.** `195bebf`

### Lara blanked out in the half turn on a rope: the ROPELOG seam
2026-09-24

**What.** When Lara turns half round on a rope she disappears for a moment. The defect
belongs to the base engine: it appears with the HD art off, at *Frame rate 30* and under
both control schemes. No fix exists, because the rope arithmetic does not produce it;
behind `-log` two lines record what decides it instead. (The squeezed body on the
tightrope turn is a different defect, the next entry.) `ROPELOG` is written once per logic
step while Lara hangs on a rope and gives her state, animation and frame, her heading
round the rope (`RopeY=`, 256 units per step of a turn, 128 steps for a half turn), the
segment, the offset and the frame's root `y`; the three lengths `Normalise` divides by
(`len=`); and the angles and position `AlignLaraToRope` gives her. `ROPELOG draw` is
written on every drawn frame while she hangs on a rope and on the frame after she lets go.
It says whether the Lara block of `DrawRooms` draws her (`drawn=`) and lists the terms
that decide it: `mesh_bits`, `SCNoDrawLara`, `ModernLaraHidden` and `IFL_INVISIBLE`. It
also gives the camera type, the camera position and the look-at point with their rooms,
the camera's distance to the look-at point (`eyed=`) and to her (`larad=`), and the
candidate `ChaseCamera` took (`cand=`, `clip=`).

**Why.** An offline probe compiles `AlignLaraToRope` and every function it calls verbatim.
On a still rope, all 65536 values of `RopeY` give continuous results: `x_rot` and `z_rot`
stay 0, `y_rot` moves at most 22 units per 1-unit step of the heading, and the position
moves by at most 2 units between neighbouring headings. No input to `Normalise` comes near
zero, for all 21 segments with four root offsets, and the half-turn step itself is clean.
The placement can only break down when the rope at her grip lies along the world X axis,
which takes a tilt past 90 degrees; a turn starts only from the plain hang, which a swing
returns to only below 6750 (about 37 degrees). The one integer defect the probe finds is a
different symptom: `Normalise` takes its reciprocal as `0x10000 / length` in integers, and
the cross product can leave it 16385 to 16455 long, where the reciprocal comes out at 3
instead of 4, so on a swinging rope `z_rot` comes out up to a quarter too large, up to
1539 units (8.5 degrees), a roll flicker that leaves the position alone. The classic Lara
draw clips nothing against her body as a whole, so a wrong angle would tilt her rather
than hide her; what hides her is therefore outside the rope code and depends on the level
geometry round the rope. A blank-out frame shows one of three things in the log: `drawn=0`
in the draw line; `eyed=` or `larad=` near zero, which points at the camera; or a jump in
`xyz=` or `pos=` in the rope line, which points at the rope.

**How.** `game/rope.cpp`: `RopeLog` and `RopeLogLength`. The lengths are taken where
`AlignLaraToRope` shifts each vector for `Normalise`, and only when `gLogEnabled` is set;
the line is written at the end of the function. `game/draw.cpp`: `RopeDrawLog`, called
from `DrawRooms` just before the Lara block. `game/camera.cpp` / `.h`: `chase_log` is set
to -1 at the top of every `CalculateCamera` pass and written by `ChaseCamera`, and
`ChaseCameraLogPick` reads it. Without `-log` nothing is computed or written, and the
arithmetic of `AlignLaraToRope` is as it was.

**Commits.** `0034725`

### Lara facing the wrong way for one tick in the jump twists: the early half turn
2026-09-24 - 2026-09-25

**What.** In the twist of the back jump (animation 212 into 213), in the two twists of the
forward jump (210 into 211, out of the standing jump's flight 77; 207 into 209, out of the
running jump's start 17 and 19) and at the end of the roll 47 (state `AS_ROLL`, 48 into
the stand 11), Lara's whole body faced the other way for one logic step and then turned
back. The defect belongs to the base engine and is drawn at every frame rate: the four
animations fire FlipEffect 0 (`turn180_effect`, `y_rot -= 0x8000`, `x_rot` negated) on
their last frame, and the effect turns the item on the step whose `frame_number` reaches
that frame (`AnimateLara`, `game/laramisc.cpp`), so that step draws the frame under the
turned yaw; but the frame, a blend of two key frames made for the yaw before the effect,
belongs to the old yaw. That frame, and the tween frames into it, are now drawn from
copies of the two key frames turned by half a turn, which land exactly where the frames
land under the old yaw; the braid hangs off the same frames. The tween frames from the
flip step to the first step of the next animation are bridged: they are drawn from a key
frame built at the frame's weight between the pose the flip step drew and the pose of the
current step. At *Frame rate 60* that is one frame per change (the halfway pose), at 165
Hz five or six, at 30 none. Behind `-log` a `TURNLOG` line names every step that takes the
turned path and a `BRIDGELOG` line every bridged step.

**Why.** Lara's playable animations carry 77 `turn180_effect` commands over the thirteen
campaign levels: 13 fire on the first frame of the roll 147, whose change turns the root
(see *The animation's root offset on a refused frame*); 12 fire on a key frame made for
the new yaw inside a key pair whose hips turn more than 90 degrees (the underwater roll
205 in eight levels, the tightrope turn 451 in four), the inside kind of the next entry;
and 52 fire on the last frame of 48, 207, 210 and 212 in every level, a frame whose key
pair turns the hips by less than 90 degrees - the early kind this entry draws. In ANDREA1
the hips turn from the step before to the flip frame by 171.9 to 179.3 degrees as drawn
and by 0.9 to 11.0 under the old yaw. Seen in play, a whole body seen from the front stood
between frames seen from behind in the back twists, for about one step, and in the forward
twist for two. The step after the flip step stands on another animation (11, 209, 211 or
213, key 0 in all 52 cases), and the pose rule refuses every tween across an animation
change, so the frames between the two steps wore the new step's pose from the first of
them on; after 210 that pose is 211's first key, which lies half a turn about her lateral
axis from 210's last frame (179.2 degrees under either yaw), a seam in the level's data,
and the first step of 211 then stood still. TROne (GPLv3) by Todesengel1931 -
https://github.com/todesengel1931 - was read for comparison before this was built: its
guard of a root turn of more than 150 degrees between two key frames, then the first key
unblended, holds 209 on its first key and leaves 213 to vanilla's blend, and nothing in it
touches the frame the effect fires on. Nothing of its code is used.

**How.** `game/interpolate_math.h` (`InterpTurnKind`): for the flip frame `f` the key pair
`k = (f - 1 - frame_base) / rate` and `k + 1` gives `INTERP_TURN_INSIDE` where the hips
turn more than 90 degrees inside it (`InterpKeyFar`), `INTERP_TURN_EARLY` where they do
not, `INTERP_TURN_NONE` on the animation's first frame. `game/interpolate.cpp`
(`InterpTurnOf`) walks an animation's commands as `AnimateLara` does, once per animation,
into a 512-slot table indexed by the animation number and checked against it;
`InterpInvalidate` empties it, and `FreeLevel` invalidates. `InterpKeyFrameTurn`
(`game/interpolate_math.h`): the offset turned as `InterpRootFlip` turns it, node 0's y
angle half a turn on (y is the outer angle of `phd_RotYXZ`'s order, so the half turn adds
exactly; a one-axis x or z hips node becomes three-axis, rounded to a step of 64), the
box's x and z extents turned, every other node copied; exact where the item's `z_rot` is
zero, whatever its `x_rot`. `LaraPoseFrames` (`game/draw.cpp`, called from
`CalcLaraMatrices` in `game/delstuff.cpp` for every set, and from `HairControl` in
`game/hair.cpp`): on the flip frame of an early animation (`LaraTurnFrame`) both frames of
the pair are replaced by turned copies; the tween frames between the step before and the
flip step stand on the same frame number and take the same path. The root blend of the
change that follows turns the previous step's offset: `GetRootAt` reports `turned`,
`InterpRootRefused` keeps it in `g_rootTurned` and `InterpRootNow` turns by `g_rootFlip ^
g_rootTurned`. The bridge: in `GetFramesNow` (`game/draw.cpp`), after `GetFramesAt`
refused, Lara's frame asks `LaraBridgeFrames`; a bridged frame is counted as a pose
(`InterpNotePose`) and not as a skip, returns 2 like a blend in time, and raises the root
latch as every refusal does. It fires where `InterpBridgeFires`
(`game/interpolate_math.h`) holds - `0 < t < 1`, `InterpTurnOf` of the previous step's
animation `INTERP_TURN_EARLY`, the previous frame its flip frame, the animation changed -
and not where the current step fires a `turn180_effect` itself. The first pose is the
previous step's pair from `GetKeyAt` (whose key arithmetic `GetRootAt` now calls), both
keys turned by `InterpKeyFrameTurn` and, where the remainder is not zero, built at the
step's factor by `InterpKeyFrameLerp`; the second is the current step's pair, built the
same way. The frame is `InterpKeyFrameBridge`: the second pose's box and root offset,
every node by `InterpKeyNodeLerp` (the node step `InterpKeyFrameLerp` now calls), in a
static buffer put into both slots. The hips take the longer way round (`InterpSlerpRot`
with `longArc`) where `InterpBridgeLong` finds the two poses more than 90 degrees apart
and the shorter way turning against the hips' own turn (`InterpHipsTurn`, the quaternion
of the turn the stack sees) both over the turned key pair the flip frame lies on and over
the pair the current step stands on. The body takes the frame through `CalcLaraMatrices`
into `Rich_CalcLaraMatrices_Interpolated`, whose `InterpRootNow` reads the bridge's offset
- the current step's own - so the root comes out as before; the classic body copies
`lara_matrices` (`specific/drawlara.cpp`) and the HD body reads them
(`specific/hd/hd_laradraw.cpp`); neither the HD switch nor the control scheme is read on
the way. The braid does not take bridged frames: `HairControl` runs on the step and its
links are blended as positions between the steps, as before; only its joint at the head
(`GetCorrectStashPoints`) follows the bridged head. Bounds (`GetBoundsAccurate`), the
shadow and the collision read the item's own frame. At `fps_mode 0` the four flip frames
change and nothing else; the bridge is not reached (`InterpAlphaNow` answers 1,
`InterpBeginFrame` returns with `g_applied` false, `InterpPoseTime` answers 0, and
`GetFramesNow`'s `if (t > 0.0F)` is not entered). What it costs: a table lookup per call
of `LaraPoseFrames`, two turned copies on the 52 frames. The log lines, behind `-log`:
`TURNLOG f= anim= frame= flip= keys= drawn=turned`, view set only, once per step;
`INTERPLOG` ends in `bridge=N`, the bridged frames of the second; `BRIDGELOG f= anim=A->B
frame=F->G hips= arc=short|long` once per bridged step.
`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/InterpTest.cpp` tests both parts: `key_build` blocks 6 and 7
(the turned offset and box, node 0's matrix with its x and z columns negated, a frame
turned twice is itself, the one-axis cases, the three kinds with their pairs) and
`key_bridge` (26 checks: the ends of the bridge against both poses, the arc of 210 into
211 with the level's own numbers, 212 and 207 kept short, the box and offset, and when it
fires).

**Decisions.** The bridge is a fast turn over the in-between frames, a motion the
animation does not carry and the draw invents. For 210 into 211 the two poses stand 179.15
degrees apart about the item's x axis and the shorter way turns against the hips on both
sides (over 210's keys 7 to 8 and 211's keys 0 to 1), so that change takes the longer way,
180.8 degrees about +x; 212 into 213 (19.5 degrees), 207 into 209 (13.5) and 48 into 11
(5.9) take the shorter way, which turns with the hips.

**Commits.** `e6aaec1`, `b5efdbf`, `b40712d`

### Lara squeezed to a sliver in the tightrope turn: the far key-frame pair
2026-09-24 - 2026-09-25

**What.** A key pair of Lara's is *far* when the drawn rotation of any of her fifteen
nodes - its own rotation multiplied onto its parents' - turns more than 90 degrees between
the pair's two keys, and a far pair is no longer drawn with vanilla's key-frame blend.
Where `turn180_effect` fires on the pair's second key - the four tightrope-turn pairs -
the first key frame is drawn in place of the blend, and the tween across it falls back to
the pose of the current logic step (the first key inside the pair, the second key on the
step that reaches it). Every other far pair is drawn from a key frame built at the weight
in hand, each node on the shortest turn between its two keys, so that every in-between
frame is a whole body turned part of the way; a node whose own turn lies within a degree
of half a turn takes instead the way whose drawn rotation lies nearer the middle of the
drawn turn, decided once for the pair. One kind of far pair is left to vanilla's blend, a
seam in the data: a pair whose hips turn less than 90 degrees and where a node from 1 on
turns more than 170 degrees both on its own and in the drawn frame. The rule holds at
every frame rate, with the HD art on or off and under both control schemes; every other
pair is drawn as before. Behind `-log` a `KEYFARLOG` line names every step that takes a
far pair, with `mode=hold` or `mode=lerp`, and a `KEYSEAMLOG` line every step on a seam.

**Why.** Vanilla's blend averages two fully multiplied-out matrix stacks element by
element (`Rich_CalcLaraMatrices_Interpolated`, `InitInterpolateAlpha` /
`InterpolateMatrix`), and an element-wise average of two rotations D apart shrinks the
frame by `cos(D/2)` and is singular at half a turn. In the tightrope turn (animation 451,
`ANIM_TROPETURN`; in ANDREA1 frames 8864 to 8916 at rate 2, 27 key frames) the hips swing
back by 176.9 degrees between key 25 and key 26 while the animation's own FlipEffect 0 on
frame 8916 turns the item by half a turn, so the key frames join up; the one frame in
between came out almost singular and Lara was flattened onto her vertical axis for one
step - a defect of the base engine, with the HD art off, at *Frame rate 30* and under both
control schemes. The same arithmetic squeezed her elsewhere wherever a node's drawn
rotation turns far: the ends of the forward twist 209 and the back twist 213, rich3's
crouch roll 219, and at the take-off of the jumps both arms stretched flat with paper-thin
hands (in the standing jump forward 76 the forearm turns 170.1 degrees in the drawn frame
and vanilla's middle frame keeps 0.086 of its breadth). The first key and not the nearer
one is held because in all four levels with a playable 451 the half turn fires on the
second key's frame, so every frame in between carries the yaw that belongs to the first
key; the second key at that yaw would face 177 degrees wrong. On pairs where no effect
fires inside the pair (209, 213, 219, the take-offs) a held key stood still for three
steps and then snapped, so those are built. The handstand from a ledge (159, `AS_GYMNAST`,
key 1 to 2) is the seam: both keys hold her wrists on the ledge while her shoulders rise
189 units past them and both upper arms flip from in front of the shoulders to behind them
(the right one 173.8 degrees on its own, 177.9 drawn); no way through that turn keeps a
hand on the ledge, while vanilla's blend walks each joint on the straight line between its
key places and keeps the wrists on the ledge, the arms shortening across the turn. TROne
(GPLv3) by Todesengel1931 - https://github.com/todesengel1931 - guards the tightrope pair:
it tests only the root node's turn between the two key frames and draws the first key
frame unblended where that turn passes 150 degrees. Reading it shaped the choice of the
first key frame and of the hips test for the hold; the limit here is 90 degrees, because
at 150 animation 213 (98.8 degrees) and 219 (94.9) would stay squeezed. Nothing of its
code is used.

**How.** The test: `game/interpolate_math.h`, `InterpDrawnRots` (every node's drawn
rotation in `InterpPoseRot`'s layout, the parent found by the bone table's pop and push
bits as the draw finds it; node 0's is its own, bit for bit), `InterpDrawnTurnCos` (the
largest turn and its node), `InterpKeyFarDrawn` against `INTERP_KEY_DRAWN_COS` (`0.0F`,
the cosine of 90 degrees), `InterpKeySeamAt` and `InterpKeySeam` against
`INTERP_KEY_SEAM_COS` (-0.98481, the cosine of 170 degrees; -1 where the hips turn far),
and `InterpKeyFarFill`, which marks one animation's pairs as one bit each, a far pair only
where it is no seam, each key frame walked once; `InterpKeyFarBit` is false outside the
table, whose width is `INTERP_KEY_FAR_WORDS` 32-bit words, 256 pairs (the longest playable
animation of Lara's has 199). The hips alone (`InterpKeyFar`, `InterpPoseFar` over node 0
with `INTERP_POSE_TURN_COS`) still decide the inside turn and with it the hold:
`InterpKeyHold` holds a far pair where `InterpTurnKind` finds the half turn inside it and
the flip frame is the pair's second key. The table: `InterpKeyFarOf`
(`game/interpolate.cpp`, declared in `game/interpolate.h`), 512 slots like
`InterpTurnOf`'s, filled for an animation on its first call and emptied by
`InterpInvalidate`. The built frame: `InterpKeyFrameLerp` - the box of the nearer key, the
offset blended in eighths exactly as `InterpRootKey` blends it, a node equal in both keys
copied word for word, a node both keys store about the same single axis blended by
`InterpLerpAngle` in that form, every other node by `InterpSlerpRot` (through
`InterpRotToQuat` and `InterpRotToAngles`, the two exact inverses of a quaternion and
`InterpPoseRot`'s matrix) and packed three-axis by `InterpPackRot`; and
`InterpKeyFrameFar`, which is `InterpKeyFrameLerp` unless a node turns past
`INTERP_KEY_HALF_COS` (one degree short of half a turn) on its own, then the ways decided
at the middle through `InterpSlerpMat` and handed to `InterpKeyNodeLerp` as `longArc`. The
draw: `game/draw.cpp`, `LaraKeyFar` (asks the table with Lara's mesh count and bone
table), `LaraKeyOf` (names the pair `frm` holds, or none for the bridge's frame),
`LaraKeyHold`, `GetFramesAt` (at rates above 1 only the tween across a held pair is
refused, so `GetFramesNow` falls back to `GetFrames` of the current step there; the
refusal counts in `pose_skips`), `GetKeyAt` (the previous step's root offset on a held
pair is the first key's, on a built pair `InterpRootKey`'s, the number the built frame
carries) and `LaraPoseFrames` (called from `CalcLaraMatrices`, `game/delstuff.cpp`, before
the still-body hold, and from `HairControl`, `game/hair.cpp`): on a blended frame whose
pair is far the held pair gets `frm[1] = frm[0]`, every other pair a built frame at the
frame's own factor in both slots, in a static buffer of `INTERP_KEYFRAME_MAX` shorts, and
a far pair under an early flip is built from its turned copies; a seam reads as a pair
that is not far, so the tween across it is accepted and both slots stay on the stored
keys. The braid follows the same frames, the HD body reads `lara_matrices`; the collision
spheres (`game/sphere.cpp`), the bounds of `GetBoundsAccurate` and `GetBestFrame`, and
`DrawAnimatingItem` are left alone. The log lines: `KEYFARLOG f= anim= frame= keys= rate=
hips= drawn= mode= node= turn=` (`InterpNoteKeyFar`), once per step, `drawn=-1` with
`mode=lerp`, `node=` and `turn=` the node that turns furthest in the drawn frame and its
turn in degrees; `KEYSEAMLOG f= anim= frame= keys= rate= node= own= turn=`
(`InterpNoteKeySeam`, which returns at once without `-log`). Over the thirteen campaign
levels' playable Lara animations the engine blends 35364 key pairs; 1204 are far, 14 of
them seams (159 key 1 to 2 in every level and rich3's 152 key 4 to 5), so 1190 are marked:
4 held (451 key 25 to 26 in ANDREA1 and rich2, key 12 to 13 in ANDREA2 and ANDREA3) and
1186 built. Animations whose frame data do not match their header's frame size are read as
the engine always read them. What it costs: 18 KB of table; filling it about 1.6
microseconds a pair, a level's 3.8 to 7.6 milliseconds spread over each animation's first
draw; per frame a lookup. At `fps_mode 0` the in-between frames of the built pairs change
and the held pairs draw as before. `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/InterpTest.cpp` tests the
rule: `pose_wrap` block 5, `key_build` blocks 1 to 5 (packing, the blend across the wrap,
a one-axis node against a three-axis one, 213's and 209's hips copied from ANDREA1),
`key_far_all` (30 checks: the walk over a hand-built tree, ANDREA1's 76, 10, 53, 1, 451
and 91 key pairs, the table's bound) and `key_seam` (15 checks: a hand-built chain at 169,
171 and 175 degrees, 159 keys 1 to 3 copied from ANDREA1, 76 and 209 far and no seam). The
subject of `5ad3689` says a far key-frame pair is drawn from its nearer frame; the code
draws the pair's first key frame.

**Decisions.** The drawn turn and not each node's own turn decides, because the drawn
rotation is what the blend averages: the own turn would miss 719 pairs whose drawn turn
passes 90 degrees (the run's 10 key 0 to 1) and take 132 whose drawn turn stays under it
(53 key 0 to 1). The limit is the rate 1 rule's 90 degrees as a constant of its own,
`INTERP_KEY_DRAWN_COS`, so it can move without moving the rate 1 rule; the nearest drawn
turns on either side are 89.925 and 90.043 degrees, and a limit of 75 would take in 1219
more pairs, the running jump's first frames among them. Nodes are blended on the shortest
turn of their quaternions and not angle by angle, because a node's two keys may be stored
on the two sides of x = 90 degrees as (x, y, z) and its twin (180 - x, y + 180, z + 180),
and angle by angle a node of 209 strays 191 degrees off the way between its keys. Near
half a turn the shorter way of a node's own turn is decided by the data's last bits and
can put an arm 180 degrees off the middle of its drawn turn (the standing jump up, 91 key
0 to 1), hence the way decided at the middle; two other rules were tried and dropped -
slerping every node's drawn rotation swings a joint through half a turn where a drawn turn
itself lies near 180 degrees (the elbow in 159 key 1 to 2 runs 274.8 degrees further than
the shortest way), and choosing the way for every node past 150 degrees lengthens 159 key
1 to 2's drawn path from 4.2 to 342.8 degrees. The seam is left to vanilla's blend because
two keys that pin the hands while the arm flips carry no turn to interpolate, and holding
key 1 would freeze her body for a pair in which it rises 189 units; the limit of 170
degrees sits where a limb's two ways round differ by 20 degrees, and any limit between
143.7 and 173.8 gives the same list.

### Level Select, a keyhole that survives a save, and the underwater pickup animation
2026-07-31 - 2026-09-14

**What.** The main menu carries a Level Select entry that opens the level-select screen
the game already had behind `PlayAnyLevel`; it sits behind an option that is off by
default, so an ordinary playthrough sees the menu as it was, and the original
`available_levels` restriction is in force, so the three dev/test levels are not offered.
Inserting a key assigns `IFL_TRIGGERED` to the keyhole's flags instead of running
`item->flags &= IFL_TRIGGERED`. `ANIM_PICKUP_UW` (130) joins the list of Lara animations
every randomized level is given, and the card-pull animation is transplanted into a level
that only has the stub rather than the interaction falling back to a plain `USEKEY`.

**Why.** A randomized campaign and any diagnosis of it need to start a chosen level
directly instead of playing up to it. The `&=` clears every flag bit unless that one was
already set, and a keyhole starts at flags 0 in the level file; the savegame writer stores
an item only when `CODEBITS`, `INVISIBLE` or `TRIGGERED` is set, so the keyhole dropped
out of the save entirely and came back as unused while the key itself was already gone,
and the door could never open, because `KeyTrigger` requires `ITEM_ACTIVE`. That is an
original-game defect, reproducible in unmodified Chronicles; it is the only `&=` of its
kind in the engine, the other 26 sites use `|=`, which is why the puzzle hole survives
save and load correctly, and the assignment keeps the original intent of clearing the
other bits while guaranteeing the one. `ANIM_PICKUP_UW` is a stub in seven of the campaign
levels - Andrea1, joby3, joby5, rich1, rich2, rich3 and richcut2 - while a randomized run
places pickups under water everywhere, so without it Lara cannot take them there.

**How.** `game/gameflow.cpp` reuses the existing level-select screen rather than building
a new one; the option is held in `tomb5/tomb5.cpp` and is the *Level Select* row of the
*tomb5 options* tab in `game/menu_frame.cpp`. `game/pickup.cpp` holds the keyhole flag and
the card-pull path. The always-list is in `TR5Randomizer/src/core/ApplyPatch.cpp`; the
animation transplant itself (`Tr5Level::copyLaraAnimFrom`) is in
`TR5Randomizer/src/core/Tr5Transfer.cpp` and uses the model transfer's splice machinery:
the animation slot exists in every level, only its frame data are Core stubs, so the
frames, rate, frame size, states and speeds of the donor set are spliced in and the
animation commands appended with their sound and flip-effect frame numbers recomputed for
the target's counting, while frame base and end, `next_anim`, `next_frame` and state
changes stay the level's own.

## 2.3 Tomb Raider III enemies

Four enemies from Tomb Raider III can appear in randomized levels. Their control code is
not this project's own: it comes from tomb3, Troye's decompilation of Tomb Raider III,
<https://github.com/Trxyebeep/tomb3>, under the GNU GPL v3 - the same licence as TOMB5
and as this project, which is what makes combining them possible at all. It was taken
over directly rather than rewritten, so that its origin stays visible, and every file
names that origin, its licence and every deviation from the tomb3 original with a
reason. No game data from Tomb Raider III ships with this project: the models,
animations, textures and sounds are read at run time from the player's own Tomb Raider
III installation, and without it those enemies simply do not appear.

### Four Tomb Raider III enemies, with tomb3's control code
2026-08-16 - 2026-08-25

**What.** The T-Rex (slot `SAS`, 31), the raptor (slot `REAPER`, 75), the Compsognathus
(slot `SAILOR`, 53) and the vulture (slot `CROW`, 43) join the enemy pool. The raptor
hunts only Lara, and the Compsognathus only attacks in a pack and gathers on Lara in its
idle mode. Each has its own hit-point and damage lines in `Balance.txt` like every other
pool enemy. They wear their own TR3 textures, carried over as extra texture pages. The
imported TR3 sounds always sit from slot 445 on, those five slots being free in every TR5
level, and an imported sound may carry several variants; the T-Rex's footstep is reachable
under the number its animation commands call while the data come from the number that
sounds as it did in TR3.

**Why.** The port was possible because the AI substructure is the same in both engines:
`CreatureActive`, `CreatureAIInfo`, `GetCreatureMood`, `CreatureMood`, `CreatureTurn` and
`CreatureAnimation` exist word for word in TOMB5's `box.cpp`, so the state machines could
be taken over as they are. Three spots were deliberately left out because TR5 has no
counterpart: tomb3's prey search over the neighbouring rooms for RAPTOR and FLARE_ITEM,
which uses a room list TR5 does not have, so Lara is always the target; `CreatureKill`
with `EXTRA_DINOKILL`, because TR5 has no Lara animation for being eaten and a wrong index
would force her into a foreign one, so the bite deals lethal damage instead; and Lara's
`AS_STOP`/`AS_DUCK` state query while the T-Rex sniffs, because the state numbers differ
between the games, so what is checked is whether Lara holds a torch and whether the T-Rex
was just hit.

**How.** New files taken over from tomb3's files of the same name: `game/trex.cpp`,
`game/trex.h`, `game/raptor.cpp`, `game/raptor.h`, `game/compy.cpp`, `game/compy.h`.
`game/crow.cpp` is not new but extended: TR5 kept only the crow branch of tomb3's
`bird.cpp`, which chooses by `object_number` between the crow's `anim_index + 14` in the
feeding state and the vulture's `+ 5` in the standing state, so the vulture's animation
offsets and its separate death handling were added back for the imported bird. The credits
name tomb3. The run-time extraction from the player's own installation lives in the
randomizer: `TR5Randomizer/src/core/Tr3Source.cpp`, `.h` read the models, textures and
sounds out of the installed game, `TR5Randomizer/src/core/Tr5Tr3Import.cpp` installs a TR3
moveable into a TR5 level, and `TR5Randomizer/src/core/ApplyPatch.cpp`, `.h` inject them
into the level being built; the installation paths are settings in the randomizer's own
options. `specific/file.cpp` decides in `LoadSamples` from the format tag how a sample
reaches the buffer: Core's own MS-ADPCM samples still go through the ACM decoder, plain
PCM goes straight into the XAudio2 buffer through `DXCreateSample`. TR3's `MAIN.SFX` holds
414 RIFF WAVs, mono PCM at 22050 Hz, which is the rate the engine expects, so no encoder
is needed and the samples can be taken over byte for byte; the variants of one sound
become one `SAMPLE_INFO` with N consecutive samples and the count in bits 2-5 of its
flags, the form the engine already reads. `game/trex.cpp` carries the footstep and bite
corrections. The textures are appended by `TR5Randomizer/src/core/Tr5Transfer.cpp` at the
same place a TR5 transfer inserts them, with texinfos and sprites drawn along after: pages
are only appended, never moved.

## 2.4 HD art from the Remaster, read at run time

With one option switched on, the engine reads the art of an installed *Tomb Raider IV-VI
Remastered* out of the player's own installation at run time and draws the levels with
it: a second, shader-based renderer beside the classic fixed-function one, sharing the
back buffer and the depth buffer and nothing else. Nothing of that art is copied into
this repository or shipped with it; with the build gate `hd_build` at 0, or with no
installation found, every path here returns on its first line and the picture is the one
the classic engine draws, and with the row *HD textures* (`hd_enable`) off the art is
built and the classic picture drawn until the row or F12 turns it on (chapter 2.6, The
HD/SD switch). The file formats are read against TRForge's published format description
(MIT, `vendor/trforge/LICENSE`), and three passages follow TRForge's own code closely -
the facial-rig rescan and the byte reader in `hd_trm.cpp`, and `read_map_file` in
`hd_bind.cpp`; the design of the HD renderer, the installation walk and the water effect
come from TROne (GPLv3) by Todesengel1931 - https://github.com/todesengel1931 - with the
author's copyright in the files' own headers and in `THIRD-PARTY.md`; everything else is
this project's own measurement over the player's files. No byte and no logic of the
Remaster's programs `tomb5.dll`, `tomb456.exe` or `tomb123.exe` is in this tree -
`hd_install.cpp` only tests that such a file EXISTS, as a marker that a folder is the
right one. Every rule of this path rests on this project's own count over the player's
files or is declared this project's free choice (the entry "Where the HD rules come
from" below); `THIRD-PARTY.md` keeps the origin ledger of every rule of this path.

### Finding an installed Remaster, reading what it holds for a level, and the settings that steer it
2026-09-05 - 2026-09-20

**What.** With the HD path built, the engine finds an installed *Tomb Raider IV-VI
Remastered*, reads what that installation holds for the level being loaded, binds it to
the level's rooms and object slots, and writes the counts into the log. The build is
`hd_build` (registry only, 1 by default), which `HDEnabled()` asks: with it at 0,
`HDEnabled()` returns before any folder is searched or any file is opened, and the two
calls in `specific/file.cpp` are the only way into the new code at all. The row **HD
textures** (on/off, `hd_enable`) on the *Graphics* page of the options frame, saved with
its neighbouring rows, switches the drawing of the level on screen, as F12 does (chapter
2.6, The HD/SD switch, Built when found). The settings that steer the path stand, each
with its default, in the manual's table under **HD from the Remaster**: `hd_build`,
`hd_enable`, `hd_objects`, `hd_motion`, `hd_reflect`, `hd_softbody`, `hd_springs`,
`hd_reach`, `hd_air`, `hd_threads`, `hd_texture_budget_mb`, `hd_install`,
`hd_install_tr3`, `hd_texture_format`, `hd_outfit` and the `hd_footsteps` subkey. The four
Tomb Raider III enemies this project ports into TR5 can be drawn from the *other* bundle:
`Tomb Raider I-III Remastered` is looked for in the same walk (`tomb123.exe` with a
subfolder `3` carrying `DATA` and `TEX`), with the registry override `hd_install_tr3`; a
slot marked `fromTr3` is looked up in that bundle only (game 3, then the siblings 1 and
2), never in the IV-VI folders and never the other way round, and the four names are
`TREX.TRM` for TR5 slot 31 (`SAS`), `VULTURE.TRM` for slot 43 (`CROW`), `COMPY.TRM` for
slot 53 (`SAILOR`) and `RAPTOR.TRM` for slot 75 (`REAPER`). Not finding the I-III bundle
costs those four models and nothing else.

**Why.** The HD art is the player's own property, read from the player's own installation
and never shipped. The two bundles sit side by side in the same library folder, so one
walk finds both, and the page cache had to learn that page 12 of Tomb Raider III and page
12 of Tomb Raider V are two different pictures. The four TR3 names are an inference and
not a measurement - they have not been checked against an I-III installation - derived
from TRForge's finding (MIT) that the HD art names a model after the engine's own symbol
for the slot unless the level's `.MAP` says otherwise: keyed on the English words that
rule matched 60 of 211 `.MAP` keys, keyed on the symbol 197, and it holds across all five
games. Because it is an inference, the log says out loud which way it went. A card that
reports 4095 MiB of texture memory is a ceiling and not a fault: `GetAvailableTextureMem`
answers in an unsigned 32 bit count of bytes, so 4096 MiB is the largest number that fits,
and every card that reaches it is nearly seven times over what the heaviest level needs.

**How.** New, under `TOMB5/specific/hd/`: `hd_install.cpp`/`.h` finds the installation -
the registry value `hd_install` first (same key as every `tomb5.*` setting,
`HKCU\Software\Core Design\Tomb Raider Chronicles\tomb5`), then every Steam library
folder; carried over from TROne (GPLv3) by Todesengel1931 -
https://github.com/todesengel1931. `hd_bind.cpp`/`.h` decides which `.TRM` belongs to
which slot: the level's own `LEVELn.MAP` first, then a hand table for the slots this
project added beyond the original 460, then the slot's own name; the slot-name table is
generated from `game/objects.h` and a `static_assert` in `hd_level.cpp` catches it
drifting away from the enum, and `read_map_file` follows TRForge's own code (MIT).
`hd_trm.cpp`/`.h` reads the header of a `.TRM`, including the rescan that gets past the
facial rig the head models carry - written against TRForge's format description, except
that rescan and the small byte reader beside it, which follow TRForge's own code closely
(MIT); TRForge's own file was not vendored because it pulls in a level library this
project does not want. `hd_scan.cpp`/`.h` reads the `.TRG`, counts groups, pages,
vertices, indices and draw ranges, binds the slots and times the BC7 decoder over every
page; it is engine-free on purpose, so that `TrgProbe` and `MapProbe` compile the same
file and measure what the game measures. `hd_level.cpp`/`.h` is the level bracket and the
`HDLOG` line. New, under `TOMB5/vendor/trforge/`: verbatim TRForge (MIT), five source
files plus `LICENSE`, `NOTICE.md` and `VERSION.txt`; those five carry no modification
notice of this project and must not - they were copied byte for byte and their first three
lines carry a hidden signature; the one change since is three comment passages left out of
`Trg.h`, recorded in `VERSION.txt`. Changed: `specific/file.cpp` calls `HDLevelLoad` after
`LoadTextureInfos` (the first moment rooms, meshes and slots are all in memory, in their
randomized state) and `HDLevelUnload` in `FreeLevel`; `specific/registry.cpp`/`.h` gained
`REG_ReadString`/`REG_WriteString` for the settings that are paths and not numbers
(`hd_install`, `hd_install_tr3`, declared in `registry.h`); `global/types.h` and
`tomb5/tomb5.cpp`/`.h` hold the settings, `hd_enable` 0 out of the box
(`tomb5/tomb5.cpp`); `tomb5.vcxproj` carries the new files and `/std:c++17` per file for
the ones that use `<filesystem>`, the engine keeping its own default. The options row and
its label live in `game/menu_frame.cpp` (`menu_rows_graphics`) and `game/gameflow.cpp`
(the frame's `CustomText` table); nothing in the randomizer's own `Language.cpp` is
involved. The TR3 bundle: `HDModelSlot::fromTr3` in `hd_model.cpp`/`.h` for the one-way
lookup, `hd_pagecache.cpp`/`.h` offering a guest's pages with `HD_PAGE_ALT_BASE` added and
taking the base off again at the one place a number becomes a file name, a `static_assert`
in `hd_level.cpp` holding the four slot numbers against the enum, and log words
`tr3_not_installed`, `tr3_model_missing` or the model with its origin, plus
`tr3_install=found/absent` on the per-level marker line. The settings table is in
`docs/Engine-Manual.md`.

### The second renderer, the seam where the engine draws HD rooms, and what a .TRG material means
2026-09-05 - 2026-09-08

**What.** Where the classic path is fixed-function with vertices the engine has
transformed, clipped and lit itself (`FVF = XYZRHW|DIFFUSE|SPECULAR|TEX2`,
`DrawPrimitiveUP`, no shader anywhere), the HD path is `vs_3_0`/`ps_3_0` with its own
vertex declaration, its own buffers and one texture per HD page. One vertex buffer and one
32-bit index buffer serve a whole level; every group's triangles are bucketed by `(pass,
page)` with a stable sort into ranges, one range being one draw call, inside the state
bracket `HDRenderFrameBegin`/`HDRenderFrameEnd`. An HD frame is drawn pass-major:
`HDFrameDraw` draws everything of the HD path that writes depth - every room's opaque and
alpha passes, then every HD object's - `DrawBuckets` then draws the classic opaque world,
`HDFrameDrawGlow` draws the glass phase and the additive pass of the same rooms and
objects, and `DrawSortList` draws TR5's own see-through polygons last. A room's identity
with the `.TRG` group it draws is a table rather than the room number, so a flipmap keeps
its art. A part's material decides how it is drawn: materials 6, 7 and 8 carry a cut-out
alpha test at their own `param[0]`; material 14 in the alpha pass is glass, drawn in a
phase of its own (`SRCALPHA`/`INVSRCALPHA`, no depth write, no alpha test, 96 parts in
eight of fifteen levels); material 13 is a four-page flipbook, its `param[0..2]` layer
numbers and `param[3]` seconds per frame; materials 3 and 17 carry a gloss drawn as a
grazing-angle lift behind `hd_reflect` (default 1); a vertex's `sway` weight is kept only
on materials 1, 7 and 8. A material is read as its **low byte**, so a destructible copy -
bit 15 set, a counter in bits 8 to 14 - is recognised as the material it copies. Static
meshes are not drawn twice: `DrawStaticObjects` returns at once for an HD room, the HD
room art carrying them baked in. A group with no triangle inside its own room (a *hollow
group*: ANDREA2 124, JOBY2 19 and 21, RICHCUT2 2, 3 and 4, TITLE 70, 101 and 103) does not
count as HD art and its room stays classic, unless one other group's art covers its faces
(*A classic room covered by another group's art is drawn as that art*, below: ANDREA2
124).

**Why.** The HD room art has to be drawn where the classic room polygons were drawn, with
the same depth, the same projection and the same effects order, or Lara, the items and the
see-through polygons would sort wrongly against the walls. The structure of the renderer
comes from TROne (GPLv3) by Todesengel1931 - https://github.com/todesengel1931. Passes 0
and 1 write depth and sort themselves out wherever they are drawn; the additive pass does
not - drawn room-major, a depth-writing draw standing behind a glow passed the depth test
and painted over it, cutting a room's lamp cones along a straight vertical line where the
next room's geometry began. `FlipMap` does not move a room: it swaps the CONTENTS of two
`ROOM_INFO` records and leaves their numbers alone, so a fixed room-equals-group identity
drew the art of the room that had gone. A page's share of dark texels is not a coverage
mask - an opaque page's alpha carries gloss or wetness and is mostly dark (ANDREA1's
facade pages 201, 211 and 207 are 95, 96 and 78 per cent dark) - so a cut-out driven by
that share discarded whole facades; over the fifteen `.TRG` files, materials 6, 7 and 8
are the only ones whose `param[0]` is an alpha reference (0.5 in every tuple but one at
0.503). The alpha test is right for a grating and wrong for glass: a pane whose sheet is
80.6 per cent below alpha 16 comes out at a test of 0.5 as a hard mask of shards, and
material 14 is the only glass in the game. `TrgVertex::sway` is a weight and not
permission - 416,153 vertices carrying one are material 8, 92,896 material 1, 46,611
material 7, against 160,620 on material 0 and 3,699 on materials 3, 6, 14 and 16, which
are ordinary geometry, glass, glow and light shafts that must not move. A material 13 part
drawn on one page left a bank of monitors and a row of ceiling panels frozen. Drawing a
room's statics again would draw every lantern twice. Without the hollow-group rule a room
whose group holds only art outside it counted as HD, its classic roomlets were dropped and
it rendered black.

**How.** `specific/hd/hd_render.cpp`/`.h` is the renderer, `specific/hd/hd_level.cpp`/`.h`
the engine-facing module; `hd_model.{h,cpp}` and `hd_object.{h,cpp}` carry the object half
of the frame order. An HD room is not drawn where it is met: `InsertRoom`
(`specific/drawroom.cpp:63`) writes the room number and the matrix on the stack at that
moment - view * world, the one `aSetViewMatrix()` has just handed the device - into a
frame list and returns, skipping its roomlets; `S_OutputPolyList` (`specific/output.cpp`)
draws the list immediately before `DrawBuckets()`, and `S_InitialisePolyList` empties it
beside the buckets and the sort list. One depth buffer serves both paths because the
classic path writes `sz = f_a - f_boo * rhw` with `rhw = 2048 / z_view`
(`specific/polyinsert.cpp:434`, `specific/drawroom.cpp:379`), which a Direct3D projection
with `_33 = f_a`, `_43 = -f_b`, `_34 = 1`, `_44 = 0` reproduces exactly after the w
division; `HDRenderSelfTest` compares the two over 50 view distances spread across the
reciprocal of z, with `D3DZB_TRUE` (`specific/function_table.cpp:107`), `ZFUNC LESSEQUAL`
(the Direct3D default) and the viewport at `MinZ 0 / MaxZ 1` read back from the device
rather than assumed. `SetD3DMatrix` (`specific/d3dmatrix.cpp`) turns the engine's 3x4
row-major matrix into a `D3DMATRIX`; the HD path draws with that as its world matrix, an
identity view, and a projection built from the live
`f_persp`/`f_centerx`/`f_centery`/`f_a`/`f_b`, taken when the rooms are collected and not
when they are drawn, because `AlterFOV` moves `f_persp` inside a frame. `MatrixCheck`
(`hd_level.cpp`) runs the engine's own three transform lines against the matrix that
really goes to the card over up to 128 of a room's vertices, once per level; those
vertices are kept aside while the vertex buffer is filled (128 per group, 192 KiB a level)
because the `.TRG` is freed at the end of the build and the buffer is `WRITEONLY`.
`HDLevelLoad` stays on the load thread and only reads and measures; the Direct3D objects
are made by `HDLevelBuild` from `S_LoadLevelFile` beside `aInit()` on the main thread, and
`HDLevelUnload` in `FreeLevel` makes no Direct3D call at all. `DXToggleFullScreen` and
`DXChangeVideoMode` replace the device rather than resetting it (`DXCreate` -> `DXClose`),
so `HDLevelDeviceLost` releases every HD object first and the rooms fall back to classic
until the next level starts; the `Reset()` path in `DXShowFrame` gets the same call,
`Reset` refusing while any `D3DPOOL_DEFAULT` object is alive. `HDFlipRoom`
(`hd_level.cpp`) swaps `g_room_group` in the same statement as the `ROOM_INFO` records and
is called from `FlipMap` (`game/control.cpp`); a loaded save follows for free, the engine
restoring a flip by calling `FlipMap` once per set flip (`game/savegame.cpp`), and the
water marks are built before any flip, on every room including the alternates.
`MaterialAlphaRef` (`hd_render.cpp`) answers materials 6, 7 and 8 with the part's own
`param[0]` and every other material with zero, and the answer travels with the draw call
in its sort key and reaches `hd_shader/hd_room.hlsl` as `gPass.x` for `clip(texel.a -
gPass.x)`; zero discards nothing, so the alpha pass (0.5, the classic `D3DRS_ALPHAREF`
128) and the additive pass are as they were to the bit. The per-page cut-out share is kept
and printed as a measurement and decides nothing (`HDPageCacheSlotCutout`,
`HDPageCacheSlotCutoutPermille`). The sway weight is taken away once, at level build, from
every vertex no part of material 1, 7 or 8 names. A material 13 part's triangles are drawn
from `flipSlot[frame]`, the frame taken from the same monotonic game clock the scroll and
the wind use, modulo the whole cycle; 27 parts in JOBY2, JOBY3, JOBY5, RICH1 and RICH2
resolve. The gloss reads material 3's strength in `param[2]` (0.333 to 1.0, 165,897
triangles) and material 17's in `param[1]` (0.05 or 0.1, 17,453 triangles) and draws
Schlick's fifth power of one minus N-dot-V times that strength, applied to the multiply so
that a surface lifts towards its own lit colour; 214 parts over twelve levels have one,
and the exponent in `param[0]` is read, logged and unused, a Blinn highlight inside the
eight-times-unrolled light loop taking the room pixel shader from 319 to 636 slots. RICH1,
RICH2 and RICH3 carry neither material, so the VCI marble is left matt. The glass phase
keeps working with the engine's three shatter paths (`game/control.cpp`,
`game/camera.cpp`, `game/objects.cpp` clear `MESH_INFO::Flags` bit 0, which
`UpdateDestructibles` reads). `hd_reflect` lives in `global/types.h` and is read in
`tomb5/tomb5.cpp`. Seams: one `HDLOG` line per room with the decision and its reason
(`hollow_group` among them) and `overhang=`, one `HDLOG flippair` line per flip pair and
one `HDLOG flip` line per swap, and the level line carrying `cutout_parts=`,
`sway_parts=`, `sway_dropped=`, `flipbook_pages=`, `flipbook_dropped=`,
`flipbook_ranges=`, `gloss_parts=` and `reflect=`, the frame line `flipbook_calls=` and
`gloss_calls=`. `HDRenderBlendOverride` exists for the diagnostic tools alone and the
engine never calls it. Tools: `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/RoomProbe.cpp` (`broom.bat`) - a
hidden window, a real Direct3D 9 device and a render target, so one room can be drawn from
a given camera into a picture file without starting the game, with `-groups`, `-plane`,
`-hasgeom`, `-shatter`, `-noreflect`, `-with <group> <dx dy dz>`, `-oldorder`, `-black`,
`-noblend`, `-paritycheck`, and a device-state check reading 58 states before and after an
HD block; `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/TrgProbe.cpp` (`-mat`, `-parts`, `-flat`, `-seam`).
