### The animation's root offset on a refused frame
2026-09-16 - 2026-09-21

**What.** At `fps_mode 1` and `fps_mode 2` a drawn tween frame whose pose the
interpolator's rule K6 refused still blends the animation's stored root offset in time,
between the offset the previous tick drew and the offset this tick draws, narrowed per
axis to the part this tick's own position step pays for. The pose, the limbs and the
rotations stay the current tick's, untouched. `fps_mode 0` draws exactly the frame it drew
before, and a frame that carries the logic tick, a slot that snapped and a tween frame
whose pose was accepted are unchanged as well.

**Why.** Every stored frame carries a bounding box and then the root offset (`frm[6]`,
`frm[7]`, `frm[8]`), which the draw applies after the item's own rotation, so the drawn
root is `item->pos` plus that offset. A climb carries its whole vertical travel in the
offsets and moves `item->pos` only once, at the wrap, through the animation command
`TranslateItem` (animation 161 `ANIM_CLIMBING` wraps with (0,-512,0), 168 `ANIM_CLIMBDOWN`
with (0,+512,0), 169 into 168 with (0,+256,0), 172 into 173 with (0,-190,0)). The root
snapshot blends `item->pos` across such a wrap, but a refused pose fell back to the
current frame's offset, so half of the position step was in the picture and none of the
offset's: 248 units of vertical error on one frame per climb cycle, presented four or five
times in a row on a 165 Hz panel. Blending the offset unconditionally errs the other way
wherever no position step pays for it: the crawl-to-crouch change (animation 274 to 222)
has an offset step of 61 units on y while `item->pos` does not move at all, and the crouch
pose - built for a root 143 units above the floor - was drawn 54, 45, 33 and 21 units too
high over four frames.

**How.** `game/interpolate.cpp` carries the refusal beside the pose flag: `g_poseOk[]`
takes a third value, `POSE_ROOT` (`POSE_NO 0`, `POSE_OK 1`, `POSE_ROOT 2`), so
`GetFramesNow` keeps returning 0 for both of its existing meanings and no call site needs
a new branch. `g_rootPrev[]` holds the offset the previous tick drew;
`g_rootStep[MAX_ITEMS][3]` holds this tick's own position step, filled by `RootStep`
(`TranslateItem`'s own inverse turned back by `y_rot`) inside `InterpBeginFrame`'s
per-item walk, one statement after `g_poseOk[i]` is set and above the `NodeMoved` exit, so
a slot that did not move reads an honest zero. `InterpRootNow` / `InterpRootRefused`
answer the draw site in `DrawAnimatingItem` (`game/draw.cpp`), once per drawn item and not
for Lara alone. The previous tick's offset is recomputed by `GetRootAt` (`game/draw.cpp`,
beside `GetFramesAt`): key index and remainder from the animation's own rate, the last
interval shortened as `GetFrames` shortens it, `InterpKeyAlpha`'s factor over the pair -
bit for bit the arithmetic that produced the picture one thirtieth of a second earlier; a
frame that is not inside the animation it is claimed to be in is refused. The blend is
`InterpRootKey`, `InterpRootLerp` and `InterpRootNarrow` in `game/interpolate_math.h`: the
key pair is blended in eighths (`InterpKeyAlpha`'s factors are quarters) and the time
blend runs at the frame's own alpha through `InterpLerpLong`, the same primitive and the
same alpha the root snapshot blends `item->pos` with, which is what makes the two halves
add up to the whole step. Swept in 1/256 steps over the wrap of animation 161, the worst
distance between the drawn root and the point the two ticks put it at is 504 units as the
picture stood before, 31 with the alpha rounded to an eighth and 1 - the two integer
truncations - at the alpha itself. `InterpRootNarrow` is the per-axis rule, in the item's
own `y_rot` frame, with `d = cur - prev` (`prev` already turned by `InterpRootFlip` on a
half-turn tick, or after a frame the previous tick drew turned by half a turn,
`g_rootTurned`): the blend may keep `min(|d|, |step|)` where offset step and position step
point against each other and nothing where they do not, and it starts from `cur` minus
that kept part instead of from `prev`. `y_rot` alone is the right frame because every
hand-written position step in `game/lara*.cpp` - the ledge grab, the vault and pull-up,
the pushblock, the ladder's corner and hang routines, crawl and duck, pole and rope, and
the water - writes `y_pos` straight and its x/z through `phd_sin`/`phd_cos` of
`pos.y_rot`, exactly as `TranslateItem` turns its three shorts (`game/control.cpp`). The
draw applies the offset through the full `phd_RotYXZ` (`game/delstuff.cpp`), so where
pitch or roll is not zero the comparison is an approximation; what that can cost is
bounded by the rule rather than by the inverse, because the kept part is clamped to `|d|`
on its own axis, so the start always lies on the segment between `cur` and `prev` and the
blend is never larger than before and never in another direction. Two draws keep their own
frame's root on purpose and say so in `CalcLaraMatrices`: the hit reaction, which wears a
frame picked by hand out of a spaz animation, and the first person still body. The HD path
takes the matrices the classic walk builds and needs no line; the randomizer and
`hd_enable` are untouched. `fps_mode 0` is byte-identical: `InterpBeginFrame` returns
before the walk whenever `alpha >= 1.0F`, so `g_rootStep` is never written, and
`InterpRootRefused` and `InterpRootNow` return at their first statement on `!g_applied`.
Seam (`-log`): `INTERPLOG`'s per-second line gains `root_fix=N`, a count of the refused
tween frames whose drawn root the rule really moved (frames whose two ticks name the same
animation and frame blend to the offset they already carry and are not counted), and
beside it, at most four lines a second and for Lara alone, `INTERPLOG root lara anim A->B
frame F->G offset_prev=(x,y,z) offset_cur=(x,y,z) drawn=(x,y,z) pos_y=N step=(x,y,z)
kept=(x,y,z)`; a transition the rule leaves at `cur` prints no line.
`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/RootProbe.cpp` links `game/interpolate_math.h` itself, so that
tool and engine run the same function, and walks Lara's own 474 animations, every wrap and
every transition with an offset step of 8 units or more on any axis, and counts the
invariant: no row where the narrowed draw leaves the segment from the frame's own offset
to the old draw. On the jump twists the previous tick drew the frame an early
`turn180_effect` fires on turned by half a turn, so the change that follows blends from
that offset turned, as `InterpRootNow` takes it. RootProbe models the case: `readTurn` and
`drawnTurned` ask the engine's own `InterpTurnKind`, `-sweep` turns the offset of such a
frame, and `-grab <a> <b> <y> <x> <z>` turns the previous offset where the leaving frame
is drawn turned or the entering frame fires the effect, and takes the whole step.
`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/InterpTest.cpp` holds the rule in its `root_narrow` group (the
ladder's whole step kept for every alpha, the crawl's nothing kept, a partial case,
same-sign and zero steps, each axis alone, the flip before the narrowing,
`LONG_MIN`/`LONG_MAX` without overflow), run by `bit.bat`; the tools are listed in
`Preparation/Tools/README.md`.

**Decisions.** On the jump twists the narrowing is left as it is: it keeps the part of the
offset step the jump's own position step pays for and draws the rest at the new frame's
offset, at most about 20 units early on one axis, which is the share of the step any
refused change draws at thirty hertz, while the pose on those frames is the new
animation's own.

### The pose between two ticks
2026-09-07 - 2026-09-25

**What.** A body's limbs move on the in-between frame and not only its position. The
engine's second matrix stack (`IMstack`, `aIFMStack`, the `phd_*_I` functions) already
blended two stored key frames; its blend factor is now one number instead of four
hard-wired branches, and the drawing code can ask for the midpoint between the poses of
two consecutive logic ticks. `InterpKeyAlpha(frac, rate)` in `game/interpolate_math.h`
produces `IM_alpha` (and `IM_alpha8`, the same factor in eighths for the integer stack),
and `aInterpolateMatrix`, `InterpolateMatrix`, `InterpolateArmMatrix` and
`aInterpolateArmMatrix` are each a loop over twelve elements instead of twelve written-out
copies of three constants. `InterpPoseAt` (`game/interpolate_math.h`) is the midpoint,
`GetFramesAt` (`game/draw.cpp`) turns it into a pair of frame pointers, and `GetFramesNow`
is what the draw sites call: `GetFrames` on a frame that carries a tick and at `fps_mode
0`, the midpoint on the frame between two ticks. The blend is vanilla's own element-wise
lerp of two 3x4 matrices - no angle is interpolated anywhere in the pose path. Animations
of rate 1 - 3619 of the game's animations, which never interpolated at all before - now
interpolate, except that `InterpPoseFar` refuses a rate 1 key frame pair whose two poses
turn more than ninety degrees at any node, `GetFramesAt` then returning 0 so that the
frame is drawn exactly as thirty hertz draws it. At rates above 1 a key pair of Lara's
where some node turns more than ninety degrees in the drawn frame (`InterpKeyFarOf`; the
hips alone, `InterpKeyFar`, until *Every node, in the drawn frame*), the pair vanilla's
own key-frame blend collapses her on, is drawn from a key frame built at the weight in
hand, the tween's weight included; only where the pair is held on its first key (the
tightrope turn) does `GetFramesAt` refuse the tween (see *Lara squeezed to a sliver in the
tightrope turn*).

**Why.** Both poses a tick apart lie on the same key frame pair, so their midpoint does
too and no third matrix stack is needed: within an interval the midpoint is `lerp(K, K',
(ap + ac) / 2)`, and where the pose crosses a key frame it is `lerp(K, K', (ap + 1) / 2)`.
The factor stays vanilla's own classification rather than the arithmetically correct `frac
/ rate`: walking the animation tables of all sixteen retail level files shows rates 1, 2,
3, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10 in use (3619, 3350, 35, 5399, 3187, 2, 2 and 120 animations), and at
rate 5 vanilla draws the four frames of an interval at 0.25, 0.75, 0.75, 0.75 - over three
thousand animations would move differently from the day the game shipped, which is a
different game and not a smoother one. The replacement of the branches had to be exact so
that `fps_mode 0` still produces the frame the build produced before: the float stack
keeps vanilla's three expressions rather than an algebraic rearrangement of them, because
`(a + b) * 0.5f` and `a + (b - a) * 0.5f` can differ in the last bit in IEEE floats, and
the integer stack keeps vanilla's shifts, because `(-3) >> 2` is -1 where `(long)(-3 *
0.25f)` is 0 - the factor is applied as `a + ((d * alpha8) >> 3)` below a half and `b -
((d * (8 - alpha8)) >> 3)` above it, which is `a + (d >> 1)`, `a + (d >> 2)` and `b - (d
>> 2)` for the three vanilla factors, negative values included. An element-wise lerp of
two rotations always lands on the short-way bisector, so the packed-angle wrap cannot
happen (1000 to 20 gives 1022 on all three axes and in both directions), and over
ANDREA1's 319 stored Lara animations no adjacent key frame pair has a per-axis packed
difference over 512 after the wrap. What the blend does instead is shorten: it walks the
chord of the arc, so a bone whose frame turns D comes out `cos(D/2)` of its length - 13 %
gone at 60 degrees, 29 % at 90, and at 180 the plane across the axis collapses, the bone's
frame is singular and whatever hangs off it lands on neither pose. Vanilla blends only
when the rate is above one; adding the rate 1 animations adds ANDREA1's 23, of which
twenty-two turn at most 52.7 degrees between two adjacent frames at every one of the
fifteen nodes (a shrink of a tenth) while the twenty-third turns her root 179.9 degrees in
one game frame (animation 205, node 0, key 0 to key 1). Ninety degrees is the last turn
whose midpoint keeps more than seventy per cent of the frame, and over ANDREA1 the rule
refuses animation 205 and nothing else; for every other rate the tween frame lands inside
the same segment the two ticks are blended on, so refusing it would itself be a jump. An
offline replay of the whole LARA table at sixty (the 337 animations ANDREA1 really stores
of 474 entries, every drawn frame, all fifteen nodes) reads a worst distance of a tween
frame from the midpoint of its two ticks of 0.00 - the blend is affine in its factor, so a
limb cannot come out beyond the two poses it stands between - and a worst shortening over
the rolls and the sprint dive of 0.89. The stretch reading first indexed `lara_matrices`
with the node number, so node 14 compared the torso with the left hand and node 9 the head
with the right shoulder; `stretch=` readings at nodes 8 to 14 taken before
`lara_lmx_of_node` named the wrong bone.

**How.** Three feed points. `DrawAnimatingItem` (`game/draw.cpp`) for every enemy, door,
machine and pickup takes `GetFramesNow` and `InitInterpolateAlpha`, and its `if (frac)`
branch is now entered on in-between frames for animations that never entered it.
`CalcLaraMatrices` (`game/delstuff.cpp`) carries Lara, and with her the HD composite, the
classic body and the mirror, all of which read `lara_matrices`:
`Rich_CalcLaraMatrices_Interpolated` takes a float alpha in place of `frac` and `rate`.
Lara's nine aim angles are blended by the root snapshot instead, being per-tick values
from the player rather than from the animation, and the four nodes her own animation does
not drive have a rule of their own (the next entry). The blend is refused when the item's
root snapped (`InterpPoseTime`, `game/interpolate.cpp`), when the animation number changed
between the two ticks (`GetFramesAt`, `game/draw.cpp`), or when the frame number did not
step by exactly one (`InterpPoseAt`, `game/interpolate_math.h`: a loop wrapping, a jump, a
frame written by hand, an item standing still); that frame is then drawn with the current
tick's pose, which is exactly what thirty hertz shows, for a sixtieth of a second. The one
exception to the animation-number rule is Lara's change after an early half turn (the tick
after the last frame of 48, 207, 210 and 212): its tween frames are drawn from a bridge
between the two poses and counted as poses, not in `pose_skips` (see *Lara facing the
wrong way for one tick in the jump twists*, *The change after it, bridged*). The one
exception to the frame-step rule is the ledge hang's lowering, whose backwards steps
`InterpPoseBack` blends (see *Ledge hang: an automatic turn and lowering at an edge*). The
snap verdict is recorded in `InterpBeginFrame`'s own item walk, one line before it writes
the blended position over the live one, because asked later from the draw the same test
would measure half the distance and a teleport could slip through. The animation's
shortened last interval - `GetFrames` reduces the rate there, comparing a relative frame
against an absolute `frame_end`, Core's own mismatch, reproduced rather than repaired - is
followed by `InterpKeyRate`. `InterpPoseFar` (`game/interpolate_math.h`) walks the two
packed rotation streams in lockstep, builds each node's frame in `phd_RotYXZ`'s own order
and compares them by `trace(A^T B) = 1 + 2 cos`; `GetFramesAt` asks it for `rate == 1`.
`InterpNoteLaraStretch` (`game/interpolate.cpp`, declared in `game/interpolate.h`, called
from `game/delstuff.cpp` on every tween frame of the view set) measures each of Lara's
bones against its own length in the skeleton and keeps the worst of the second with its
node, animation and frame (`INTERPLOG stretch=0.87@node3(anim232 f5843)`; a rigid pose
reads 1.00); it walks the bone table in mesh tree order (`LM_`, the head last) while
`lara_matrices` is in draw order (`LMX_`, the head ninth), so it reads every node's matrix
and its parent's through `lara_lmx_of_node` (`game/delstuff.h`, beside `lara_matrices`, a
`constexpr int[15]` written with the enum names, its walk bounded by the table's fifteen
entries, Lara's own mesh count). The table is written out, not derived; it is the draw
order's inverse (LM 14 is LMX 8, LM 8..13 are LMX 9..14, the rest unchanged), and the HD
seam's three reads in `hd_laradraw.cpp` use the same table, with a `static_assert` that it
has a matrix for every node of the composite. Log only: the drawn picture does not depend
on it. `HairControl` needed nothing: it is called from inside `ControlPhase`'s tick loop
(`game/control.cpp`) and `DrawHair` (`game/hair.cpp`) builds its matrices from the already
blended positions. The HD path followed with no change to `specific/hd/`, `HDObjectNode`'s
`interpolated` branch simply being entered on in-between frames as well. `game/sphere.cpp`

Deliberately left on vanilla's own pair: `GetBoundsAccurate` and `GetBestFrame`, which
produce bounding boxes for clip windows, shadows and lighting - the same approximation
vanilla already makes on every interpolated tick frame. `INTERPLOG` carries `pose_items`,
`pose_skips`, `pose_far`, `pose_hd` (Lara's own HD body as well as HD items), `lara_pose`
and `stretch=`, documented in `docs/Engine-Manual.md`.
`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/InterpTest.cpp` holds the rule (`pose_wrap`, and the pose
factor against the four hard-wired branches it replaced over 441 matrix element pairs for

`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/ModelProbe.cpp` (`-poserisk`, `-tween60`). `InterpPoseFar` is

### The arms between two ticks
2026-09-08 - 2026-09-09

**What.** The four of Lara's fifteen nodes that her own animation does not drive are
blended in time like the rest of her. With a weapon in her hands the two arms are driven
by the weapon slot's animation through `lara.right_arm` / `lara.left_arm`, and with the HK
in states 0 to 4 the torso and the head are read from it as well. `InterpArmPrev` keeps
each arm's animation number, frame number and `frame_base` pointer at the tick and hands
the previous one back with the frame's time alpha. It answers false - and the arms are
drawn as before - at `fps_mode 0`, on a frame that carries a tick, on a frame drawn live,
with no previous tick, when the arm's animation changed, when its `frame_base` moved, or
when its frame number stepped by more than one in either direction, because a pistol arm
counts down as well as up. It is not first-person only: `InterpArmPrev` asks `g_applied`
and not the camera, so the same four nodes interpolate in third person too. Both arm
chains descend from the same root, the torso the drawn body has.

**Why.** The arm chain indexes the frame data by the frame number and not by the key, so
it reads one stored pose per game frame however the animation's rate is declared
(ANDREA1's weapon slots are not all rate 1: `HK_ANIM` has 13 animations at rate 1, two at
2 and fifteen at 4). Writing those frames raw left the hands and the weapon stepping on
the logic tick while the background moved every frame - a hand that crept for five frames
and leapt on the sixth at 60 Hz and above; at thirty hertz it is invisible. The refusals
are the cases where the two frames are not two poses of one continuous movement.
`g_prevArm` must be invalidated with the rest of the previous state because its `base[]`
is a `short*` into the level's frame data - memory `FreeLevel` returns to the
`game_malloc` pool and the next level allocates over. The collapse of the two stacks had
to move up to the torso: done inside the right arm's own `phd_PushMatrix_I` it left the
left arm pushed off the torso level with stack one on key frame A and stack two on key
frame B and blended at the factor the collapse had left behind - the arm's alpha, which
nothing set back. For a rate 1 animation the body's factor and the arm's alpha are the
same number and the error is zero; for every other rate the left shoulder sat at `lerp(A,
B, alpha)` while the drawn torso sat at `lerp(A, B, blend)`, so the arm drifted off the
body through the tick and snapped back on the next - a visible shake of the rifles at any
rate above thirty: in animation 90 at rate 2, with the shotgun idle in hand, the body's
factor is half the frame's alpha, and the left hand ran ahead through the tick and jumped
back on its first frame while the right never jumped.

**How.** `InterpArmPrev`, `InterpBlendFloat` and `g_prevArm` (cleared in
`InterpInvalidate` beside `g_prevAim`) in `game/interpolate.cpp` and `game/interpolate.h`;
`InterpArmStack` in `game/draw.cpp` and `game/draw.h`; the six weapon branches of
`Rich_CalcLaraMatrices_Interpolated` in `game/delstuff.cpp`. The draw takes one of two
shapes: the pistol, uzi and revolver branches walk the three arm nodes twice from the same
shoulder - once with the previous tick's frame into a scratch of three matrices, once with
this tick's into the output - and blend them with `InterpBlendFloat`; the shotgun, HK and
crossbow branch already holds both stacks in the weapon's own animation, so
`InterpArmStack` collapses them to their blend at the body's factor on the torso level,
before either arm is pushed, and sets the arm's factor, after which stack one walks the
previous tick's frame and stack two this tick's. For the right arm the move of the
collapse changes nothing, because a translation applied to both stacks alike commutes with
their blend. With the HK in states 0 to 4, where the torso is collapsed once already, the
call takes the torso to its midpoint in time and both arm chains hang off that one joint.
`Rich_CalcLaraMatrices_Normal` is untouched and tick frames and `fps_mode 0` never enter
this branch's blend (`InterpArmPrev` answers false there), so thirty hertz is byte for
byte what it was. Seams: `INTERPLOG` carries `arms=<blended>/<refused>/<tween frames>`,
counted in the draw where the weapon is known, so empty hands, a flare and a torch read
nought. `ARMLOG` (behind `-log`) writes one line per drawn frame while a weapon is in
Lara's hands or on the way there or back (`LG_READY`, `LG_DRAW_GUNS`, `LG_UNDRAW_GUNS`,
`LG_FLARE`), written right after `CalcLaraMatrices(0)` in `game/draw.cpp` so that it reads
the view set `lara_matrices` - the table the HD body is skinned from
(`specific/hd/hd_laradraw.cpp`) and the classic body drawn from. Three calls in the draw's
own order (`game/interpolate.cpp`, declared in `game/interpolate.h`): `InterpArmLogPath`
notes which path built her (`GetFramesNow`'s `frac`, the body's blend, the held first
person body, whether the HD body is on), `InterpArmLogNote` notes what was done with the
arms (the weapon type, both answers of `InterpArmPrev`, the arms' alphas and the previous
tick's frames), and `InterpArmLogFrame` writes the line; a frame built by
`Rich_CalcLaraMatrices_Normal` never reaches the second call, which the line shows as
`ok=-1/-1`, and empty hands write nothing. The line carries its own serial,
`GlobalCounter` (so that the frames of one tick can be grouped), whether the frame is a
tween and at what alpha, the body path and factor, Lara's animation, frame and state, the
weapon type and `gun_status`, the weapon item's animation, frame and state, each arm's
animation, frame and the previous tick's frame the blend used, `InterpArmPrev`'s two
answers and the arms' alphas, the aim angles for both arms plus torso and head, and the
view-space positions of the hips and of shoulder, elbow and hand of each arm, with the
right hand matrix's first column for a hand that turns rather than moves; the hand taken
relative to the hips is what the arm does, because the camera and the hips move smoothly.
Without `-log` the three functions return at their first line; at `fps_mode 0` the line is
still written (`tween=0`, `a=1.000`) and is the reference a sixty run is held against.
`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/AnimMap` maps the weapon slots' animations and rates.

### The camera on the in-between frame
2026-09-07 - 2026-09-09

**What.** The eye, the target and the roll are blended with the rest of the snapshot, and
the whole view is rebuilt for the in-between frame: the interpolator calls `phd_LookAt`
again with the moved eye, and a second time in `InterpEndFrame` with the live one.
`camera.pos.room_number` is never written; the room walk of a blended frame is seeded
instead with the room that contains the blended eye (`InterpEyeRoom`). The frame is drawn
live from end to end when `camera.fixed_camera` changed, when a change of `camera.type` or
`camera.old_type` leaves the smooth family (chase, look and combat, which hand over to
each other), or when the eye or the target jumped more than 1024 units, the target test
being scale-aware.

**Why.** Moving `camera.pos` does nothing on its own: the world-to-view matrix, `CamPos`,
`CamRot`, `D3DMView` and the device's own view transform are built by `phd_LookAt`, once
per logic tick, at the end of whichever camera routine ran. The second rebuild with the
live eye keeps the tween frame's matrix from being handed to the next frame, which would
leave the world half a step ahead of the camera looking at it on every second frame.
`old_type` is tested beside `type` because `CalculateCamera` resets `type` to
`CHASE_CAMERA` at its own end unless a heavy camera's timer is running, so `old_type` is
what the view was actually built as. The roll has to travel with the eye because three
cameras hand `phd_LookAt` a roll that is not zero - first person rolls with the head bone,
a flyby rolls along its track, a cut scene rolls with the scene - and rebuilding the view
without it would snap a first-person frame upright and back on every other frame. The room
is not interpolated because it drives `DrawRooms`' whole portal walk and every clip
window; but seeding that walk with the logic room while the eye has crossed a portal plane
between two ticks makes `GetRoomBounds` refuse the portal (`x ^ p->normal[0]` flips sign)
and `SetRoomBounds` drop it a second way (`tooNear == 4`), so the room behind it is
missing for one frame with the sky in the hole and the hole's edge on the portal's own
line. The aim test is scale-aware because the first person camera has to express a look
direction through a target position, the engine's camera having no field for one: it puts
the target 0x5100 (20736) units down the line of sight, where one degree of turn moves the
point 362 units, so an absolute threshold of 1024 read any turn past about three degrees
between two ticks as a cut - ten to seventeen false cuts a second in a quiet room, an idle
animation turning her head by more than that. And a type change is not by itself a cut
because `game/larafire.cpp` sets `COMBAT_CAMERA` while the guns are up while
`CalculateCamera` (`game/camera.cpp`) resets the type to chase at its own end, so
`camera.old_type` moves chase - combat - chase around every draw and every holster, bursts
of five or six type changes a second, which the engine itself hands over smoothly (the eye
walks to the new camera's place at `camera.speed` and the target is Lara either way, which
is why the eye test never fired): taking each for a cut drew that tick live and the next
tween frame half a tick back, so the picture went forward, back, forward at every weapon
draw. A cut makes the whole frame live because a cut that left the camera live and the
world at its halfway values moved the entire level against the eye - in first person,
where the eye hangs in Lara's head, that produced copies of her body, moving room seams
and a near zone measuring a distance the picture did not have; it costs one frame of
thirty hertz at the one moment the picture jumps anyway.

**How.** `phd_LookAt` records the roll it was handed in `CamRoll` (`specific/3dmath.cpp`),
the one place that catches all three cameras; in first person the value is read through
the camera's own getter `GetFirstPersonRoll()` instead, because `fpRoll` is private to
`game/camera.cpp`. It is blended the short way round like any other angle.
`phd_GenerateW2V`, which `phd_LookAt` calls, carries game state inside it - `lara.poisoned
+= (lara.dpoisoned - lara.poisoned) >> 4`, an exponential ramp written when there was
exactly one `phd_LookAt` per logic tick - so the ramp is guarded at its source in
`aGenerateW2V` and `phd_GenerateW2V`, which covers every caller including `S_DrawPickup`
(`specific/output.cpp`), whose own `phd_LookAt` runs once per drawn frame while a pickup
icon is on screen; Core's arithmetic is untouched, including the fact that
`phd_GenerateW2V` ends by calling `aGenerateW2V` and so steps the ramp twice per
`phd_LookAt`. `InterpEyeRoom` (`game/interpolate.h`, `game/interpolate.cpp`) answers with
the room that contains the blended eye - `GetFloor` from the logic room, the very call
`camera.cpp` makes at every tick - and `DrawRooms` (`game/draw.cpp`) seeds its walk from
that; nothing is written back, `camera.pos.room_number` keeps the logic room and `outside`
and `camera_underwater` are still read from it, `g_applied` is the gate, and the
correction lives in the walk both paths share, so it mends the classic picture as well as
the HD one. `InterpCamAimCut`, `InterpCamAim`, `INTERP_CAM_FAR_TARGET` (4096) and
`INTERP_CAM_DIR_RADIUS` (1024) in `game/interpolate_math.h`: beyond the far-target
distance a target is treated as a direction - pulled back onto a sphere of 1024 units
about its own eye, with the 1024-unit threshold applied to the change of direction alone
while the eye's own travel keeps its own test - and the branch is chosen once for the pair
of camera states (far if either length is beyond the shell), both offsets taking the same
scale, the radius over the longer of the two, because choosing per camera put a cliff in
the middle of the rule. At the direction radius the threshold is a turn of 41 to 57
degrees in one thirtieth of a second, over 1200 degrees a second, while a real cut still
measures 1448 at a right angle and 2048 at a half turn; the chase camera is untouched, its
target sitting on Lara about a sector and a half out, under the shell, where the
comparison is the absolute one to the bit. `InterpCamTypeCut` (`game/interpolate_math.h`)
lets a hand-over inside the smooth family through, and `game/interpolate.cpp`
`static_assert`s the three type values the header mirrors against `camera_type`, because
the header is built without the engine. Still a cut: a fixed camera taking over
(`FIXED_CAMERA`, or `fixed_camera` changing), a heavy camera, a cinematic, a spot camera
stepping, the binoculars (where the eye jumps to Lara's head and the eye and aim tests
catch it), any eye jump over `CAM_SNAP`, and any aim swing over the sphere threshold. The
cut test runs at the top of `InterpBeginFrame`, beside the cutscene test, and not after
the items, effects, hair links, particles and aim angles have been blended. The
first-person filters `fpVel`, `fpSpd`, `fpRel` and `fpSmoothSlow[]` are left alone: they
are tuned as per-logic-tick exponentials, `FirstPersonCamera` stays inside
`CalculateCamera` at thirty and sees exactly one sample per tick, and only its output -
`camera.pos`, `camera.target` and `fpRoll` - is interpolated. `INTERPLOG` counts the
hand-overs it now lets through as `handover=` and only the changes that leave the family
as `type=`. `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/InterpTest.cpp` holds the rule: `camera_aim` (the
old rule and the new one side by side over a swept first person camera, 500 cases of turn
plus eye travel, and a chase camera), `camera_shell` (a target walked out through the
shell one unit at a time, 500 steps, and jittered on it for thirty ticks), `camera`
(twelve checks over the type table - the six hand-overs are none, the six leaves are cuts)
and a `portal walk` section of 13 checks on ANDREA1's own portal records. All of it lives
past `InterpBeginFrame`'s `alpha >= 1` return, so `fps_mode 0` reaches none of it. The
entry that follows, "The drawn eye at a corner", keeps the blended eye out of a pillar or
a door jamb the straight blend cuts, and seeds the walk from the room that holds the eye.

**Commits.** `766896d`, `9b4f7b8`, `73819d5`, `e6debb7`, `82e1b12`, `a7b3ec9`

### The drawn eye at a corner
2026-09-27

**What.** On a frame drawn between two logic ticks - `fps_mode` 1 and 2, in both control
schemes - the blended eye is tested before the view is built: `GetFloor` from the logic
room, then `GetHeight` and `GetCeiling`, and the point has to lie between the two. An eye
the logic room refuses is tested from the previous tick's room; if that room holds it, the
eye stays where it is and the portal walk starts in that room. An eye neither room holds
is moved to the nearest open point of the chord between the two tick eyes, with the target
and the roll taken at the same blend factor. When no point of the chord opens, the eye
stays and that frame draws no sky, so what its walk leaves undrawn is the clear colour,
black. A blended eye the logic room holds - nearly every frame - is drawn exactly as
before, and no tick eye moves. A flyby is left out and drawn as before. `-log` gains
`CAMLOG`: a `tick` line per pass of the chase, combat, fixed and look cameras (none during
flybys, binoculars or cutscenes), a `draw` line per frame the rule acted on and a `sum`
line per second.

**Why.** In play at 165 Hz the picture flashed black for one or two video frames at doors
and pillars of indoor rooms (in ANDREA1 at room 40's east door and at the pillars of rooms
3 and 11; indoors, so black rather than sky). Both causes lie in the draw. The chord
between two open tick eyes cuts a corner block or a pillar for two or three drawn frames:
`GetFloor` from the logic room then follows the pillar's floor data up into the room
above, and the walk draws one room. And the room seed: the first drawn frames after a tick
apply the new tick's room to an eye still beside the old tick eye, where that room's
sector is a wall. The logic camera is not the cause: `MoveCamera` tests every tick eye
against its room and pulls or pins it in (`game/camera.cpp:2789`-`2849`); only the blended
points between the ticks leave the room.

**How.** `ModernCameraChordClamp` (`game/modern_camera.cpp:302`) is pure: from the blended
point it scans the chord outward on both sides at once in steps of a thirty-second of its
length (`MODERN_CAMERA_CHORD_SCAN`, `game/modern_camera.h:315`), tests an end itself when
a scan reaches it, halves each bracket it found twelve times toward its open end
(`MODERN_CAMERA_CHORD_BISECT`, `modern_camera.cpp:367`, `:377`) and returns the nearer
answer - the newer tick eye's side on a tie - or none. It builds its points with
`InterpLerpLong`, the interpolator's own blend, so a point it tests is the point drawn.
`ModernCameraDrawnEye` (`:427`) is the order: the logic room, the previous tick's room
(`:468`), the chord (`:474`), none (`:478`); a chord answer equal to a tick eye is
reported as `tick` (`:497`). `CameraEyeTest` (`game/camera.cpp:1062`) is the engine's
test, the five terms of `ModernCameraEyeInRoom`; it saves `trigger_index`, `tiltxoff`,
`tiltyoff`, `OnObject` and `height_type` before `GetFloor`, `GetHeight` and `GetCeiling`
and writes them back after (`:1065`-`1090`). `InterpBeginFrame` calls the rule after the
blend (`game/interpolate.cpp:1617`) unless either tick is a flyby (`:1608`; entering or
leaving one is a cut, `:656`), moves the eye and the target to the answer for `chord` and
`tick`, rebuilds the view with the roll at the same factor (`:1647`) and raises
`g_skyWithheld` for `nosky` (`:1632`); `InterpEyeRoom` returns the rule's room for
`prevroom`, `chord` and `tick` (`:1149`); `ClearEyeFix` clears all of it at the top of
every `InterpBeginFrame` (`:1305`) and in `InterpEndFrame` (`:1749`), which puts the tick
eye back as on every frame (`:1709`). `SkyDrawPhase` reads `InterpSkyWithheld()`
(`game/draw.cpp:550`), leaves out the moon, the HD dome (`HDFrameSky` is called nowhere
else), the flat layers, the horizon and the stars, and returns once the storm's clock has
stepped (`:603`). `nosky` needs both tick eyes to fail as well, since the chord's ends are
among the points searched, so it happens only where the logic camera itself left an eye
that neither tick's room holds; at `fps_mode` 1 the live frame between two such blended
frames still draws that eye with its sky. The seams: `CameraTickLog`
(`game/camera.cpp:1220`, at the end of `CalculateCamera`, `:1707`) with `CameraEyeNear`
(`:1147`) for the distances, fed by `CamTickWant`, `CamTickLos` and `CamTickIdeal` in
`ChaseCamera` and `CombatCamera` (`:2372`, `:2471`, `:2496`, `:2604`, `:2677`, `:2699`),
which store only behind `gLogEnabled`; `InterpLogEyeFix` (`game/interpolate.cpp:1189`),
called by `DrawRooms` after the walk and the sky (`game/draw.cpp:2315`); the sum in
`LogSecond` (`game/interpolate.cpp:873`). `CAMLOG tick` prints `f=`, `eye=(x,y,z)/room`,
`ideal=(x,y,z)/room` or `-`, `want=(x,y,z)` or `-`, `target=(x,y,z)/room`, `los=` 1, 0 or
-1, `los_lp=` 0 to 8 or -1, `pull=` 8 to 1, 0 or -1, `lead=yaw,pitch`, `mc_pull=`,
`snaps=`, `kind=` (`open`, `wall`, `door->room`, `below:units`, `above:units`), `face=`
and `corner=` (units, -1 for none). `CAMLOG draw` prints `frame=` (`ROOMLIST`'s serial),
`tick=`, `alpha=`, `eye=(x,y,z)`, `prev=(x,y,z)/room`, `cur=(x,y,z)/room`, `kind=`, `fix=`
(`prevroom`, `chord`, `tick` or `nosky`), `alpha2=`, `moved=`, `walk_room=`, `rooms=`,
`outside_logic=` and `sky=`. `CAMLOG sum` prints `flagged=`, `prevroom=`, `chord=`,
`tick=`, `nosky=` and `max_moved=`. `CameraEyeTest`'s calls touch no game state:
`GetFloor` writes only the room through its pointer, here a local
(`game/control.cpp:1253`-`1340`); `GetCeiling` writes no global, and the ceiling callbacks
it runs write only the height they are handed (`game/objects.cpp`, `game/traps.cpp`);
`GetHeight` writes the five globals the test saves and restores, and runs floor callbacks
that write only `height_type`, `OnObject` and the height - no item, no random number,
nothing a savegame holds. `fps_mode 0` does not reach the rule: `InterpAlphaNow` answers 1
there (`game/interpolate.cpp:1086`-`1087`) and `InterpBeginFrame` returns at `alpha >= 1`
(`:1328`) before the camera block, the only caller of `ModernCameraDrawnEye`; the rule's
state is cleared on every frame (`:1305`). The rule moves only the frame's copies of the
camera, which go back in `InterpEndFrame`, so the logic camera keeps its eye, target and
room; `ChaseCamera` and `CombatCamera` carry three calls each that store what `CAMLOG`
prints and return at once without `-log`. ModernTest's `camera_chord`
(`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/ModernTest.cpp`) holds the rule on the niche map's 2x2
pillar: chords past its four corners against a brute force, an open chord, a chord solid
from end to end, solid ends with an open middle, one solid end, and the order over two
rooms - none, prevroom, chord, tick, nosky. InterpTest compiles no engine file (`bit.bat`
builds `InterpTest.cpp` alone against `game/interpolate_math.h`), so the room order and
the sky flag are held in ModernTest through `ModernCameraDrawnEye`, the function the
engine calls.

**Decisions.** The rule acts on the drawn eye alone: no tick eye moves, the tick eye keeps
no clearance margin and `mgLOS` gets no diagonal corner test - that test mends none of the
eight events and would change the camera at every pillar, and no margin is kept;
`CAMLOG`'s `face=` and `corner=` count how often a tick eye stands that close to a face or
a corner. A frame whose eye neither tick's room holds shows the nearest open point on the
chord between its two tick eyes and never a position of its own. The fallback colour is
the clear colour, black. Both control schemes take the rule, because the blend is the
interpolator's and not a scheme's, and `fps_mode` 1 and 2 alike. Flybys are left out:
`CalculateSpotCams` sets a flyby's eye straight from its spline
(`game/spotcam.cpp:458`-`483`) and `MoveCamera` never tests it, so a flyby passing outside
every room would fail at both ends of every chord and, under the rule, lose its sky or
stall at the tick rate; a flyby at a corner keeps the plain blend and whatever that draws.
The net can still fire on an eye the logic itself left untested: `MoveCamera` keeps its
ideal when the ceiling meets the floor height or a height is `NO_HEIGHT`
(`game/camera.cpp:2837`-`2843`), and a fixed camera or the first person head eye is never
room-tested; an outdoor stretch of that kind alternates sky and black at the tick rate,
and `CAMLOG`'s `nosky=` count shows it. The see-through and wall-fill frames of the near
plane are a separate matter: the entry *The Modern eye clear of a wall*.

### The Modern eye clear of a wall
2026-09-28

**What.** In the Modern scheme the orbit's tick eye is moved square off every closed axis
face of its sector that stands nearer than the reach of the near plane's visible
rectangle, to exactly that reach, at the end of `MoveCamera`: after its own `mgLOS`
pull-in and `CameraSnaps`, before its floor and ceiling clamp. The reach comes from the
projection the frame uses, 33 units at 16:9 and 39 at 21:9. Only x, z and the eye's room
change, each axis by at most the reach. `-log`'s `CAMLOG tick` line ends in `clear=`: the
units moved, 0 when there was nothing to do or the pass ran no Modern orbit, -1 when the
moved point opened in no room and the eye stayed. The rule belongs to the logic camera, so
`fps_mode` 0, 1 and 2 change alike.

**Why.** The near plane stands 20 units in front of the eye (`InitWindow(0, 0, w, h, 20,
20480, 80, ...)`, `specific/gamemain.cpp:260`; `phd_znear` holds it shifted up by
`W2V_SHIFT`, `specific/3dmath.cpp:796`, and the HD renderer clips at the same `f_mznear`,
`specific/hd/hd_level.cpp:638` and `:1248`). `AlterFOV` sets the focal length `phd_persp =
(winh * 320 / 240 / 2) * cos(fov / 2) / sin(fov / 2)` (`specific/3dmath.cpp:139`-`140`,
`GAME_FOV` 80 degrees, `global/types.h:55`), and a view-space point is on screen while
`|x| <= z * (W / 2) / persp` and `|y| <= z * (H / 2) / persp`. The corners of the
rectangle the screen shows at z = 20 therefore lie `R = sqrt(20^2 + (20 * (W / 2) /
persp)^2 + (20 * (H / 2) / persp)^2)` from the eye: at 1920x1080 persp is 858 and R 32.5,
at 2560x1080 R is 38.1, at 2560x1440 persp is 1144 and R 32.5 again. A closed face nearer
than R can cross that rectangle at some view angle, and whatever lies behind it shows at
the screen's edge; a face at R or more never can. Nothing kept the eye that far off. When
no eighth of the ray clears the four probes of `ModernCameraRayBounds` at 384 units - her
back to a wall - the `mgLOS` point stands (`game/camera.cpp:2125`-`2136`), and `mgLOS`
(`:1801`) steps one sample back from the first one in a wall, so that point lies anywhere
in the last eighth before the face, down to 0 units from it. `MoveCamera` smooths the eye
towards it by 1/speed a tick (`:2858`), runs `mgLOS` again only for an eye outside its
floor or ceiling (`:2892`) and asks no wall. So the Modern orbit's eye often stood nearer
than 33 units to a closed face, mostly at the `pull=0` fallback and at times 0 or 1 unit
from it.

**How.** `ModernCameraNearRadius` (`game/modern_camera.cpp:646`) is the formula in
doubles, rounded up to a whole unit, 0 without a focal length or a near plane; whole
numbers would leave a long at a 4K window. `ModernCameraWallClearance` (`:663`, declared
under the formula and the rule at `game/modern_camera.h:526`-`560`) is pure and takes its
open test as a callback of the type `ModernCameraDrawnEye` uses (`MODERN_EYE_OPEN`,
`:508`). It answers 0 at once when no edge of the eye's sector lies within the radius;
otherwise it asks the eye itself (not open: 0, untouched), then, for each edge within the
radius, the point one unit past it at the eye's height from the eye's room - the probe
points of `CameraEyeNear` (`game/camera.cpp:1182`), so `face=` and the rule read the same
faces - and moves x to `(x & ~1023) + radius` for a closed west face or to `(x & ~1023) +
1024 - radius` for a closed east face, z likewise. The moved point is asked last: open, it
answers the units moved, `|dx| + |dz|`, with the room it resolved to; closed, it answers
-1 and nothing moves. A radius outside 1 to 512 answers 0, since two faces of one axis
within it would need a sector narrower than 1024. The design asked all four probes on
every tick; the code asks only the edges within the radius, so nearly every tick asks
nothing. `ModernCameraClearWall` (`game/camera.cpp:2778`) hands it `camera.pos` with its
room, the radius from `phd_znear >> W2V_SHIFT`, `phd_winwidth / 2`, `phd_winheight / 2`
and `phd_persp`, and `ModernCameraWallOpen` (`:2750`), which is `CameraEyeTest` (`:1097`),
and writes x, z and the room back when the eye moved. `MoveCamera` (`:2800`) reads the
flag `modern_cam_clear_wall` (`:280`), which `ChaseCamera` and `CombatCamera` set to their
`modern_orbit` just before they call it (`:2536`, `:2740`), and clears it at once, so
`FixedCamera`, its one other caller, never runs the rule. It calls the rule after the
`CameraSnaps` block (`:2927`), before the floor and ceiling clamp (`:2930`-`2950`, the
same three cases and the same 255 as `ModernCameraEyeY`),
`CheckForRichesIllegalDiagonalWalls` in RICH1 and RICH2 and the final `GetFloor` into
`camera.pos.room_number` (`:2955`), so all of them apply to the pushed point. The open
test runs `GetFloor`, `GetHeight` and `GetCeiling`; `GetHeight` writes `tiltxoff`,
`tiltyoff`, `OnObject`, `height_type` and `trigger_index` and runs floor callbacks. The
rule runs inside `MoveCamera`, in the tick, where the camera already calls `GetHeight`
freely (`mgLOS`, `CameraCollisionBounds`, the clamp that follows), so nothing needs saving
there; `CameraEyeTest` puts the five back all the same, which is harmless. The pure
function calls nothing of the engine. The seam: `cam_tick.clear` (`:273`), written only
behind `-log`, cleared with the rest of `cam_tick` at the top of every pass (`:1337`) and
printed last on the tick line (`:1312`). The classic scheme keeps its camera: the flag is
`modern_orbit`, 0 there, and `CameraCollisionBounds(&ideal, 384, 1)` still resolves its
eye (`game/camera.cpp:2523`, `:2729`); the first person, binocular and fixed cameras, the
look camera and the flybys never set the flag. In the Modern scheme `fps_mode` 0, 1 and 2
all draw the moved tick eye, and the interpolator blends the moved eyes as it blends any
others. The faces are asked at the eye's height before the floor and ceiling clamp; an eye
that the clamp then raises or lowers is not asked again. ModernTest's `camera_wall_clear`
(`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/ModernTest.cpp`) holds the rule on the niche map: the focal
length and the radius at the screen sizes above, an eye nearer than R to a face moved
exactly R off it on that axis alone, an eye at R or beyond left where it is, a concave
corner moving both axes, a refused moved point answering -1 without a move, and a sweep of
a 7-unit grid that leaves no closed face nearer than the radius.

**Decisions.** The radius is computed from the projection the frame uses (`phd_znear`,
`phd_winwidth`, `phd_winheight`, `phd_persp`), never a constant, so it follows the
window's aspect and the field of view. The rule runs for the Modern orbit only; the
classic scheme stays as it is. The push is square to the face and at most the radius,
never along the ray - a wall along the ray would let the eye slide far - and never round
her beyond that. Convex corners are left out: an eye seldom comes within the radius of
one. A room dropping out of the picture is a matter of the portal walk, not of the near
plane. The floor and the ceiling need nothing: the clamp that follows keeps 255 from both.

**Commits.** `a1f392c`, `e471965`, `dd343c0`

### A level camera that follows Lara is blended between its ticks
2026-10-01

**What.** At *Frame rate 60* and at *Display*, under both control schemes, a level camera
sequence that follows Lara while she keeps her controls - the X-ray corridor of Escape
with the Iris, and one sequence each in the level files andy1, Andy2, andy3 and rich3 and
a second one in rich2 - is drawn between its ticks like any other flyby; its first tick
and the tick after its last stay camera cuts. At *Frame rate 30*, and on every tick
outside such a sequence, every frame is drawn as before. With `-log`, `INTERPLOG`'s
`spot=` counts for such a sequence only the frames of its first tick and of the tick after
its last.

**Why.** In the X-ray corridor the whole picture juddered at a frame rate of 60 and above,
under the classic scheme as well, and not at 30. The cause is the upstream pair of lines
at the top of `ControlPhase` (`game/control.cpp:256`-`257`), `if (bTrackCamInit)
bUseSpotCam = 0;`, which runs on every call, the calls that run no tick included - at
*Display* most calls run none. The tick's `TO_FLYBY` trigger sets `bUseSpotCam` again
(`:2685`-`2693`), and `CalculateSpotCams` sets `bTrackCamInit`
(`game/spotcam.cpp:530`-`531`) on every tick of a sequence whose first camera tracks Lara.
The interpolator read `bUseSpotCam` alone: its snapshot at the start of every tick took 0,
its cut test after the tick saw 1 and counted a flyby cut, so the first frame after every
tick was drawn live at the tick's state, and the in-between frames after it, with the flag
back at 0, were blended from the tick before - the picture jumped a tick forward and fell
back, thirty times a second. On those in-between frames the drawn-eye rule also ran on the
flyby's eye, which its own comment leaves out.

**How.** `InterpLevelCamHolds(useSpotCam, trackCamInit)` (`game/interpolate_math.h:123`):
a level camera sequence holds the view when either flag is set. From a tracking sequence's
first tick to the tick that runs `CalculateCamera` again the pair is never 0, where
`bUseSpotCam` alone is 0 between the ticks; outside a tracking sequence `bTrackCamInit` is
0 and the answer is `bUseSpotCam`'s. `InterpSpotCut` (`:131`) and `InterpEyeRuleRuns`
(`:139`) are the cut test's flyby term and the drawn-eye rule's exclusion as pure
functions, so InterpTest calls what the engine calls. In `game/interpolate.cpp`,
`LevelCamHolds()` (`:450`) hands the two flags of `game/spotcam.h` to the predicate, and
every read of the flag the interpolator makes goes through it: the snapshot stores it in
`g_prevCam.spot` (`:1116`, the field's comment at `:152`); the cut test compares the two
(`:686`); the drawn-eye rule is off while either end of the blend is held (`:1741`); and
`CameraRollNow` (`:464`) asks `FirstPersonActive` (`game/camera.cpp`), which refuses a
flyby by `bUseSpotCam` alone, only while no level camera holds the view, so a tracking
sequence's roll is `CamRoll` at both ends of the blend, as for every other flyby. No other
cut reason, blend or snapshot field changes. On the entry tick the predicate goes from 0
to 1, and every frame of that tick is a cut. On a continuing tick `InitialiseSpotCam`
finds the same sequence still tracked, clears `bTrackCamInit` and returns without
restarting it (`game/spotcam.cpp:126`-`128`), and `CalculateSpotCams` sets it again
(`:531`): the predicate is 1 throughout and there is no cut. On the exit tick no trigger
fires and the `CalculateCamera` branch of `ControlPhase` (`game/control.cpp:670`-`672`)
clears `bTrackCamInit`: every frame of that tick is a cut. When one call runs several
ticks the reset at its top runs once, and the predicate is 1 either way. The `GF_OFFICE`
branch of `ControlPhase` (`game/control.cpp:641`-`645`) starts a sequence through the same
test in `InitialiseSpotCam`, so it leaves the flags as the trigger does. A sequence whose
first camera does not track never sets `bTrackCamInit`, so its frames count exactly as
before, the title's flybys among them. `InitSpotCamSequences` (`game/spotcam.cpp:94`),
which `DoLevel` runs at every level start (`game/gameflow.cpp:1021`), clears the flag, so
a savegame loaded inside the corridor or a level left inside it starts clean. At *Frame
rate 30* `InterpAlphaNow` answers 1 (`game/interpolate.cpp:1152`-`1153`) and
`InterpBeginFrame` returns at `:1411`, before the cut test, the roll and the drawn-eye
rule; at *Frame rate 60* the frame that carries a tick returns there too. InterpTest's
`level_camera()` (`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/InterpTest.cpp:1157`) with `sim_call` and
`sim_walk` (`:1034`, `:1102`) holds the rule: the predicate; a walk at 165 frames to 30
ticks a second through a tracking sequence in which only the entry tick and the exit tick
cut; a call of two ticks inside the sequence; nothing outside a sequence; and a flyby that
does not track, which counts as with `bUseSpotCam` alone.

**Decisions.** The interpolator's cut rule changes for both control schemes, inside a
level camera sequence that tracks Lara at *Frame rate 60* and above, and nowhere else. The
repair is in the interpolator's reads of the flag, not in the upstream reset, which stays
as it is. Every read of the flag the interpolator makes goes through the one predicate,
the roll's included. So the draw-time readers of `bUseSpotCam` outside the interpolator
still see 0 between the ticks of such a sequence: `ModernLaraHidden` (`game/camera.cpp`)
then measures the camera, which stands far beyond the 122 units at which she is hidden,
and with the first person view on `FirstPersonActive` hides her head on the in-between
frames of such a sequence and shows it on the frames that carry a tick
(`specific/drawlara.cpp`, `specific/hd/hd_laradraw.cpp`). A cutscene that starts while a
tracking sequence holds the view runs with `bTrackCamInit` still set; where she then
stands off the sequence's tiles, the first tick after it counts one flyby cut, at a moment
the camera changes its type anyway.

### Particles on the same time axis
2026-09-07

**What.** Everything that moves but is not a body is drawn between two logic ticks as
well: the sparks, the fire and smoke sparks, the blood, the drips, the flying shards of a
smashed object, the rain, the snow, the underwater dust and the shockwave's expanding ring
are walked back from the state the game holds, while the gunshells, the rats, the bats,
the spiders, the bubbles and a rope Lara hangs from join the root snapshot.

**Why.** A particle does not need a snapshot, because it already carries what one would
have held: every particle simulation in this engine settles the velocity first and then
moves the position by it, so the stored velocity is the step the last tick took and
`previous position = current position - step` is exact rather than an estimate - a
thousand sparks and two thousand raindrops for a subtraction and no memory at all. The
walk is backwards and never forwards: `cur + vel * alpha` would draw the particle at tick
+ alpha, a whole logic step ahead of everything around it - sparks running out in front of
the gun that made them, rain falling through a floor that has not arrived yet - and it
would look perfectly smooth while doing it. The six that joined the snapshot have a place
but no usable step: a gunshell's bounce negates the fall speed and writes the position
back; rats, bats and spiders rewrite both the angle and the speed after the position
moves; a bubble's drift is a sine of a rotation that has already advanced; and a rope is a
constraint solve with no velocity in its drawn segments at all - and Lara hangs on it, so
an uninterpolated rope would leave her hands by half a step on every second frame.

**How.** `InterpTrailLong(cur, step, alpha) = InterpLerpLong(cur - step, cur, alpha)` in
`game/interpolate_math.h`, written as the snapshot's own lerp of a reconstructed previous
position and not as `cur - step * (1 - alpha)`: the two are the same algebra and not the
same integer, because a C cast truncates towards zero, and the wrong form is out on 16,384
of the 40,965 step pairs a TR5 particle can carry. Ten draw sites ask
`InterpParticleAlpha()` once before their loop and take no branch at all when it answers
1: `spark[1024]` (`S_DrawSparks`, `Xvel >> 5` plus the outdoor wind), `fire_spark[20]`,
`smoke_spark[32]`, `blood[32]` (`DrawBlood`), `Drips[32]` (`Yvel >> 5` and the wind if the
room is outside), `debris[256]` (`Speed * sin(Dir) >> W2V_SHIFT`, `Yvel >> 4`),
`Rain[1024]` (`xv + 4 * SmokeWindX`, `yv << 3`), `Snow[1024]` (`xv`, `(yv >> 1) & 0xFC`,
and nothing for a settled flake), `uwdust[256]` and `ShockWaves[16]` (the radius: `Speed`
and `Speed >> 1`) - all in `specific/specificfx.cpp`, with `game/tomb4fx.cpp` and
`game/draw.cpp` beside them. Two thirds of the spark array hangs off an item or an effect
and stores an offset from a body the root snapshot has already blended; the walk back is
applied to the finished world position, which is the same number as blending both halves,
and leaves the "let go of the thing you came off" code above it writing the live position,
which is game state. `Gunshells[24]`, `Rats[32]`, `Bats[64]`, `Spiders[64]`, `Bubbles[40]`
and `RopeList[8]` with 24 links each cost 16.7 KB of statics - 10.1 for the 184 movers
with their pointer table, 1.2 for the bubbles, 5.6 for the ropes, taking the whole
snapshot to about 44 KB - and not one line of their own drawing code: `DrawGunshells`,
`DrawRats`, `DrawBats`, `DrawSpiders`, `DrawBubbles` and `DrawRope` read the same globals
and find the blended values. They carry the root's snap rule, and "was this slot alive on
the last tick" is their identity test, because a bubble slot is freed by writing its size
to zero and handed straight to the next bubble. Deliberately left at thirty: the
lightning, because `UpdateLightning` re-rolls its segments out of the random generator on
every tick, so a bolt's previous shape is a different bolt and blending them would draw a
shape the game never draws; a shard's tumble, whose two rotations are unsigned bytes
shifted up by eight and would wrap the wrong way half the time (where it flies is
interpolated); and splashes and ripples, whose vertical term steps its velocity on the
same line as the position and whose life is decremented in two places, so the walk back is
not exact. Two approximations are marked where they are made: a snowflake's sideways drift
is ramped towards the wind after it has moved, and a dust mote's sink is a quantised
reading of a field stepped after the move - a unit or two out of a step of sixty-odd, on a
sprite four pixels wide. `INTERPLOG` carries `particles=` and `particle_kinds=`, one bit
per draw site, because a guard that never fires looks exactly like thirty hertz and there
is no other way to see it.

**Commits.** `8975d1d`

### Every per-frame counter on the logic tick
2026-09-07 - 2026-09-09

**What.** Every counter in the engine that measured time in drawn frames steps once per
logic tick, so a death fade, a rain shower, a level caption, a footprint and a corpse last
exactly as many seconds at sixty as at thirty. One criterion serves all of them:
`InterpIsTweenFrame()` (`game/interpolate.h`, `game/interpolate.cpp`) is true when the
frame being drawn carries no logic tick, and every guarded counter steps only when it is
false. At `fps_mode 0` it is false always, so the thirty hertz behaviour is the old
behaviour line for line. `DoScreenFade` also clamps the walked fade value to the fade's
end value once the step has carried it past (`InterpFadeClamp`,
`game/interpolate_math.h`).

**Why.** A counter stepped per drawn frame runs at double speed the moment the engine
presents twice as often. The latch is set from the cadence rather than from `alpha < 1`,
because a cutscene frame and a frame with no previous state are drawn live and still carry
no tick, so every fade through every cutscene would otherwise have run at double speed. It
lives for the whole loop iteration and not just the draw, because two counters sit outside
`DrawPhaseGame` - `gfLegendTime--` before it and `cutseq_busy_timeout--` after it - one
reading the previous frame's latch and one this frame's. It is false in every modal loop:
`S_DumpScreen` calls `InterpNoteClassicPresent()` whenever the present it is about to make
waited the full two ticks and `S_DumpScreenFrame` calls it always, without which a modal
loop entered straight after an in-between frame would inherit a `true` nothing inside it
could clear, and `RenderLoadPic`'s `do { ... } while (DoFade != 2)`
(`specific/output.cpp`) would never end, `DoScreenFade` being the only thing in the build
that sets `DoFade` to 2. The fade clamp is the one place where stepping on the tick was
not enough: `SetFade(start, end)` (`specific/specificfx.cpp`) sets `FadeStep = (end -
start) >> 3` and `DoScreenFade` walks `FadeVal` by it once per logic tick, reading `a =
FadeVal << 24` before the step and, on the ninth call, putting `FadeEnd` over `a`; for the
fade-in every level starts with - `SetFade(255, 0)`, from `DoLevel`, `DoTitle` and
`RenderLoadPic` in `game/gameflow.cpp` - the step is -32 and the eighth step lands on 255
- 256 = -1, which shifted into the colour is `0xFF000000`, alpha 255, black. At thirty
presents a second that value is read exactly once, by the ninth call, which overrides it;
above thirty every in-between frame between the eighth and the ninth tick drew it, so
every fade-in carried one whole logic tick of full black, two frames at sixty, 33 ms. The
fade-out direction (`SetFade(0, 255)`, step 31) lands on 248 and never overshoots, and
`Fade()`'s grey tile clamps inside its own step.

**How.** The counters and where they are: `Fade()` (`game/tomb4fx.cpp`) - the grey walks
on a tick, the tile is drawn every frame; `DoScreenFade()` (`specific/specificfx.cpp`) -
nine steps on nine ticks, `a` read before the step so the in-between frame draws the same
grey, and `InterpFadeClamp` applied right after the step; `FlashFader -= 2`
(`specific/output.cpp`) - `DrawFlash()` every frame, the walk on a tick; `FlashIt()` and
`DrawPickups()` (`game/health.cpp`), the second the whole slide-in animation, returning
early; the sky lightning machine and `aWibble++` (`game/draw.cpp`); rain and snow
(`specific/specificfx.cpp`) - the simulation loop on the tick, the draw loop every frame;
a spark letting go of its item - the random threshold rolled on the tick;
`GnFrameCounter++` (`specific/output.cpp`) - on the tick in a game frame, per present in a
modal loop; `RegeneratePickups()` moved from above `ControlPhase`'s loop into the tick
body (`game/control.cpp`); `gfLegendTime--` (`game/gameflow.cpp`); `cutseq_busy_timeout--`
(`game/deltapak.cpp`); `ammo_change_timer--` and `PoisonFlag--` (`game/health.cpp`); the
F12 bump-mapping debounce (`specific/output.cpp`); the underwater dust simulation
`DoUwEffect` and the gas cloud's `yo`/`sTime`/`mTime` in `DrawGasCloud`
(`specific/specificfx.cpp`); `print->Active--` (`game/footprnt.cpp`); the monitor screens'
scan band in `DoMonitorScreen` (`specific/file.cpp`). The resolution caption's
`resChangeCounter` (`specific/output.cpp`) counts 120 logic ticks, which is vanilla's own
120 frames at thirty; it is the one deliberate difference at `fps_mode 0`, and it is the
version that cannot leave the caption standing (a step scaled by a measured rate truncates
to zero above the target). Two per-frame rolls are deliberately left: the enemy muzzle
flash's random Z rotation (`DrawBaddieGunFlash`, `game/objects.cpp`) and the steel door's
lens flare colour (`DrawSteelDoorLensFlare`, `game/tower.cpp`), as is Lara's cutscene
speech head (`game/deltapak.cpp`) - the rule is that a counter carrying state or a cadence
is guarded and pure noise is not. The corpse fade left the draw path entirely:
`PrintObjects` (`game/draw.cpp`) only marks the bodies it drew, one byte per item slot,
and `StepAfterDeathFade()` (`game/draw.cpp`, called from `ControlPhase`) does the counting
and the killing. That also removes a latent bug - `KillItem` was being called from inside
the walk of the room's own item list, and for a spawned item (`item_num >= level_items`)
it ends with `item->next_item = next_item_free; next_item_free = item_num;`
(`game/items.cpp`), rewriting the very link the loop was about to follow. Only bodies in a
room that was actually drawn age at all, exactly as at thirty, which is why the tick does
not sweep all 512 slots; the mark is wider than the old increment (`after_death > 0`)
because the skeleton writes that field directly (`game/skeleton.cpp`). The dead test
`!(wibble & 3)` is left dead on purpose: `ControlPhase` steps `wibble = (wibble + 4) &
0xFC`, so it is always true, and repairing it would change how long every body in the game
lies there. The fade clamp changes no thirty hertz picture, the ninth tick having drawn
`end` anyway, and `fps_mode 0` is byte-identical by the same arithmetic; `SetFade(255, 0)`
runs at a level start, at the title and at the loading picture and nowhere else, so a
black frame anywhere else is a different fault. Noted and not changed: `S_DrawLoadBar`
(`specific/drawbars.cpp`) draws only the bar onto whatever the back buffer holds and
presents, with `D3DSWAPEFFECT_DISCARD` and one back buffer (`specific/dxshell.cpp`), whose
content after a present the D3D9 contract calls undefined. `TICKLOG`, one line a logic
second under `-log`, prints the guarded counters so that the same line comes out of a
thirty and a sixty hertz run of the same scene.
`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/InterpTest.cpp`, section `fade`, holds the rule: the nine
ticks of 255 -> 0 and of 0 -> 255 draw what they always drew, the eighth step of 255 -> 0
lands on -1 unclamped and the frame after it now draws 0, the eighth step of 0 -> 255
stays 248, and -1 shifted into the colour is alpha 255.

**Commits.** `9b4f7b8`, `ab139d8`, `e0448e4`, `89e93ca`

### The inventory ring at the frame rate
2026-09-15

**What.** The inventory ring presents at the rate the option asks for and keeps its logic
at thirty steps a second. `S_CallInventory2` (`game/newinv2.cpp`) keeps its own modal loop
and its own present, and that present asks for `InvFrameMinTicks()`
(`game/inventory_interp.cpp`), `gPresentMinTicks` being raised around that present only
and put straight back to two. The loop body runs its logic once per two ticks through an
accumulator of `ControlPhase`'s shape (`InvInterpBeginFrame`), and on a frame with no step
the spin of the selected icon, the brightness ramp, the row slide, the two ring fades, the
ammo selector's fade and spin and the examine zoom are blended, while every discrete value
is held. Nothing else moved: the pause screen, the load and save screens, the death menu,
the F4 outfit screen and the loading fade still wait their two ticks, and the randomizer
is untouched.

**Why.** At sixty the ring was the one thing on screen still presenting at thirty. The
accumulator is clamped to one step's worth of credit, with one difference from
`ControlPhase` that is written out where it lives: the ring's body draws as it steps, so
the step can run at most once per frame, and a hitch that banked four steps would
otherwise make the ring step on every frame until the debt was paid - the ring running at
the frame rate, which is what this change exists to stop. The blended values are handed to
the draw at the read rather than written into the ring, because `draw_current_object_list`
steps and draws in one pass: the spin and the brightness sit inside the very loop that
draws each icon and the slide is stepped at the bottom of the same function, so a value
written before that body is stepped over by the body itself and one written after it is
too late for the picture. It is the step frame that is blended: in the game the draw comes
before the tick and the drawn states are `T1, mid(T1,T2), T2`, while in the ring the step
comes before the draw, so the same arrangement would draw `C1, mid(C0,C1), C2` - a picture
walking backwards on every second frame. The factor the ring's accumulator produces
through `InterpRefreshAlpha` is 0.5 on the frame whose step ran and 1.0 on the next, which
is the even, monotone order.

**How.** `game/inventory_interp.cpp` and `game/inventory_interp.h` hold the snapshot and
nine accessors, each returning the live value whenever there is nothing to blend. Six take
the previous generation and the live one - the values vanilla steps before it draws them;
three - the row slide, the current slot and the ammo fade - take the two previous
generations, because their subject has already been stepped by the loop that draws it,
which keeps each of them exactly one step behind the spin, the relation they have at
thirty. On a tween frame `S_UpdateInput` is not called and `input`, `dbinput` and the six
`go_` flags of `do_debounced_joystick_poo` are shadowed to zero and restored;
`GameTimer++` (the stats page's clock, `GameTimer / 30`), `UpdatePulseColour`
(`game/text.cpp`), the keymap cheats, `GnFrameCounter`, `objlistmovement` and
`curobjinlist`, `combine_ring_fade_val` and `normal_ring_fade_val`,
`ammo_selector_fade_val`, `examine_mode`, `stats_mode`, `keypadpause--` with its six
tones, and every discrete piece of state are held; `LookCnt` and `med_hotkey_timer` step
once per logic step, which is the rate they had. The ring raises the build's own tween
latch for itself (`InterpNoteMenuFrame`, `game/interpolate.cpp`) now that its present no
longer comes through `InterpNoteClassicPresent`, so `Fade`, `FlashFader`, `DoScreenFade`,
the F12 debounce and `resChangeCounter` inside `S_OutputPolyList` (`specific/output.cpp`)
stay guarded. The row's slot and its offset are taken from one generation (`InvDrawCur` /
`InterpRingSlot`), because the step that puts `objlistmovement` back to 0 moves
`curobjinlist` in the same breath and a frame drawing the new slot with the old offset put
the whole row seven eighths of a slot to the side; a slot left over from a list that has
since been rebuilt falls back to the live one, and the option list under the row keeps the
live slot, which is the relation it already has at thirty. `InvInterpCut` drops the
snapshot so that the next step frame draws live on opening or closing a mode, the ammo
ring taking over, the combine ring being built, the list being rebuilt by a combine, a
separate or a weapon hot key, the load/save screen, and opening and closing the ring
itself; a rebuilt list needs no call site, each slot's `invitem` travelling in the
snapshot. `INVLOG` (new, `-log` only, behind `gLogEnabled`) writes an open line, one line
per logic second with `frames=`, `steps=`, `tween=`, `alpha=min/max`, `budget=`, `blend=`
and `cuts=`, a cut line with its reason, and a close line; `blend=` names the motions that
really blended, because a field that never blends simply looks like thirty.
`InterpRingStep`, `InterpRingAlpha`, `InterpRingSlide` and `InterpRingSlot` live in
`game/interpolate_math.h` so that the offline test runs the engine's own arithmetic.

### The title menu at the frame rate, one tap one row
2026-09-07 - 2026-09-15

**What.** The title screen is drawn at the rate the option asks for, with its fly-by
interpolated through the normal draw path, and one tap of a direction still moves one row
on every page it reaches. On the call in which the menu would read an edge for the second
time, its input is shadowed: `input` and `dbinput` are put aside, zeroed for the length of
that one call and put back byte for byte the moment it returns (`TitleInputShadow`,
`game/gameflow.cpp`).

**Why.** `DoTitle`'s loop is `TitleOptions(); DrawPhaseGame(); ControlPhase(nframes);`, so
the menu is walked once per present while the debounced input it walks with, `dbinput`, is
written once per tick inside `ControlPhase`'s tick loop (`specific/input.cpp`) and nowhere
else. At two ticks per present the two rates are the same and every edge is read exactly
once; at one, every second `ControlPhase` runs no tick, `dbinput` keeps standing and the
next `TitleOptions` reads the same press again - one tap of Down moved the cursor two rows
and *New Game* could not be selected. A menu only has to be told which of its calls is
reading an edge for the second time, which costs it no frames. The shadow is restored
rather than left zeroed for a reason the code really has: `SetDebounce` is cleared inside
the first tick of a `ControlPhase` call (`game/control.cpp`), so a call that runs three
ticks writes `dbinput` on one of them and a zero left behind would swallow the edge for
the other two.

**How.** The question is asked of the engine's own tick counter and not of a clock of its
own: `g_tickSerial` steps once per logic tick at every frame rate and is readable as
`InterpTickSerial()` (`game/interpolate.cpp`, `game/interpolate.h`), so the rule holds at
`fps_mode 1`, at `fps_mode 2` where four or five frames fall inside one tick, on the first
iteration after `DoTitle`'s priming `ControlPhase` and through a hitch.
`GameFrameMinTicks()` (`specific/output.cpp`) therefore gives the title what it gives a
played frame - the `InventoryActive` test remains as the guard for any future path into
`DrawPhaseGame` from a menu - and the fly-by is drawn through `DrawPhaseGame` with the
root and camera interpolation underneath it. Everything `TitleOptions` reaches steps on
`dbinput`, which the shadow covers: the level select, the whole options tree and the
options pages; `JoyMenuStep` has a latch of its own and the two direct `keymap` reads in
the key-mapping screen are idempotent. One counter behind the title needed the guard the
rest of the build has: `DoCredits`' roll (`StartPos--`, `specific/alexstuff.cpp`) is one
pixel a present and asks `InterpIsTweenFrame()` now.
