### The cut scenes at the frame rate
2026-09-28

**What.** A cut scene is drawn between its steps like the game around it. The camera's eye
and target are blended between the last two ticks by the interpolator's own camera block,
and every actor - Lara, actor 0, included - is drawn from its node table blended between
the same two ticks: `game/cutseq_interp.cpp` copies the decoded tables at the start of the
tick, writes the blend into them before `DrawPhaseGame` draws and puts the tick's values
back after it. A cut in a camera track (the eye or the target stepping more than 256
units) draws the frame live, an actor whose root jumps more than 1024 is drawn at the
tick's values while the others glide, and a node with an axis exactly half a turn from its
previous value keeps the tick's three values. The braid, which a cut scene swings inside
the draw, swings once per tick. New: `game/cutseq_interp.cpp` and `.h`,
`game/cutseq_decode.h` (the track decoder, lifted unchanged out of `game/deltapak.cpp` so
that a tool compiles it), `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/CutseqProbe.cpp` with `bcp.bat`, the
`-log` seam `CUTLOG`, and a `cutseq` section in `InterpTest`.

**Why.** At sixty and at 165 hertz every cut scene stepped at thirty - camera, actors and
Lara - while `FPSLOG` presented sixty or 165 pictures a second, because `InterpBeginFrame`
returned at `GLOBAL_playing_cutseq`. The return was there because the cut scene camera is
decoded from a frame index and `frigup_lara` moves Lara inside `DrawPhaseGame`, so a
restore was taken to undo it. That does not hold: `DecodeAnim` is the only writer of the
actors' node values (`xrot_run`, `yrot_run`, `zrot_run`), and their only readers are
`do_new_cutscene_camera` (the camera's two nodes) and `updateAnimFrame`, which
`DrawCutSeqActors`, `frigup_lara`, `GrabActorMatrix` and `GetActorJointAbsPosition` call -
the last two only from the scenes' control routines, inside the tick. The decoder keeps
its own state per node (`RTDECODE`) and only the tick advances it, so the decoded outputs
of two ticks can be blended and restored like `items[]`, and the tick sequence is the one
a thirty hertz run has. The tracks cut as a film cuts: over the 44 cut scenes of
`DATA/CUTSEQ.BIN`, `CutseqProbe` counts 371 camera cuts in 33 cut scenes (0.48 % of the
steps), the smallest a jump of 294 units, while the eye's 99th percentile is 78 units a
frame and the fastest drive 222 a frame (cut scene 30) - so 256 parts every cut from every
motion; 35 of the cuts step no more than 1024 on both the eye and the target, so a 1024
Manhattan rule on the two would have blended them as motion. The braid was a live fault of
its own: `frigup_lara` runs `HairControl` once per drawn frame, so at sixty and 165 the
braid's simulation ran two to five and a half times per tick.

**How.** The snapshot is `g_prev` and `g_saved`, x, y and z per node for ten actors of up
to forty nodes, 2,400 bytes each; the largest actor in the file has 30 nodes and the
largest scene 115. `CutseqInterpOpen` (`game/cutseq_interp.cpp:132`) is called at the end
of `init_cutseq_actors` (`game/deltapak.cpp:3578`), after the tables are laid out, and
invalidates the whole interpolation (`InterpInvalidate("cutseq open")`);
`CutseqInterpClose` (`:170`) at the teardown in `handle_cutseq_triggering`
(`game/deltapak.cpp:2237`), before the next credits scene opens; `CutseqInterpSkip`
(`:188`) at the end of `do_cutseq_skipper_stuff` (`game/deltapak.cpp:3723`).
`CutseqCapturePrev` (`:200`) runs in `InterpCapturePrev` beside the hair capture
(`game/interpolate.cpp:1007`), at the start of the tick and so before
`do_new_cutscene_camera` (`game/camera.cpp:1413`) decodes; a capture before frame 0 was
decoded leaves no previous table. `InterpBeginFrame` asks `CutseqBlendable` (`:226`) where
the return stood (`game/interpolate.cpp:1366`) - the scene's first tick is drawn live -
then `CutseqCameraCut` (`:247`, `game/interpolate.cpp:1404`) beside `CameraCut`, and after
`g_applied` is set `CutseqApply` (`:270`, `game/interpolate.cpp:1429`), so
`InterpParticleAlpha` and `InterpEyeRoom` take the blended frame as on any other;
`CutseqRestore` (`:335`) runs in `InterpEndFrame`'s restore block
(`game/interpolate.cpp:1743`) and in `CutseqInterpInvalidate` (`:194`, called from
`InterpInvalidate`, `game/interpolate.cpp:1863`), because the decoder adds its next deltas
to whatever the tables hold. The order in the game loop is `InterpBeginFrame`
(`game/draw.cpp:466`), `frigup_lara` (`:476`), `DrawRooms` (`:480`) with
`DrawCutSeqActors` inside it (`:2489`), `InterpEndFrame` (`:518`); `DoLevel` draws at
`game/gameflow.cpp:1153` and ticks at `:1172`, `DoTitle`, which plays the credits, at
`:923` and `:925`. The arithmetic is in `game/interpolate_math.h` so that `InterpTest`
runs it: `INTERP_CUTSEQ_SNAP` 256 (`:150`, beside `INTERP_CAM_SNAP`),
`INTERP_CUTSEQ_ROOT_SNAP` 1024, `INTERP_CUTSEQ_ACTORS` 10 and `INTERP_CUTSEQ_NODES` 40
(`:2000`-`:2002`), `InterpLerpAngle10` (`:2007`, the difference folded into -512..511 and
the result masked to ten bits), `InterpHalfTurn10` (`:2014`, a difference of exactly 512),
`InterpCutseqCameraCut` (`:2022`, eye and target measured apart), `InterpCutseqRootStep`
(`:2034`, node 0 at three times its value, as `updateAnimFrame` draws it) and
`InterpCutseqBlend` (`:2051`: the root blended as a position, every other node as three
ten-bit angles, a node with a half-turned axis kept whole at the tick's values). Two rules
of the camera block are left out of a cut scene: the drawn-eye rule
(`game/interpolate.cpp:1681`), because a cut scene camera's room comes from
`IsRoomOutside`, which matches no room within a sector of a room's walls and keeps the old
one, so the rule would withhold the sky; and the braid's blend (`:1490`), because the
snapshot is taken before the draw steps the braid and the frames after the step would pull
it back. The braid's guard is `if (!InterpIsTweenFrame())` around the two `HairControl`
calls in `frigup_lara` (`game/deltapak.cpp:3289`). `InitPackNodes`, `GetTrackWord`,
`DecodeTrack` and `DecodeAnim` (`game/deltapak.cpp:2917`-`:2935`) forward to the templates
`CutseqInitPackNodes`, `CutseqTrackWord`, `CutseqDecodeTrack` and `CutseqDecodeAnim` in
`game/cutseq_decode.h`, which hold their bodies unchanged and include no engine header.
The seams, `-log` only: `CUTLOG open cutseq=17 frames=2097 actors=3 nodes=48 fps_mode=1`;
`CUTLOG cut cutseq=25 frame=1622 why=camera eye=27494 target=30686 actor=-1 node=-1
step=-1` once per cut tick (`why=` also `actor` with the root step, `halfturn` with the
node, `open`, `skip`, `close`; `frame=` is the index `DecodeAnim` decoded); `CUTLOG close
cutseq=17 frames=4194 ticks=2097 blended=2084 live=2110 cuts=12 actor_cuts=1 halfturns=3
hair=2097 eye_rooms=- hair_lag=69` as `CutseqProbe -cutlog 17` predicts it (the tool
prints `-` for `eye_rooms=`, which needs the level's rooms), where `hair=` counts the
braid's steps (`CutseqNoteHair`, `game/deltapak.cpp:3296`), `eye_rooms=` the blended
frames whose room walk starts in another room than the tick's
(`game/interpolate.cpp:1182`) and `hair_lag=` how far Lara's blended root stood from her
previous tick's, which is how far the braid trails. `INTERPLOG`'s `cutscene=` keeps its
place and now counts frames between two ticks of a cut scene drawn live for a reason that
is not a cut (an actor larger than the snapshot, a scene never opened), nought in a
healthy log; `cutscene_cut=` at the end of the line counts the frames a cut scene camera's
cut drew live. `CutseqProbe` (`bcp.bat`, x86 like `SaveDiff`, because it instantiates the
decoder with `global/types.h`'s structs) reads a `cutseq.bin` in place, decodes every cut
scene with `game/cutseq_decode.h` and measures it with `game/interpolate_math.h`; `-frames
<n> <a> <b>` prints the decoded eye, target and roots, `-cutlog <n>` the `CUTLOG` lines a
run at sixty writes. `InterpTest`'s section `cutseq`
(`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/InterpTest.cpp:5522`) holds the rule: ten-bit angles across
the wrap (1000 to 24 and 24 to 1000 land on 0, every 0.5 blend of a 147 x 205 sweep lies
on the shorter arc), the half turn refused, the cut rule at 255, 256 and 257 with eye and
target apart, the root test at 1023 and 1026 drawn units, and the apply-and-restore round
trip on a four-node table. At `fps_mode 0` every new call that writes a node table sits
behind `alpha >= 1`, which returns before the cut scene branch, or behind `g_applied`, and
`InterpIsTweenFrame()` is false, so the braid steps on every frame as before. The decoder
and the tick sequence are those of a thirty hertz run, so `TICKLOG` reads the same at
every setting.

**Decisions.** The decoded outputs of the last two ticks are blended, not a snapshot of
two generations: the draw comes before the tick in `DoLevel` and `DoTitle`, so the
previous tick and the live tables are the pair. The camera needs no snapshot of its own:
`g_prevCam` is filled every tick in a cut scene too, and the camera block with
`RebuildView` blends it. A cut in the track is a step of the eye or the target above 256
Manhattan. An actor's root jumping above 1024 draws that actor live. An exact half turn on
a node axis draws that node at the tick's values, all three axes, because the other axes
of such a node turn with it. The credits are cut scenes like the others. The drawn-eye
rule and the braid's blend are left out of cut scenes. The braid steps once per tick and
is drawn where the tick left it, so on a frame between two ticks it trails Lara, at sixty
by half her step and at the display's rate by up to a whole step; `hair_lag=` bounds it
from above. No root threshold parts every jump from motion: a lone jump under 1024 without
a camera cut is blended as a slide for one tick.

### The level warm-up
2026-09-07

**What.** `WarmUpLevel()` (`specific/file.cpp`) runs after the load thread has joined and
the HD build is done, with the loading bar still on screen, and calls
`IDirect3DResource9::PreLoad` for every classic texture page (`specific/texture.cpp`,
`CreateTexturePage`), every HD page slot (`HDPageCacheSlotTexture`) and every HD model's
vertex and index buffer (`HDModelPreload`, new in `specific/hd/hd_model.cpp` and
`specific/hd/hd_model.h`). `PreTouchDrawBuffers()` (`specific/polyinsert.cpp`) writes
through `SortBuffer` (2.5 MB), `SortList` (256 KB) and `Bucket` (30 x 2080 vertices, 2.4
MB) from the same place. One line goes into the log: `WARMUP pages=112 hd_pages=143
hd_buffers=94 ms=38.2`.

**Why.** Nearly every texture in this engine is `D3DPOOL_MANAGED`, and a managed resource
lives in system memory until something draws with it - Direct3D uploads it at that first
bind, so the frame that first shows a wall, a texture or an enemy pays for the upload, and
a level shows most of its art in its first seconds. `PreLoad` is Direct3D's own answer to
that: it draws nothing, touches no render state, costs nothing for a resident resource and
is documented to be ignored for one in `D3DPOOL_DEFAULT`. The three draw buffers are plain
statics living in `.bss`, which Windows hands out as demand-zero pages - roughly 1300
first-write faults, every one of them in the first frame that draws anything. Writing
through them cannot change a pixel: `InitBuckets` and `InitialiseSortList` reset all three
at the top of every frame, and nothing reads a byte of any of them that was not written in
the same frame first. What the pass cannot cover is named rather than guessed at - the
water mark tables, a room's first light list, the driver's first use of a shader or a
vertex declaration, and Windows paging the process in.

**How.** The warm-up runs in every frame-rate mode, being by construction unable to change
what is drawn. Its numbers and the `first_frame` and low-`sec=` late lines that answer for
the rest are documented with the profile seams.

### The frame-rate seams and the offline proofs
2026-09-07 - 2026-09-15

**What.** New files `specific/profile.cpp` and `specific/profile.h` carry `PROFLOG`, a
per-frame breakdown taken with `QueryPerformanceCounter` in seventeen phases: `logic`
(`ControlPhase`, timed at its call site in `game/gameflow.cpp` because `ControlPhase` has
early returns), `gather`, `rooms`, `sky`, the HD path's three shares of the gather
(`hdroom` in `InsertRoom`, `hdobj` in `HDObjectBegin`/`Node`/`End`, `hdlara` in
`HDLaraDrawFrame`), `output` with `hddraw`, `hdlight`, `hdobjdraw` and `hdglow` inside it,
`buckets`, `sort` and `sortdraw` as whole-frame totals, and the present split into `spin`
(the frame finished and waiting for its slot) and `flip` (`Present` itself). It writes one
line a second with mean and worst per phase, one line for every frame that missed its slot
with all its phases and the second of the level it happened in, one `first_frame` line per
level, and a short line for an interval that presented nothing of the loop's own - `pause
at=<s>s frame=<ms> work=<ms> presents=<n>`. `FPSLOG` (`specific/hd/hd_level.cpp`) carries
`fps=` (the rate the budget was taken from), `logic_ticks=` (`GlobalCounter`'s difference
over the second), `budget=` (the slot the frame was judged against) and `real_fps=` (the
rate worked out from the mean present interval). `TICKLOG`, `INTERPLOG` and `INVLOG` each
write one line per logic second. All of it is behind `-log`.

**Why.** A frame count cannot say where a frame's milliseconds went. The budget must be
the slot the frame really waited for and not what `fps_mode` says, because only the game
frame's own present ever drops below two ticks - measured against `fps_mode` alone, every
menu second reported thirty slow frames and up to thirty late ones. An interval of 5516 ms
whose own work was 32 ms is not a slow frame but a loop that was somewhere else, so those
are counted as pauses, never as late, and are kept out of the second's mean and maximum. A
logic second is the unit for `TICKLOG`, `INTERPLOG` and `INVLOG` because `GlobalCounter`
steps thirty times a second by construction in both modes and stands still while the ring
is up, so the same line has to come out of a thirty and a sixty hertz run of the same
scene: a number that doubles is a counter that was missed, one that halves is a guard that
also stopped a tick frame.

**How.** Every seam is `ProfBegin(...)` / `ProfEnd(...)`, both of which are `if
(gLogEnabled)` around a call, so without `-log` not one clock is read, no accumulator
moves and no string is built. `ProfPresent()` sits in both present functions
(`specific/output.cpp`), so the profile knows how many pictures went out during an
interval and recognises a modal loop drawing behind its back; an interval that exceeds its
own work by more than a second catches what presents nothing at all. `buckets`, `sort` and
`sortdraw` are whole-frame totals because each is called from three or more places;
`SkyDrawPhase` has a phase of its own because it is the one place in the frame that draws
buckets and a sort list outside `S_OutputPolyList`, which makes the printed remainder
`outrest = output - hddraw - hdglow`. `sort` and `sortdraw` are separate phases because
`SortPolyList` is a quicksort and `DrawSortList` is vertex copying and `DrawPrimitiveUP`,
and the line carries `sortn=`, how many entries the list held. `PROF_LOGIC` is
deliberately not cleared by `ProfileFrameBegin`, because `ControlPhase` runs between the
present and that call; `ProfileFrameEnd` clears it once it has reported it and once the
second's totals have taken it. The definition is written down in `specific/profile.h` and
in `docs/Engine-Manual.md`: the loop is draw, present, logic, so the game step that
follows a frame is counted into the next frame's line, `logic` is not part of `work`
(`ProfileFrameBegin` to `ProfileFrameEnd`), and the invariant to check a log against is
`work + logic <= frame`. `FrameBudgetMs()` / `MissedSlotMs()` (`specific/hd/hd_level.cpp`
and `specific/profile.cpp`) read `gPresentMinTicks` at the moment the frame is judged,
which is why `DrawPhaseGame` (`game/draw.cpp`) restores the two after `ProfileFrameEnd`;
`PresentSlotMs()` (`specific/output.cpp`) is the single definition both logs call, so they
cannot disagree about a frame whose slot is the panel's period rather than a whole number
of ticks. `INTERPLOG` (`game/interpolate.cpp`, with the ring's own line in
`game/inventory_interp.cpp`) carries `lara_step`, how far Lara moved on screen from one
picture to the next, measured on the position that was drawn rather than the one the logic
holds - over the same walk it must read half at sixty what it reads at thirty - and
`alpha=` is a `min/mean/max` distribution, because bound to the display every frame has a
factor of its own and a maximum pinned at 1.00 is the clamp firing. Two offline tools
stand beside the logs: `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/SaveDiff.cpp` (`bsd.bat`) compares two
savegames field by field by name, taking every offset from the engine's own
`global/types.h` with `offsetof`, which is why it is built for Win32 - the structs are
`#pragma pack(1)` but carry pointers; and `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/InterpTest.cpp`
(`bit.bat`) includes `game/interpolate_math.h` itself rather than a copy, so there is no
twin to keep in step. It asserts the short-angle lerp over a sweep of 16,256 angle pairs
with the 128 exact half-turns stepped over and asserted separately, the position lerp over
a level's whole coordinate range, the snap thresholds against the engine's own speeds, the
cadence over a simulated minute at both settings and through a hitch, the counter rule at
both rates including the nine-step screen fade, the pose factor against the four
hard-wired branches it replaced over 441 matrix element pairs for every `(frac, rate)` the
retail levels can produce - 336,471 animation frames' worth, maximum difference 0 units on
both stacks - the pose in time at rates 1, 2, 4 and 5, the display-bound loop at 60, 120
and 144 Hz with the vblanks on their own grid and their own phase (ten simulated seconds
run 300 logic steps against 600, 1200 and 1440 frames, the factor never clamped, no frame
drawing what the one before it drew, and a 200 ms hitch caught up less the two ticks
vanilla's own `if (nframes > 10)` cap discards), the particle walk-back against an item
whose previous state really is remembered, and the ring's cadence and the title's shadow.
The recipes are in `docs/Engine-Manual.md` under *Frame rate*.

### The zoom at the frame rate (#225)
2026-10-19

**What.** The binoculars' and the sights' zoom is drawn between two logic ticks like the
camera: on a frame between two ticks of a zoom the field of view lies between the two
ticks' values at the frame's alpha, so at 165 Hz every frame of a zoom draws a value of
its own. `InterpCapturePrev` (`game/interpolate.cpp`) keeps `BinocularRange` and
`CurrentFov` before the tick; `InterpBeginFrame` sets the blended field of view after the
camera's blend; `SkyDrawPhase`'s three `AlterFOV` calls (`game/draw.cpp`) go through the
new `InterpZoomFOV`, which blends the range at the same alpha for the sky's `GAME_FOV -
range` and the view's `GAME_FOV - 7 * range`; `InterpEndFrame` sets the field of view the
classic code would have left. The rule is two inline functions in `game/modern_camera.h`,
`ModernCameraZoomTweens` and `ModernCameraZoomLerp`. `ALTERFOV` ends with `alpha` and
`tween`, `INTERPLOG` with `zoom=`.

**Why.** In the display-bound mode (`fps_mode` 2) on a 165 Hz display the zoom of the
revolver's and the HK's sight still ran at 30 FPS and stuttered while zooming in and out.
The interpolator blended the eye, the target and the roll, the poison sway, Lara's pose
and root, the arms and the nine aim angles, the items, effects, braid, particles and
ropes, but not the field of view: every frame of a tick drew one value and the next frame
jumped by a whole step of the zoom.

**How.** The zoom as the classic code runs it, once per tick: `BinocularCamera`
(`camera.cpp`, `BinocStep`) steps the range by 64, or 32 with the walk key, under the duck
key (in) or the sprint key (out), and clamps it to 128 to 1536; the view's field of view
is `GAME_FOV - 7 * BinocularRange`, from the range before the tick's step; `SkyDrawPhase`
sets the sky's own, `GAME_FOV - BinocularRange`, and back to `7 *` after the sky, on each
frame from the tick's range. One step of the range is 7 x 64 = 448 units of the view's
field of view, 2.46 degrees (182 units a degree); with the walk key 224. The entry sets
the range from 0 to 128 (`control.cpp`, the three sights; `newinv2.cpp`, the binoculars),
the exit sets it to 0 and calls `AlterFOV(GAME_FOV)` (`control.cpp` for a sight,
`camera.cpp` for the binoculars). Everything `AlterFOV` feeds follows the value it is
given: `phd_persp`, `f_persp`, `f_mpersp` and their inverses, which the classic and the HD
paths project with (the HD rooms take `f_persp` when they are collected, the HD sky and
the pickup display when they draw). `ModernCameraNearRadius` is computed in the chase and
first person cameras only and is not reached while the binoculars run. The rule: a frame
between two ticks draws the zoom between them when the zoom ran at both ticks (both ranges
at least 128) and both ticks' fields of view are a zoom's (at most `GAME_FOV - 7 * 128`);
it then draws `from + (to - from) * alpha`, the camera's own `InterpLerpLong` arithmetic,
with `from` and `to` the field of view before and after the tick for the frame's first
value, and `GAME_FOV - factor * range` before and after for `SkyDrawPhase`'s. At alpha 1
the value is `to`: a frame on a tick draws the tick's own. A blended value that equals the
classic one is set as the classic call sets it. `InterpEndFrame` sets the last classic
value again when a blended one was set, so the next tick finds `phd_persp` as a 30 Hz run
leaves it. At `fps_mode` 0 `InterpBeginFrame` returns at `alpha >= 1` before the zoom,
`g_zoomOn` stays false, `InterpZoomFOV` calls `AlterFOV(short(GAME_FOV - factor *
BinocularRange))`, the expression `SkyDrawPhase` passed before, and `InterpEndFrame` sets
nothing: no byte changes. The same holds on every frame at alpha 1, on a camera cut and on
the first frame after an invalidation. Outdoors the frame's room walk still projects with
the value from before the sky, as at thirty; between two ticks the two values now lie
closer. RoomProbe's log reader takes the last `ALTERFOV` line before a walk dump, on a
blended frame the blended value the walk used. InterpTest's group `zoom` holds the rule:
the blend at alpha 0, 0.5, 1 and 1.5, the steps of 448 and 224 out and in, the clamp's
ends 3808 and 13664 and a range held there drawing one value, the view's 7 x and the sky's
1 x of one blended range, the entry, the exit, GAME_FOV before and after the tick as cuts,
alpha 0 blending and alpha 1 not, and a zoom in of 19 steps, held, out of 19 steps, then
the exit, ticked at 30 Hz and drawn at 165 Hz, in which every frame of a moving zoom has
its own value and none moves backwards.

**Decisions.** The entry and the exit stay the cuts they are at thirty: the frames there
are camera cuts, drawn live, because the eye moves between Lara's head and the chase
camera, and a field of view blended over a live camera would be the one thing on the
screen moving between two pictures that jump. A field of view the zoom did not set before
the tick (GAME_FOV after the binoculars were taken from the inventory, whose return
invalidates the seam) is refused by the second test. The zoom takes the frame's alpha, not
the corner rule's `camAlpha`: the zoom steps at a fixed rate, like the poison sway. The
first value blends the field of view itself, not the range, because indoors the tick
leaves the value from the range before its step; blending the range there would make a
frame at alpha 1 draw a tick ahead. The rule lives in `modern_camera.h` beside the drawn
eye, the camera's other state between two ticks, a header with no engine include that
InterpTest includes for the two inline functions. `BinocularCamera` is not changed: it
runs on the tick only, and its value is the `to` of the blend.

## 2.6 Modern controls and the options menu

Beside the engine's own Tank control the game offers a second scheme, **Modern**, in
which the left stick steers Lara relative to the camera and the right stick moves a free
orbit around her. With it come an adjustable pad dead zone, a second keyboard set and a
second pad set of bindings, chord bindings behind a Modifier, an optional second action
key and four hold-or-toggle modes; the options menu that carries all of them is one
table-driven frame instead of five hand-written pages. Every one of these is a stored
setting whose default is the engine's own behaviour, and every statement added to an
existing engine file sits behind a test on that setting, inside a new file nothing
reaches without one, or in menu and settings code — so the shipped default is the engine
as it was. Origins, as facts: the movement design is TROne's (GPLv3) by Todesengel1931 —
https://github.com/todesengel1931 — re-derived here in this engine's own units and state
numbers, with 32 test expectations (28 `modern.*` and 4 `combatmode.*` cases of their
`tests/test_controller.cpp`) taken across verbatim and named as such in the test's own
header; none of their modern-control code is in this tree. The orbit camera shares only
the idea that a camera angle is a state: TROne's world angle (its copy of 2026-09-13)
never returns behind the player, this one falls home. The scheme is TROne's design
reworked here almost throughout: of the 32 constants of the design 16 stand as TROne's
design has them, 9 were re-measured in this project's own play, 5 do not apply and 2 of
unknown origin are not taken. The turn rate (`MODERN_TURN_RATE`, 30 degrees a tick, the
top of the thumb's measured 15 to 30), the camera's return behind her in 0.67 s and the
ends of its orbit rate (`game/modern_camera.h`) are this project's own choices; a handful
of option names are read out of a plain text file of the player's own installation. The
same statement stands in the origin block of `game/modern_move.h` beside the code.

### Modern control: the stick turned into the classic direction bits
2026-09-17 - 2026-09-20

**What.** The setting `control_modern` (default 0 = Tank) makes the left stick steer Lara
relative to the camera instead of relative to her own heading. It is not a new way of
moving her: a pure function turns "stick direction plus a remembered world heading" into
exactly the `IN_FORWARD` / `IN_BACK` / `IN_LEFT` / `IN_RIGHT` / `IN_WALK` / `IN_LSTEP` /
`IN_RSTEP` bits the keyboard has produced since 1996, and `game/lara.cpp` does the turning
at the classic automaton's own rate — with one named exception, a direct write to
`pos.y_rot` in ten standing and running states so that a half turn on the spot does not
cost twenty-three ticks. The direct turn moves her heading toward the course the stick
asks for at `MODERN_TURN_RATE` 5461 (30 degrees a tick); a reversal turns at that same
rate the short way round, a tie broken by her own last turn, and there is no one-tick
snap. While she is running the turn keeps `IN_FORWARD` however much turn is left; from a
stand it is withheld only past 90 degrees (`MODERN_SNAP_FORWARD_STAND`, states 2, 6, 7,
20) and handed over anyway after `MODERN_STAND_FORWARD_TICKS` (8) ticks of standing,
turning and arriving nowhere. She steers in the air: in `AS_FORWARDJUMP`, the only
airborne state whose routine reads a turn bit, the heading moves toward the stick's course
by `MODERN_AIR_TURN_RATE` 728 (4 degrees a tick, four times the classic 182) and the
classic `IN_LEFT` / `IN_RIGHT` are withheld so she is not turned twice. Under water the
left stick moves her on a flat circle relative to the camera, at `MODERN_SWIM_TURN_RATE`
2730 (15 degrees a tick) with a pitch of `MODERN_SWIM_PITCH_RATE` 728 a tick, her swim
attitude following the camera's own. She can run while she fires. The yaw step the right
stick gave the orbit on its last tick, and only that step, is added to the held reference
and the held course before the course is read, so the camera the player turns takes her
course with it. At Tank nothing of it runs. A camera cut while the stick is held keeps her
course until the stick is let go (*A camera cut keeps the held course until the stick is
let go* below).

**Why.** The scheme gives the player a control relative to the camera beside the engine's
own Tank control, and it survives a 1:1 engine because it only sets the classic bits: the
engine's `input` word carries the same bits at the same values, and TR5's state numbers
are the numbers the design was measured against. The held world course exists because the
obvious alternative does not work — reading the camera fresh every tick under a chase
camera that swings to stay behind Lara is a feedback loop that spins her in circles. The
direct turn exists because the automaton's fastest rate (1456, about 8 degrees a tick) is
too slow to follow the stick; it is barred from the air, the ladder, the water and every
interaction pose because there `y_rot` belongs to the animation and an outside hand on it
puts a pose crooked. 30 degrees a tick is the rate a thumb can circle the stick at (15 to
30); the older lid of 3277 sat below it, so a faster circle broke out of the turn and she
ran off or stopped, and a one-tick flick above 90 degrees snapped a whole turn into one
frame where this project's rate takes six ticks. Withholding forward past 45 degrees of
turn dropped a running Lara into `AS_STOP` for single ticks, a stumble on about a fifth of
the run ticks; a gate that asks how much turn is left can never open for a stick circling
at exactly her own rate, so the second question is asked in ticks, and a held stick never
reaches that counter (thrown a half turn and held she is inside the 90-degree gate by tick
4), which leaves the ledge the standing gate protects untouched. The classic forward jump
turns 1 degree a tick, 1 to 36 degrees over 40 ticks, too little to steer; 4 degrees a
tick was tuned in play. Nothing in this engine writes `lara_item->pos.y_rot` while she
aims — only her arms and torso move, in `larafire.cpp`, `lara1gun.cpp` and `lara2gun.cpp`
— so the refusal to run while aiming guarded a collision that does not exist here. The
water's old 6 degrees a tick left up to 59 consecutive ticks more than 45 degrees off the
stick. Carrying the camera's own player step is what keeps the re-latch rule honest: the
held course re-latched only when the left stick's own direction moved, which also ignored
the camera when the player moved it, so the course stood still and then paid the whole
jump in one tick - a jolt of up to the turn rate itself, in the water and running alike,
and under water a kick of the roll lean as well.

**How.** `game/modern_move.h` / `.cpp` (new) is the pure translation: eight numbers in
(stick x/y, camera yaw, Lara's yaw, a situation struct), a result struct out, no engine
header and no engine global, so the test compiles the engine's own file rather than a
copy. Its arc tangent is the C library's `atan2` scaled to the 16-bit convention — over
all 131,769 integer stick pairs a controller can produce the worst disagreement with the
engine's `phd_atan` is 5 of 65,536 units (0.03 degrees), against a smallest threshold of
384. `game/modern_state.h` / `.cpp` (new) is the one file that knows the engine: the
per-tick state, the reset on every break in the tick chain it can see, the blocked-wall
counter (measured from Lara's own position, never a collision internal, so a wall, a crate
and a corner read alike), the camera yaw of the tick taken from the camera's own two
points, the direct turn's one write to `pos.y_rot`, the air turn as the third arm of the
turn chain, and `MODERNLOG`. The seam is one call, `ModernUpdateInput`, in
`specific/input.cpp` between the block that puts the stick on the four direction bits and
the block that reads the key roles, guarded by `tomb5.control_modern && ControlMethod == 1
&& !FirstPersonActive() && !bUseSpotCam && !GLOBAL_playing_cutseq && !bDisableLaraControl
&& lara_item && !InventoryActive && gfLevelId != LVL5_TITLE && !(input & IN_LOOK)`.
`S_UpdateInput` is also called from eight menu loops, where the direction bits steer a
menu, so the seam tests `GlobalCounter`, which `game/control.cpp` raises exactly once
immediately before its own call: a call that does not follow a fresh count leaves the
input word untouched, and the tick right after a break in the chain is skipped so the
blocked counter is never measured against a position from before the break. That counter
cannot see a level change or a savegame restore, because between two levels not one tick
runs — so the held course is also forgotten by one line in `game/gameflow.cpp` beside
`InterpInvalidate("level start")`, which covers the savegame restore as well. The
inventory is deliberately not a reset: the world did not move while the ring was open. The
exempt-state table is `ModernStateIsClassic` (`game/modern_move.cpp`), answering state by
state from 0 to 138 — 95 classic, 44 modern when the translation was built, eight of them
retired again for the water. A direction bit stays classic wherever its state's own
routine in `lara_control_routines[]` reads it as something other than the direction she is
asked to go: which way to shimmy, whether to let go of a rope, which way to push a block —
the hangs and shimmies, the ladder, block push and pull, the poses grouped as 89-104, and
TR5's own extension past 104 (states 107-138). States 25, 26 and 27 (the back flip and the
two side flips) are classic, read out of the routines themselves: `lara_as_leftjump` sets
`AS_TWIST` on `IN_RIGHT`, `lara_as_rightjump` the mirror, `lara_as_backjump` reads
`IN_FORWARD | IN_ROLL` to end the flip early; 28 and 29 (`lara_as_upjump`,
`lara_as_fallback`) read no direction bit and stay modern. The constants, each with its
origin in the file's own comment: `MODERN_WALK_BELOW` 0, so the stick's own magnitude can
never produce `IN_WALK` — the pad has a dedicated walk key, and a stick still travelling
toward the speed asked for read 20 to 60 of 128 on the first tick of 19 of 32 pushes from
rest and latched the automaton into `AS_WALK` (the constant and `cfg->walk_below` remain,
provable under an explicit config); aim window `MODERN_AIM_WINDOW` 0x0400 with its
hysteresis doubled once aligned; spin enter 0x5000 and exit 0x2800 (turn on the spot above
112.5 degrees of error, run again below 56.25); `MODERN_STAND_SPIN` 0x3000, because
standing `lara_as_stop` can only express "turn" without `IN_FORWARD`; `MODERN_STEER_STEP`
0x0180, the noise floor, with `MODERN_RECENTER = MODERN_STEER_STEP`, so any stick movement
above that floor re-seats the course on the camera of that tick while a stick that is not
moving keeps its course whatever the camera does underneath it; `MODERN_AIM_SECTOR`
0x2000; blocked after `MODERN_BLOCK_FRAMES` 6 ticks of moving under `MODERN_BLOCK_EPS` 4
world units while asking to go forward and turn at once; `MODERN_TURN_RATE` 5461 with
`MODERN_TURN_RATE_VANILLA` 1456, `_MIDDLE` 2184 and a third rate of 3277 kept beside it as
named alternatives; `MODERN_DIRECT_TURN` 1, a second gate so that the direct turn can be
told apart from the scheme without a rebuild; full stick deflection 128; and five
build-time switches, `hold_course`, `back_turns`, `jump_dir` and `block_turn` on with
`MODERN_AIM_STRAFE` 0, each switching exactly one rule. `MODERN_STATE::last_course` /
`have_course`, `MODERN_RESULT::course_step` and `MODERN_SITUATION::cam_player_step` carry
the reversal and the camera's step, which `ModernTranslate`'s step 2a applies. The direct
turn is allowed in ten states: standing, walking, running, the three turns on the spot,
the wall splat, the landing, the sprint and `AS_COMPRESS` (0, 1, 2, 6, 7, 12, 14, 15, 20,
73). The translation stops aiming on the tick she jumps, so a side flip and a back flip
both survive firing; with no weapon drawn the directional jump stands aside (`sit->drawn`)
and the jump key gets the ordinary standing jump in the direction she is facing. Under
water, `ModernStateIsSwim`, `ModernWaterTurnRate` and `ModernWaterMove`
(`game/modern_move.cpp`) with the one write to the engine — turn, attitude, bank, stroke —
in `game/modern_state.cpp`; the surface rates are the engine's own, measured out of
`game/laraswim.cpp` and `game/larasurf.cpp` (surface turn 728, surface side 364, pitch
limits ±15470, swim roll 546), auto stroke on so the jump key is not needed to move, and
the pitch cap costs the modern dive 75 degrees against Tank's 85 because the pointer is
the camera's elevation with `pitch_home` taken out. `specific/input.cpp` / `.h` wire the
air turn into the turn chain and `specific/dxshell.cpp` supplies the stick. Byte identity
at the defaults holds by construction, and `tomb5_options tomb5;` is a global, so
`control_modern` reads 0 before any registry is opened. Seam behind `-log`: `MODERNLOG`
prints one `init` line per break in the tick chain and one line per real logic tick — 30
lines a second at every `fps_mode`, `mode=off` earning a line like any other, with `f=`
being `GlobalCounter` so a gap in it is the scheme standing aside. Tests:
`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/ModernTest.cpp` with `bmt.bat` links no game, no level and no
pad — it compiles the engine's own `game/modern_move.cpp` beside itself. It holds the 32
ported expectations plus sweeps no hand on a pad can reach: 16,384 blocked
stick/camera/state combinations with no violation of "forward and a turn bit never go out
together while she is blocked" and the counter-proof beside it (the same sweep unblocked
turns while running in 1,208 of 2,048), 2,997 stick pairs inside a raised dead zone
silent, 10,240 ticks after a 180-degree camera cut with the held course unmoved, eleven
checks on what the level-start reset is worth, and the groups `reversal`, `spin_sweep`,
`air_turn`, `turn_chain`, `circling`, `firing_run` and `cam_steer`; 34 single-edit
mutations of the scheme were tried against the finished tests and all 34 were caught.
`TOMB5 Code/tomb5.vcxproj` lists the new files and `Preparation/Tools/README.md` the test.

### The modern camera: a free orbit on the right stick
2026-09-17 - 2026-09-20

**What.** With Modern control on, the right stick moves the camera on a sphere around
Lara. The angle the player dials is held as a WORLD yaw
(`MODERN_CAMERA_STATE::world_yaw`), so her own turning does not move the camera at all;
only the return does, at a half-life of 122 ticks (4.07 s) for a 90-degree offset while
she is moving, and eight times as fast while the eye is clipped. The engine's
`camera.target_angle` receives `world_yaw - lara.y_rot` every tick, so nothing downstream
changed. The stick reaches the eye in the same tick it is pushed: the eye is turned about
the target by exactly this tick's stick step before `MoveCamera`'s damping sees it, and
the elevation step goes straight into `camera.actual_elevation`. At a wall the dialled
angle stays and the distance shrinks — both orbit cameras keep exactly one candidate,
clipped by `mgLOS` at any distance, and the clipped point is walked back toward the target
along the ray until clearance is found rather than snapped onto the sector grid. Below a
measured eye-to-target distance Lara is not drawn at all. Fixed level cameras are
discarded exactly as first person discards them, with the rich2 sniper camera excepted,
and a discarded one leaves no trace: over a Camera tile the orbit keeps its damping, a
trailing eye is not pulled onto its ideal place in one tick, and the tile edges are not
counted as camera cuts; flybys and cutscenes are untouched in every mode. A heading change
of more than 150 degrees in one tick that the modern turn did not cause hands the orbit a
pending swing of half a turn, paid out over 20 ticks on an eased profile and cancelled the
moment the stick is pushed. The camera's own rate is a setting: 0 to 100 maps linearly to
364..2184 yaw units per tick (60 to 360 degrees a second), pitch always half the yaw,
default 40 = 1092 units (180 deg/s), re-read every tick so a change on the pause menu is
felt the next tick. Under water the orbit's elevation becomes the attitude her body swims
toward. At Tank there is no orbit. Under the rich2 sniper camera the stick reads against
the sniper view, and a stick held through the cut into or out of it keeps her course until
it is let go (*A camera cut keeps the held course until the stick is let go* below).

**Why.** The orbit is the camera half of the modern control: a scheme that steers relative
to the camera needs a camera the player aims. It is built on the engine's own chase and
combat cameras rather than as a new camera so that distance, damping, collision and the
interpolator keep working as they do, and the combat camera gets the identical
substitution because `game/larafire.cpp` sets `camera.type = COMBAT_CAMERA` on every tick
a weapon is ready or being drawn — an orbit built into `ChaseCamera` alone would have
stopped answering the stick the moment a weapon came up. An offset from her heading swung
the camera behind her whenever she turned, where a world-angle camera stands still while
she spins under it; a world yaw minus this tick's heading is exact regardless, where an
offset carrying a per-tick heading delta drifts on every rounding and loses any tick the
orbit does not run. Without the lead the eye lagged the orbit by most of a second:
`MoveCamera` walks `pos += (ideal - pos) / speed` at speed 10 and the angle had no damping
of its own, so the eye needed about 25 ticks to reach the orbit's rate; with the lead the
first tick answers the stick in full at both damping speeds and at both ends of the speed
setting. Feeding a wall's displacement back into the yaw wrote `ChaseCamera`'s quadrant
snap onto a world cardinal into the state, so the next tick asked for the cardinal plus
one stick step, was blocked again, and the stick was swallowed - about a third of the
ticks pushed against a wall did not advance or ran against the stick. Above 60 degrees of
elevation the ideal eye's horizontal radius falls below 768 units (half a sector), close
enough that the measured eye-to-target vector reads as her own running direction, and her
course jumped by more than 45 degrees; hence the pitch limit of 60 degrees. The lead's arc
grows with the radius, and after a flyby, a cutscene, a room change or a released fixed
camera the eye walks in from thousands of units out — unscaled the lead reached 2856 units
in one tick against `INTERP_CAM_SNAP` 1024; scaled by the radius ratio the swept step is
407, 609 and 812 units at the three distances the engine sets (1536 behind her, 1024 in
the puzzle states, 2048 on the rope). Answers from the orbit must expire when the orbit
stops, because `ModernCameraActive()` reads the option, `lara_item`, the title, the
spotcam, the cutscene and first person but not which camera the engine is running, and a
frozen world yaw steered her along the bearing the chase camera had before a cut.
`CameraCollisionBounds` snapping a clipped point onto the sector grid made the eye's
picture and the movement reference disagree by 60 degrees or more on about half the pushed
ticks. The fixed-camera discard is decided at the top of `CalculateCamera` because taken
further down it would have handed the orbit the trigger's own object: a trigger carrying a
Camera and a Target command makes `game/control.cpp` set `camera.item` and the whole shot
is then built around that item — an orbit around a door at 1536 units with Lara out of the
picture; twenty floor triggers in the shipped campaign carry both commands on one tile
(Andrea1 4, Andrea2 1, joby2 1, rich1 4, rich2 3, rich3 7, counted over the player's own
`.trc` files). The discard kept the level camera from taking the view, but two side
effects of its trigger still reached the orbit. `TO_CAMERA` writes `camera.speed` = the
camera word's code bits + 1 (`game/control.cpp:2576`; the three Camera tiles Lara crosses
in Andrea1, rooms 19, 42 and 225, all carry 0x0000, so 1), `RefreshCamera` sets
`camera.type = FIXED_CAMERA` again on every tick she stands on the tile
(`game/control.cpp:2818`), and `ChaseCamera` forces speed 1 while `camera.old_type` is
FIXED (`game/camera.cpp:2178`-`2179`): speed 1 switches off the eye damping in
`MoveCamera` (`pos += (ideal - pos) / speed`) and the target damping in `CalculateCamera`
(`game/camera.cpp:1261`), so a trailing eye landed on its ideal place in one tick. And
`MoveCamera` records `camera.old_type = camera.type` (`game/camera.cpp:2531`), which was
FIXED during the discarded pass; FIXED is outside the interpolator's smooth family
(`InterpCamSmoothType`, `game/interpolate_math.h:93`), so every entry and exit of the tile
counted as a camera cut and drew its tick live.

**How.** Origin: OWN, as `game/modern_camera.h`'s own header states before a line of
arithmetic; the orbit falls home behind her at `MODERN_CAMERA_RETURN` whenever she is
moving and the thumb is off the stick. `game/modern_camera.h` / `.cpp` (new) hold the pure
half and no engine header: the state (`world_yaw`, `stick_step`, the last return step),
the config with an origin comment on each field, `ModernCameraUpdate` (the wall, then the
stick, then the return, in that order), `ModernCameraReset`, `ModernCameraHidesLara`,
`ModernCameraSwimPitch`, `ModernCameraSpeedRates` (the speed mapping, 18 or 19 units per
setting), `ModernCameraCarryStep` (a 64-bit numerator, because 3·n³·4096 passes 2³¹ at n =
56) and `ModernCameraTickFollows` (the "exactly one tick apart" arithmetic including the
wrap the engine meets every thirty-six minutes). `game/camera.cpp` / `.h` hold the seam in
eight places: the axes (`ModernCameraStick`, fed from `specific/input.cpp` on every poll,
read once per logic tick), the tick (`ModernCameraOrbit`, from whichever of `ChaseCamera`
/ `CombatCamera` runs), the angle (`camera.target_angle`, which `UpdateCameraElevation`
already adds to her heading), the height (`camera.target_elevation`, replacing the two
lines `ChaseCamera` opens with, because those accumulate her slope pitch tick after tick),
the wall, the draw (`ModernLaraHidden`), the water (`ModernCameraSwimTarget`) and the log;
plus `ModernCameraLeadEye` (scaled down by the radius ratio whenever the eye is further
out than `camera.target_distance`), `ModernCameraRayBounds` (the walk back along the ray,
with `CameraCollisionBounds`' y-correction kept and the function itself untouched),
`ModernCameraCarryFromAnim` (its rule is "a heading change this turn did not make", since
`CreatureKill`'s grab, the lift, the electric grab and the ceiling trapdoor also write
`lara_item->pos.y_rot`), `ModernCameraArm`, and `ModernCameraWorldYaw` /
`ModernCameraPlayerStep`, which decline unless the `GlobalCounter` stamp
`ModernCameraOrbit` writes is exactly one tick old (`game/control.cpp` steps the counter,
then runs `S_UpdateInput` and `CalculateCamera` in the same tick body; the subtraction is
done in the counter's own unsigned width). `game/draw.cpp` gains one term,
`!ModernLaraHidden()`, on the single condition every path that draws her passes, braid and
shadow included. `specific/dxshell.cpp` hands the right stick over as axes
(`joystick_read_rx` / `ry`) rather than only as four buttons. `game/modern_state.cpp`
seats the movement reference on `ModernCameraWorldYaw()`, and in first person, where the
orbit does not run, `ModernWaterMove` asks for her own current attitude instead. The
constants: `MODERN_CAMERA_PITCH_MIN` -10923 (60 degrees above her), pitch max 15470 —
`ChaseCamera`'s own elevation clamp (84.98 degrees) — pitch home -1820, `ChaseCamera`'s
own resting elevation, never 0 because that line reads 0 as "unset";
`MODERN_CAMERA_RETURN` 377 of 65536 per tick with a floor of 4 so the fall really arrives;
wall factor 8 on the return, a 14.7-tick half-life while a wall lasts; hide distance 122 =
the near clip plane (20) plus her standing radius (102), the distance at which the plane
stops being in front of her and starts being inside her; invert pitch 0, because the
classic look camera already turns stick-forward into "look up"; pitch return 0;
`MODERN_CAMERA_CARRY_FLIP` 27307 with `MODERN_CAMERA_CARRY_TICKS` 20;
`MODERN_CAMERA_PULL_STEPS` 8 and `MODERN_CAMERA_PULL_PUSH` 384; `MODERN_CAMERA_LEAD_MAX`
8192. Removed with the wall rule they served: `ModernCameraNoteWall`, `modern_cam_push` /
`_push_at`, `wall_push`, `MODERN_CAMERA_FOLLOW_WALL`, `MODERN_CAMERA_WALL_DEAD`,
`MODERN_CAM_ANGLE_RADIUS`, `MODERN_CAM_CLIP_DEAD` and the `angle_radius` fields; `wall` /
`clip` is now the candidate loop's own `mgLOS` answer, and the classic quadrant snap (3072
Manhattan) no longer fires in Modern at all. The discarded level camera's two side effects
are closed in `CalculateCamera`, both behind `modernDiscard` (`game/camera.cpp:1115`),
which is false under Tank, in first person (`ModernCameraActive` refuses it,
`game/camera.cpp:319`) and for the rich2 sniper camera (`sniperCam`), so those stay as
they were: right after the discard is decided the pass sets `camera.speed = 10`
(`game/camera.cpp:1130`-`1131`), the chase speed the reset at the end of the function
hands every pass (`game/camera.cpp:1393`); and the discard branch runs `ChaseCamera` with
`camera.type` set to `CHASE_CAMERA` and puts the level's type back afterwards
(`game/camera.cpp:1342`-`1346`), so `MoveCamera` records `old_type` CHASE and
`ChaseCamera`'s speed-1 rule stays quiet, while the reset's hold of a heavy camera and
`DiscardedFixedCameraTimer` see the type they saw before. Inside `ChaseCamera` and
`MoveCamera` nothing else reads `camera.type` or `camera.speed`: beside the speed-1 rule,
the speed it hands `MoveCamera` (`game/camera.cpp:2181`) and the record, only
`MoveCamera`'s reuse of the last ideal compares `camera.old_type == camera.type`
(`game/camera.cpp:2403`), which now holds on a tile as it does off one. On a look or
combat pass the branch further down writes its own speed over the 10. A known and accepted
difference: `lara_as_switchon` and `lara_as_switchoff` set `camera.speed = 6`
(`game/lara.cpp:3176`, `3187`), and on a lever whose trigger also carries a Camera command
the orbit runs at 10 instead on the ticks the level camera is discarded. The forced fixed
camera Core uses for three animations - the floor trapdoor lift (`game/traps.cpp:1061`),
the ceiling trapdoor pull (`:1120`) and the turn switch (`game/switch.cpp:606`) - is set
as `FIXED_CAMERA`, with speed 1, by `game/camera.cpp:1053`-`1058` and discarded under the
orbit the same way (its `camera.number` is -1, so it is never the sniper camera): its eye
ran undamped for the whole animation and its start and end counted as camera cuts, and now
it keeps the damping and counts no cut, a change the player sees - the orbit eases through
a trapdoor pull or a wheel turn instead of snapping. During the ledge hang's move and on
the ten ticks from its hand-over on, the chase camera's look-at point is looked up from
the room it was in the tick before and accepted from that room or from hers, so it follows
her down over the edge instead of standing still and then jumping (*Ledge hang: an
automatic turn and lowering at an edge* below). The orbit does not trip the 60 fps
camera-cut detection, swept rather than argued: over the whole sphere at the chase radius
(about 128,000 sample pairs) the worst tick of a fully pushed stick moves the ideal eye
309 units Manhattan against `INTERP_CAM_SNAP` 1024, and `InterpCamAimCut` fires on none of
them. Seam behind `-log`: `MODERNLOG`'s init line carries `cam_return`, `cam_return_min`,
`cam_wall_factor`, `cam_hide_dist`, `cam_invert`, `cam_pitch_return`, `cam_speed`,
`cam_yaw_rate`, `cam_pitch_min`, `cam_pitch_max`, `cam_pull_steps` and `cam_pull_push`;
the tick line carries `cam_off`, `cam_pitch`, `cam_ret`, `cam_world`, `clip`, `view_err`,

### A camera cut keeps the held course until the stick is let go
2026-09-26

**What.** With Modern control, a left stick held through a camera cut - into or out of the
rich2 sniper camera, the one level camera Modern keeps - leaves Lara on the course she was
running. The thumb still steers the held course, but from the cut until the stick is let
go its direction is read against the camera the course was seated on, not against the view
of the tick. Let go and pushed again, the stick seats a fresh course on the camera of that
tick: inside the sniper view it means the sniper view's directions, after the cut back the
chase camera's. With `-log` the `MODERNLOG` tick line ends in `cut=` and `latch=`.

**Why.** The held course is re-seated on the camera of the tick whenever the stick's own
direction has moved `recenter` (384 units, 2.1 degrees) from the direction it was last
drawn from (`MODERN_STATE::last_off`), and a thumb is never still: its drift from
`last_off` passes 384 within seconds. Under a camera that moves by itself the re-seat
costs the little that camera moved. Across a cut the camera of the tick is another camera:
the seam hands the translation the orbit's world yaw under the chase camera and the
measured eye-to-target vector under the sniper camera, and the two differ by the angle
between the views. So under the rich2 sniper camera a cut taken with the stick held ended
within a few ticks in a re-seat onto the other camera, before the stick was let go, and
the course jumped by the angle between the two views (11,268 to 32,343 units) while the
stick itself had moved little; a stick held through several cuts swung her course to and
fro between the sniper view and the chase camera.

**How.** The seam marks the cut: `game/modern_state.cpp:349` keeps whether the reference
of the tick is the orbit's world yaw (`ref_orbit`), and `:429`-`431` set
`MODERN_SITUATION::cam_cut` (`game/modern_move.h:583`) on the tick that source differs
from the previous tick's; the two statics behind it (`:67`-`68`) are cleared by
`ModernResetControls` (`:84`-`85`), so the first tick after a break in the chain is no
cut. The source switch is the signal rather than `camera.old_type` because the reference
is what the latch protects and the source is what hands it over, whatever camera type took
the view - a sniper camera fired as heavy (`old_type` 5) switches it the same way. Where
`old_type` changes, the source switches on the same tick. The translation
(`game/modern_move.cpp`) sets the latch in its step 2b (`:1504`-`1505`) when a cut arrives
while a course is held with `hold_course` on, and the re-seat (`:1535`) then seats on the
held reference instead of the camera of the tick; the course minus the reference is
`last_off` all through a hold, so a latched re-seat turns the course by exactly the
stick's own change. `ModernRelease` clears the latch with the course (`:252`), the aiming
branch clears it because it reads the camera fresh (`:1579`), and `ModernResetState`
(`:313`) and the empty situation (`:1440`) start at 0. The rule has its own switch beside
the five, `MODERN_CUT_LATCH` 1 (`game/modern_move.h:424`, `MODERN_CFG::cut_latch` at
`:508`, filled at `game/modern_move.cpp:292`), and its state `MODERN_STATE::cut_latch`
(`game/modern_move.h:553`). `MODERNLOG`'s tick line appends `cut=` (`sit.cam_cut`) and
`latch=` (`cut_latch` after the translation) after `old_type=`
(`game/modern_state.cpp:659`, `:667`-`668`, the legend at `:625`). Tests:
`camera_cut_latch()` (`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/ModernTest.cpp:6201`, run after
`sweeps()`) with its helpers `thumb` and `cut_twin` (`:6124`, `:6144`): a held course
through one and two cuts against a twin whose camera never cuts, the release and the push
seated on the new camera, the stick rolled far under the latch, the cut back, the mirror
of sweep (c), the player's camera turn under the latch, `hold_course` off and aiming. With
`cut_latch` 0 the translation works as it did without the latch. Tank never reaches the
latch: `ModernUpdateInput` runs only behind `modern_seam` (`specific/input.cpp:1289`,
`:1420`), which needs `tomb5.control_modern`. The sniper camera stays the level camera
Modern keeps (`sniperCam` and `modernDiscard`, `game/camera.cpp:1133`-`1135`), with the
measured vector of the sniper view as its reference. Without a cut the re-seat takes the
camera of the tick, and the player's own camera turn (step 2a) moves reference and course
together, latch or not.

**Decisions.** The latch drops when the stick is let go, on a tick the translation leaves
classic (which forgets the course anyway), when aiming reads the camera fresh, and when
the stick is turned past 45 degrees (below); there is no timeout. While it stands, a stick
rolled to a new direction is read against the reference the course was seated on - the
camera before the cut - and not against the view on the screen; a direction relative to
the new view is had by letting go and pushing again. A second cut while the latch stands
changes nothing, the cut back to the first camera included. The signal is the switch of
the reference source, not `camera.old_type`. The latch ships on. It also drops when the
stick is turned more than 45 degrees from its direction at the cut (*A held course also
ends when the stick is turned past 45 degrees*). The small course steps under the sniper
camera between the cuts stay: they are re-seats of the thumb against the measured vector,
which turns as she runs past the sniper's fixed position.

**Commits.** `89b12d4`, `1802637`

### At a diagonal wall the stick is read in the view on screen
2026-10-01

**What.** With Modern control in The 13th Floor and Escape with the Iris, where Core
pushes the camera off the 45-degree wall panels that stand in the corners of some rooms,
the left stick is read against the view on screen on every tick after that push moved the
camera, and against the angle the player dialled everywhere else, as before. A stick held
through the moment the push begins or ends keeps the course it was running, by the
existing cut latch, until it is let go. With `-log` the `CAMLOG` tick line ends in `diag=`
and the `MODERNLOG` tick line in `ref_view=`.

**Why.** Beside a diagonal wall, with the camera close to her, the direction Lara ran in
did not answer the stick as the picture showed it: the stick's position came out as her
own running direction. The cause is in `MoveCamera` (`game/camera.cpp`). After the Modern
orbit has walked its ray, cleared the wall and been clamped to floor and ceiling, the
upstream lines call `CheckForRichesIllegalDiagonalWalls` (`game/tower.cpp:76`-`138`) in
those two levels: for every static 36, and in Escape with the Iris static 27, within 4096
units whose collision box grown by 512 holds the eye, `ItemPushCamera` (`:140`-`187`)
moves the eye to the nearest side of that box grown by 384. The panels' boxes are 1526
(static 27) and 1486 (static 36) units wide and of no depth, standing on the diagonals of
corner sectors. The orbit's ray walk does not know the panels, so its ideal lies behind
one, and the push throws the damped eye back in front of it on every tick: pinned a few
hundred units from her, across the dialled ray and not along it. The stick was read in the
orbit's world yaw (`ModernCameraWorldYaw`), which geometry does not move, and with
`clip=1` the return ran eight times as fast, so the frame went on turning while the
picture stood. Wherever the push moved the eye - in Escape with the Iris on the push
planes of rooms 8 and 10, at both ends of the X-ray corridor - the reference lay up to
about a quarter turn from the view on screen; a close eye alone, clipped or not, keeps the
frame on the picture. The world yaw is the reference since 'The modern camera: a free
orbit on the right stick', which repaired a close eye whose measured vector had become her
own running direction, at a steep pitch or with a wall pulling the eye in along the ray.
That holds while geometry moves the eye along the dialled ray. The diagonal-wall push
moves it across, after the orbit's resolution and unknown to it, so the dialled angle no
longer describes the picture. Before that entry the reference was the measured vector, the
picture itself, which is the rule this entry gives back for the pushed ticks.

**How.** `ModernCameraOrbitIsView(now, orbit_at, pushed)` (`game/modern_camera.cpp:980`,
declared at `game/modern_camera.h:458`): the orbit ran on the tick before
(`ModernCameraTickFollows`) and its eye was not pushed. In `game/camera.cpp` the flag
`modern_cam_pushed` (`:228`) is cleared at the end of every orbit pass beside the orbit's
stamp (`:623`) and by `ModernCameraResetOrbit` (`:350`); `MoveCamera` keeps the eye before
the upstream call and hands it to `ModernCameraNotePush` (`:2833`) after it, both only
when `clear_wall`, the flag that only the Modern orbit's pass sets (`:2996`-`3009`); the
two upstream lines stay word for word. `ModernCameraWorldYaw` (`:768`) and
`ModernCameraPlayerStep` (`:803`) ask the helper instead of the stamp alone, so on a tick
after a push `game/modern_state.cpp:373` takes the measured vector, and the player's own
camera step does not turn the held course. The source switch sets `cam_cut` (`:458`) as
before, which arms `MODERN_CUT_LATCH` for a stick held through it. With `-log`,
`cam_tick.diag` (`game/camera.cpp:275`) holds the units the push moved the Modern eye,
|dx|+|dy|+|dz|, printed last on the `CAMLOG` tick line as `diag=` (`:1336`, legend
`:1277`-`1281`); the `MODERNLOG` tick line ends in `ref_view=`
(`game/modern_state.cpp:702`, legend `:666`), 1 while the modern camera is active and the
reference is the measured vector. The comments in `game/modern_state.cpp` (`:360`-`369`,
`:435`-`436`, `:454`-`457`) and `game/modern_move.h` (`:589`-`590`) name the case. Tests:
`camera_push_view()` (`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/ModernTest.cpp:7694`, run after
`camera_stamp()`): the helper at the wrap, at a gap and against the stamp over all 65536
stamps; a walked episode of 172 pushed passes, declined on exactly the 172 ticks after
them; and through the engine's `ModernTranslate` a stick held into and out of a push
against a twin whose reference never moves, the release and push seated on the measured
view, the switch back to a turning orbit with the stick held, and `hold_course` off. The
classic scheme never reaches the new lines: `clear_wall` is `modern_cam_clear_wall`, which
`ChaseCamera` and `CombatCamera` set to their `modern_orbit`, 0 unless
`ModernCameraActive()`. Core's push and its second call in the look camera stay as they
are, and the world yaw stays the reference wherever the push did not move the eye, close
eyes along the ray included. RICH3 carries eight static 36 panels, but its level is not in
Core's list, so the push never runs there.

**Decisions.** Any distance the push moves the eye counts, and the measured vector is then
the reference for the next tick; there is no threshold. One mechanism holds a course
across the switch, the cut latch, armed by the reference source switch as for the sniper
camera. The push is told apart from the orbit's own resolution by comparing the eye before
and after the upstream call, which leaves the upstream lines as they are. The frame goes
back to the dialled angle on the first tick the push does not move the eye, though the
damped eye needs some 5 to 15 ticks of `MoveCamera` to walk back to the dialled ray: a
stick held through the end of a push keeps its course by the latch, and a stick pushed
fresh in that window, or in a gap of a tick in which the push moves nothing, is seated on
the dialled angle, up to some 50 degrees off the picture. In the X-ray corridor of Escape
with the Iris the level's tracking camera runs instead of the orbit (*A level camera that
follows Lara is blended between its ticks*); the orbit is not seated on the level camera's
last view when that camera hands the view back.
