### A held course also ends when the stick is turned past 45 degrees
2026-10-01

**What.** With Modern control, a left stick held through a camera cut keeps the course
Lara was running, as before, but now only until the stick is let go or turned more than 45
degrees from where it pointed at the cut. On the tick it is turned that far the hold ends
and she runs on: from then on the stick is read in the view on screen - the measured view
under a level camera, the sniper camera or the diagonal-wall push, the angle the player
dialled under the Modern orbit. It holds at every cut: into and out of the rich2 sniper
camera, into and out of a level camera that follows her (the X-ray corridor of Escape with
the Iris), and where Core's diagonal-wall push begins or ends. With `-log` the `MODERNLOG`
tick line ends in `latch_drop=`.

**Why.** Through the X-ray corridor the steering felt sluggish, as if the turn angles were
unequal. The turns are not unequal: the per-tick turn to the left and to the right is of
the same order under every camera, and no turn goes the long way round. The cause is the
latch of *A camera cut keeps the held course until the stick is let go*: a stick held
across a cut is read against the camera before the cut until it is let go, and a stick
steered by the picture is turned within seconds of every cut. In the corridor a hold is
armed at its entry and exit and at the end of every diagonal-wall push; within a second or
so the stick had left its direction of the arming tick by more than 45 degrees, and for
the rest of the hold it was read against the camera before the cut, under the level camera
almost a quarter turn off the picture.

**How.** `MODERN_CUT_REAIM` 8192 (`game/modern_move.h:450`), and `MODERN_STATE::cut_off`
(`:586`), the stick's direction on the tick the latch was armed. In `ModernTranslate`
(`game/modern_move.cpp`) step 2b (`:1554`-`1559`) arms the latch only when it does not
stand and keeps `offset` - the stick's own direction, which the translation already takes
for itself - in `cut_off`, so a further cut under the latch moves neither. The new step 2c
(`:1570`-`1577`) ends the hold when the latch stands with `hold_course` and
`cfg->cut_latch` on and the stick's direction lies more than `MODERN_CUT_REAIM` from
`cut_off`, the short way round (`ModernWrap`): it clears `have_ref`, `cut_latch` and
`cut_off` and sets `MODERN_RESULT::latch_drop` (`game/modern_move.h:633`), and the branch
below seats the course on the camera of the tick exactly as a fresh push seats it (`ref`,
`course`, `last_off`, `have_ref`). Of what `ModernRelease` (`game/modern_move.cpp:289`)
does - it clears `have_ref`, `spin`, `aligned`, `aiming` and the latch - the drop leaves
`spin`, `aligned` and `aiming` alone, and the tick does not return early as a release
does, so she keeps running. 2c runs after 2b: on a tick that carries a cut and a turn past
the bound together, the cut is taken first and the seat is on that tick's new camera.
`cut_off` is cleared with the latch by `ModernRelease` (`:296`), the aiming branch
(`:1652`) and `ModernResetState` (`:358`), and `latch_drop` starts at 0 on every tick
(`:1462`). `MODERN_STATE` is not part of a savegame. With `-log`, `game/modern_state.cpp`
prints `latch_drop=` last on the `MODERNLOG` tick line (`:707`, `:717`, legend `:674`).
The comments that stated the old rule - the latch's switch and field
(`game/modern_move.h`), step 2b and the table of the held course
(`game/modern_move.cpp:1417`-`1423`), the `latch=` legend
(`game/modern_state.cpp:662`-`664`) - now state the new one. Tests: `camera_cut_reaim()`
(`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/ModernTest.cpp:6841`, run after `camera_cut_latch()`) with
`reaim_sit`, `reaim_arm` and `reaim_pair` (`:6760`, `:6774`, `:6790`): the arming tick's
direction is the translation's own `offset`; a quarter turn ends the hold and leaves
course, reference and latch as a fresh push of that stick, on the camera of the tick, with
the tick still active and sending bits; a roll of 200 units a tick ends it on the first
tick its sum from the arming direction passes 8192 and not before, and a roll out to 8000
and back keeps it; a second cut under the latch keeps the remembered direction, so 9000
from the first cut ends the hold though it is 3000 from the second; a cut after the drop
arms the latch again with that tick's direction; a cut and a turn past the bound on one
tick seat on the new camera; exactly 8192 keeps the hold and 8193 ends it, on either side,
with integer stick pairs searched for those exact gaps; across +32767/-32768 the step is
the short one; with the movement keys, forward then forward and right (45 degrees exactly)
keeps the hold and right alone ends it; a flick of 5000 under the latch re-seats against
the held reference as before; the release, aiming and `ModernResetState` clear the
direction with the latch; and with `cut_latch` or `hold_course` off nothing latches or
drops. In `camera_cut_latch()` the check of a stick rolled half a turn under the latch now
states the new rule (`:6561`-`6574`). Tank never reaches the rule: `ModernUpdateInput`
runs only behind `modern_seam` (`specific/input.cpp:1397`, `:1554`), which needs
`tomb5.control_modern`. The latch's arming signal, the reference source switch
(`game/modern_state.cpp:458`) and the source of the reference on each tick, the
diagonal-wall rule (`ModernCameraOrbitIsView`, `modern_cam_pushed`) included, are those of
the entries above; under a standing latch a stick that moves `recenter` or more but stays
within 45 degrees of its direction at the cut is still read against the held reference.

**Decisions.** The turn past 45 degrees ends the hold at every cut, the sniper camera's
included, because every cut arrives as the one `cam_cut`: a stick rolled far under the
latch ends the hold and is read against the view of the tick. The turn is measured from
the stick's direction on the arming tick, not from tick to tick, so a slow roll ends the
hold once its sum passes the bound; a further cut under the latch keeps that direction, so
a row of cuts cannot walk it round. The bound itself keeps the hold: 8192, one movement
key added to another, keeps it, and a quarter turn ends it. The drop is not a release: she
does not stop. The bound is a constant, not a config field; `cut_latch` switches it with
the latch. After a push's end or a corridor exit the drop seats the course on the orbit's
dialled angle, which can still lie off the picture while the eye walks back to the dialled
ray; under the sniper camera a drop reads the held stick in the sniper's view from that
tick on, and her course can swing by up to half a turn at once. A stick that never turns
45 degrees from its direction at the cut is held until it is let go.

**Commits.** `cc9ca690` (re-aim ends the latch), `d0f28483` (the suites), `f9181b9f` (the
record), `567737ec` (corrections after reading)

### The pad: radial dead zones, a second binding set and a Modifier for chords
2026-09-18 - 2026-09-20

**What.** Modern control has its own pad table and its own way of reading the sticks. Both
sticks are read through `ModernStickDeadZone`, a radial dead zone with rescaling, beside
the per-axis square the hardware holds — the stick is dead in either. The widths are
chosen by `joystick_is_xinput`: XInput radial 31 on the left stick and 34 on the right
(the hardware's own 7849 and 8689 of 32767), per-axis 30 and 33; the DirectInput fallback
radial 24 on both, per-axis 18 and 20. A *Dead zone* slider (`tomb5.dead_zone`, 0 to 100,
default 50, registry value `dead_zone`) scales all eight: at 50 it reproduces the tuned
constants exactly, at 0 there is no zone at all and at 100 twice the tuned one; it is
offered only under Modern, like *Camera speed*. The right stick becomes the camera, so its
four button roles (bits 16-19) are masked rather than raised and the medipacks move onto
the D-pad (bit 20 up, bit 21 down); the D-pad no longer reaches the movement stick under
Modern. Switching the control type repairs the bindings the new scheme cannot honour and
keeps every other binding the player made. The pad keeps two complete binding sets, one
for *Action* **One key** and one for **Separate**, the setting seating one and parking the
other. Any pad role may be a chord: a *Modifier* role plus a button; twenty-eight pad
roles exist — the sixteen movement and interaction roles, the Modifier, the six weapons
and the five cheat roles — and with the Modifier unbound the pad behaves exactly as
before. The value column prints `Mod+<Button>` for a chord and `---+<Button>` for one
whose Modifier is unbound, and bit 13 of the PS5 DirectInput page is named *Touchpad*.

**Why.** DirectInput's own zone was 500 of 1000 on the right stick and 150 of 1000 on the
left, and a per-axis zone zeroes each component on its own: the directions she was steered
in piled onto the four world cardinals and emptied just beside them, with about a fifth of
pushed ticks having one axis exactly zero. Over 360 sampled directions the per-axis zone
put about two thirds exactly on a cardinal; the radial zone puts only the four cardinals
themselves there and keeps the direction to within a third of a degree. A radial zone
alone covers only the disc inside the square the hardware held, so every rest position in
the square's corners — out to 1.41 times the half-width — stopped being dead and a pad
lying on the desk could turn the camera by itself; asking both costs the axis snap
nothing, because a push the per-axis zone snapped is by definition one it let through and
therefore always has a component outside the square. The DirectInput widths are 24 and not
the first 62: that number was sized from a comment's claim, where the pad measures rests
within 10 of 128, so 24 is above the hardware's gate and below the shared 31, which had
been throwing away every real left-stick push between 18 and 31. The right stick cannot be
a camera and four buttons at once, and a scheme that takes bits away must leave the roles
that sat on them somewhere usable — without a repair, switching to Modern left the player
with no medipack buttons at all, and pressing *Reset* in Modern wrote bits 20/21 into the
registry so that back under Tank every D-pad Up tapped forward and ate a small medipack.
The stick repair is needed because `specific/dxshell.cpp` does not OR the D-pad onto the
stick's two axes, it assigns ±20 of 128 over them: under Tank that is right, because a
direction bit has no size, but under Modern the size is the speed and the direction is a
course — over the whole square of stick values with D-Pad Up held, 770 of 66,049 positions
stopped her outright and nearly all the others had their course bent, by up to 177
degrees. Two binding sets keep a Separate player's layout and a One-key player's apart.
The Modifier exists because the pad has no free buttons left for fifteen hotkeys and a
chord costs none; the two XInput-ordered default tables name no spare button, so their
Modifier stays unbound rather than take one a player needs. A registry written before the
chords existed must not have the new mask laid over its buttons: that would have put six
buttons on two roles each — Look and Save both on R3, Sprint and Load both on L3, Jump and
Pistols both on Cross — and silenced every plain role while the touchpad was held.

**How.** `game/modern_move.h` / `.cpp`: `ModernStickDeadZone` with its `axis_zone`
argument, `MODERN_DEAD_LEFT` 31, `MODERN_DEAD_RIGHT` 34, `MODERN_DEAD_LEFT_DINPUT` 24,
`MODERN_DEAD_RIGHT_DINPUT` 24, `MODERN_DEAD_AXIS_LEFT` 30, `MODERN_DEAD_AXIS_RIGHT` 33,
`MODERN_DEAD_AXIS_LEFT_DINPUT` 18, `MODERN_DEAD_AXIS_RIGHT_DINPUT` 20 — each per-axis
width the hardware's own number divided the way that path divides its axes and floored —
and `ModernDeadZoneUser(base, user) = (base*user+25)/50`, pure with both arguments
guarded, applied at the two `ModernStickDeadZone` calls in `specific/input.cpp`.
`specific/dxshell.cpp` keeps the left stick's own two axes (`joystick_read_lx` / `ly`)
beside the pair the D-pad writes over, exposes the D-pad as four digital buttons, and
publishes the raw axes `joystick_raw_lx` / `_ly` / `_rx` / `_ry` before every classic gate
on both paths, so the smallest effective zone is a true zero; `joy_x` / `joy_y` still
carry the D-pad so it still steers the menus and the binding page in either scheme, and
`joy_fire` still carries its four bits so they stay bindable. `dead_zone` is the last
field of `tomb5_options` (`global/types.h`), so no existing offset moves, and
`tomb5_options` is registry-only, so the new field changes no file format and no savegame;
`tomb5/tomb5.cpp` reads, writes and clamps it, and `game/modern_state.cpp` prints the
effective widths as `dead_l` / `dead_r` with a `dead_user=` field on the `MODERNLOG` init
line, beside a `MODERNLOG pad` line giving the four raw resting axes and `xinput=` so the
numbers can be re-measured on any pad. The modern set is derived rather than hand-written:
`jLayout[16..31]` copied roles 0-12 from the same per-controller-style source
`ApplyJoyDefaults()` resolves (refactored around one record per style, `JoyDefaultRecord`)
and overrode only the two medipack roles — checked side by side for all four styles
(`PS5-DInput`, `PS5-XInput`, `Xbox`, `Generic`), roles 0-12 identical and roles 13 and 14
the only ones that differ — and that unread snapshot was retired once `ApplyJoyScheme`
recomputed the repair on demand. `ApplyJoyScheme()` (`specific/input.cpp`) is the switch's
rule: a role bound to a bit the active scheme has taken for something else, or still
sitting on the other scheme's own default for itself, goes to this scheme's default for
that role, and every other binding is kept; Modern cannot honour bits 16..19, Tank cannot
honour 20..23; where freeing a bit collides with a role that already holds it, the older
role is unbound exactly as the binding page does and then gets its own default when that
button is free. It is idempotent and is deliberately not `ApplyJoyDefaults()`. It runs
from the Control-type row in `specific/LoadSave.cpp` in both directions, and once inside
`S_UpdateInput`'s `if (tomb5.control_modern)` block for a session that starts in Modern
with a table written by Tank, which has to wait for a pad to really answer because
`joystick_is_xinput` is set by the poll and not by the init. One named cost: a binding the
player chose that equals the other scheme's default for that same role cannot be told
apart from one nobody repaired, so it follows the switch, and because the registry keeps
the table but not which scheme wrote it that one-time seat repeats on every launch; it can
only ever reach the two medipacks. `game/pad_scheme.h` is pure arithmetic with no engine
include: `JOY_ROLES` 28, `JOY_ROLE_SECOND` pinned to the literal 15, `JOY_ROLE_MODIFIER`
16, `JOY_ROLE_WEAPON_FIRST` 17, `JOY_ROLE_CHEAT_FLY` 23 through `JOY_ROLE_CHEAT_SKIP` 27,
`PadSetSeat`, `PadBitDown` and `PadRoleFires` — one function deciding whether a role
fires, read by every pad producer, the medipacks, save/load and both hotkey families.
`specific/input.cpp` holds the four Separate default tables `jSepPS5DInput`,
`jSepPS5XInput`, `jSepXbox`, `jSepGeneric` beside the four untouched One-key tables, plus
`jSplitParked`, `joy_split_seated`, `JoySplitSet`, `JoySplitDefaults` and `ApplyJoySplit`,
which swaps the sets unconditionally and calls `ApplyJoyScheme()` only once a scheme has
been seated. The chord flag lives in its own array with its own registry names per set
(`JChord`, `SJChord`) and is never folded into the button value; the Separate set has its
own names `SJDck..SJBmd` / `SJSec` (`specific/registry.cpp`), and `LoadSettings()` reads
`SJChord` unconditionally and lets only its absence decide, because `REG_ReadLong` writes
its default when a name is missing and `specific/winmain.cpp` calls `LoadSettings` a
second time whenever the first returns `REG_Setup` 0, which a virgin registry always does.
Capture, in `game/menu_frame.cpp` and `specific/LoadSave.cpp`: with the Modifier held the
next other button is stored as a chord, a plain binding and its chord twin coexist as two
rows, and binding the Modifier onto a used button clears every role there. Defaults on the
two DirectInput-numbered tables (PS5 DirectInput, generic): Modifier on the touchpad
click, quick save Modifier+R3, quick load Modifier+L3, flare Modifier+R1, the four weapons
Modifier+Cross/Circle/Triangle/Square, HK, crossbow and the cheats unbound; the two
XInput-ordered tables keep their earlier plain defaults, and `game/gameflow.cpp` carries
the button names. Format compatibility runs both ways: an older build ignores
`JChord`/`SJChord` and reads the chord roles as plain bindings, and one *Reset to
defaults* restores a whole row in either build. A table walk prints all four styles
through both directions of the switch, and a sweep holds three properties the rule may
never break — idempotent, no two roles sharing a button afterwards, no role left on a bit
the scheme cannot honour — over both directions, all four styles and four starting tables;
`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/ModernTest.cpp`'s `deadzone` group sweeps the whole 257 × 257
domain for all four pairs and answers zero points that were dead before and are alive now,
and its D-pad block catches all eight D-pad readings and nothing else in a sweep of 66,049
stick pairs, with the counter-proof that the raw ±20 would have made her walk;
`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/MenuTest.cpp` covers the role tables.

### The pad's scheme repair never displaces the Modifier
2026-09-27

**What.** Flipping the *Control type* row repairs the pad bindings the new scheme cannot
honour (the entry above); that repair no longer unbinds the Modifier. A role whose
repaired default is the Modifier's own pair is left unbound instead, remembered in its
set's yield mask, and seated on its default again by the next repair that finds that
default free and not blocked. On the PS5 DirectInput page at *One key* the small medipack
now waits while the Modifier holds the touchpad under Tank and is back on d-pad up under
Modern, and every chord keeps its Modifier through both flips.

**Why.** With the Modifier on the touchpad and chords on some hotkeys, a flip to Tank and
back left the binding page showing every chord as `---+L3`, `---+L2`, `---+R1`
(`game/menu_frame.cpp:1347`-`:1352` prints `---` for an unbound Modifier), and a
Touchpad+button press bound the plain touchpad, because the capture records a chord only
while a Modifier is bound and otherwise takes the highest bit down, which the touchpad's
bit 13 is (`:2007`-`:2031`); the `PADLOG` line read `mod=-1`. The mechanism is in the
tables and the repair: at *One key* on that page Tank's Small Medipack default is bit 13
(`jDefPS5DInput`, `specific/input.cpp:189`) and Modern's is d-pad up, 20. Into Tank the
medipack on 20 is on a blocked bit - Tank keeps the d-pad moving Lara - and goes to 13;
the repair's displacement then found the Modifier on (13, plain) and gave it its own One
key default, which is none. Back into Modern the medipack follows the switch to 20, and
nothing gave the Modifier back. The Separate DirectInput row escapes the collision by
leaving both medipacks unbound (`game/pad_scheme.h`, `JOY_SEP_PS5_DINPUT`); the One-key
Tank row does not.

**How.** The repair's rule moves out of `ApplyJoyScheme` into `game/pad_scheme.h`, pure
arithmetic like the rest of that header, so that MenuTest runs the engine's own rule:
`PadSchemeRepair` (`:246`-`:320`) with `PadPairTaken`, `PadChordSet` and
`PadModifierHolds` beside it. Part 1 is the repair as it was. Part 2: before a role takes
its default, `PadModifierHolds` asks whether the Modifier holds that pair; if so the role
is set to -1, its chord flag cleared and its bit set in the yield mask (`:262`-`:269`),
and the displacement loop skips the Modifier (`:281`) - a role displaced there whose own
default the Modifier holds is remembered the same way. Part 3 (`:298`-`:319`): every role
in the mask that is still unbound is seated on its default when the bit is not blocked and
the pair is free; a role the player has bound in the meantime leaves the mask.
`ApplyJoyScheme` (`specific/input.cpp:403`) calls it on the active set (`:424`). The mask
is `jYield` beside `jChord` and `jSplitParkedYield` beside `jSplitParkedChord`
(`:264`-`:265`), exchanged with them by the Action row (`ApplyJoySplit`, `:533`-`:539`),
cleared by *Reset* (`:346`), reached as `JoyYieldSet` (`:479`), and stored beside
`JChord`/`SJChord` as `JYield`/`SJYield` (`specific/registry.cpp:67`-`:71`, read at `:532`
and `:610`, written at `:732`-`:733`), so a medipack waiting under Tank at shutdown still
returns after a restart into Modern. Behind `-log`, new lines (`specific/input.cpp:427`-
`:438`): `PADLOG repair role=<n> default=<bit> held by the modifier, left unbound` when a
role yields and `PADLOG repair role=<n> seated=<bit>` when it is seated again; the `PADLOG
mod= chord= split=` line is unchanged. The repair runs only on a scheme flip, on an Action
flip once a scheme is seated and once at a Modern start, never per frame; without a bound
Modifier it gives exactly what it gave before, and the Separate set, whose Tank medipacks
are unbound, repairs as before. MenuTest's family `pad_scheme_repair`
(`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/MenuTest.cpp`) holds the rule on all four pages and from both
schemes.

**Decisions.** The repair never displaces the Modifier: it is the anchor of every chord,
and one default outranks none of them. A role left unbound for it is remembered per
binding set, in the registry beside the chord masks, and seated again by the next repair
that finds its default free. The defaults stay as they are: Tank's One-key Small Medipack
keeps bit 13 wherever no Modifier holds it. A Modifier on a bit the new scheme blocks is
still repaired like any other role, and *Reset* at One key still clears a player's
Modifier.

### The keyboard: two binding sets, bindable hotkey roles, and the look key's turn on the spot
2026-08-30 - 2026-09-20

**What.** The keyboard keeps two complete binding sets, one per control type, both
persisted: the classic (Tank) set stays under the registry names `Key0..Key33` and a
Modern set lives under `MKey0..MKey33`. Switching *Control type* seats one and parks the
other, so Modern bindings survive a flip to Tank and back. The Modern default row is a
hand-on-the-left layout around W/S/A/D: forward W, back S, left A, right D, duck C, dash
Left Shift, walk Left Alt, jump Space, action E, draw Q, flare F, look R, roll Left Ctrl,
inventory Escape, step left Z, step right X, pause P, select Return. Fifteen keys the
engine used to read directly from the keyboard became rebindable roles: the small and
large medipack, quick save, quick load, the six weapons of `DoWeaponHotkey`, whose order
is fixed and no longer level-dependent (1 pistols, 2 shotgun, 3 uzis, 4 revolver, 5 HK, 6
crossbow), and the five cheat roles; their defaults are the keys the engine already
answered to — 0, 9, F5, F6, 1-6, F2, F7, F8, F11, F1 — identical in both rows but for
quick load, which is F9 under Modern and F6 under Tank. *Reset to defaults* restores the
active scheme's own defaults and recomputes the conflict table. Under Modern the four
arrow keys and Return also drive any menu that owns the input. Separately, while the look
key is held with no weapon ready, the modern translation is bypassed and `IN_LOOK` itself
is kept from the engine for those ticks (latch `modern_look_tank`), so `LookLeftRight` and
`LookUpDown` never eat the direction bits and `AS_TURN_L`, `AS_TURN_R` and `AS_FASTTURN`
run with their real animation — Tank turning on the spot inside the modern scheme. On such
a tick the stick is read by sector: `ModernTankSector` lets exactly one axis through, at
the stick's magnitude rather than its component — inside `MODERN_TANK_TURN_SECTOR` (9102,
50 degrees either side of the horizontal) a pure turn, outside it a pure step, with no
diagonals. With a weapon ready the sector stands aside and the classic look keeps the
bits.

**Why.** At base `DoWeaponHotkey` let two of its four keys change meaning on `gfLevelId`:
key 1 drew the pistols early and the HK later, key 2 the shotgun early and the crossbow
later. `gfLevelId` is the level's identity, not its position, so under a rolled level
order "from the 13th Floor on" means "in levels that happen to have a high id", scattered
unpredictably through the run - and because the weapons are scattered too, Lara can carry
an HK in the first level, where no key draws it, and the pistols in the last, where key 1
reaches for the HK. Keys 5 to 8 were free in play; only the save/load screen uses 1 to 4,
which is a different context. At base `SaveSettings()` wrote `Key0..17` from the active
row, so the first exit in Modern would have overwritten the classic keys with the Modern
ones. A hard-wired `keymap[DIK_*]` read cannot be rebound, and the two keyboard name
tables named none of `DIK_F1..DIK_F12`, so eight of the new default keys would have
printed a null pointer on the binding page. The reset never called `CheckKeyConflicts()`,
so `conflict[]` stayed stale after a reset until the next capture. The look-key bypass is
needed because on a bypass tick the classic word is built from `move_x` / `move_y` with `>
8` / `< -8` per axis — Core's own arithmetic, written to sit behind the hardware's
per-axis zone — while in the modern scheme the pair has come through the radial zone
instead, so 8 of 128 is a window of about 3.6 degrees either side of the exact horizontal,
where a thumb pushes "left" at a median of -100 to -106 degrees. Most pushed ticks came
out as a turn plus back or forward and only about one in seventeen as a pure side, and
`lara_as_stop` lets `IN_BACK` and `IN_FORWARD` overwrite the turn goal, so the turn could
not be started and she stepped backwards instead; the camera has no part in it, the
pattern being the same at every camera offset. Diagonals are refused because this mode
exists to place her exactly, and the magnitude is used because the component shrinks
toward the sector's edge and would fall back under the very threshold the sector exists to
clear. With a weapon ready the look bit survives twice over — the `IN_TARGET` swallow
releases it from the seventh tick of a hold (`LookCnt` 100), and `game/control.cpp` puts
it back with `input |= IN_LOOK` on every tick of a binocular or lasersight session — and
on exactly those ticks the classic direction bits are what aim the head, the binoculars
and the crosshair, where one surviving axis would make a diagonal impossible.

**How.** `game/key_scheme.h` is pure arithmetic with no engine include: `KEY_SCHEME_ROLES`
34, `KEY_ROLE_SECOND` pinned to the literal 18, `KEY_ROLE_MEDI_SMALL` 19 through
`KEY_ROLE_CHEAT_SKIP` 33, `KEY_SCHEME_MODERN_ROW`, `KeySchemeConflicts` (Core's own double
loop run against the active scheme's default row, with arguments saying whether the
Secondary role and the five cheat roles are live, since an inert role's key must claim
nothing), `KeySchemeSeat` and `KeySchemeRowSound`. `specific/input.cpp` holds `short
layout[4][KEY_SCHEME_ROLES]` — row 0 Core's Tank defaults unchanged, row 1 the active set
every existing reader and writer already uses, row 2 the Modern defaults, row 3 the parked
set — plus thirty-four `static_assert`s tying the header's bare scan codes to their `DIK_`
names, `key_scheme_seated`, `KeyDefaultRow`, `KeySchemeSet(long modern)` and
`ApplyKeyScheme()`; `Key()`'s fallback reads `KeyDefaultRow()` instead of `layout[0]`, and
ten hard-wired `keymap[DIK_*]` reads became `Key(role)` one for one with the same guard,
timer and ammo-cycle condition. `KeyboardButtons` and `GermanKeyboard` now name F1, F2,
F5-F9 and F11; F3, F4, F10 and F12 stay nameless on purpose, because the outfit changer
(`specific/hd/hd_outfitmenu.cpp`), `IN_E` and `specific/output.cpp` own them and a capture
must keep refusing them. `specific/registry.cpp`'s `LoadSettings()` stores the two sets by
name while Tank is still seated, because it runs in `WinMain` before
`tomb5.control_modern` is read; the one-time seat is a single `ApplyKeyScheme()` call in
`specific/gamemain.cpp` after `init_tomb5_stuff()`, and `SaveSettings()` writes `Key*`
from `KeySchemeSet(0)` and `MKey*` from `KeySchemeSet(1)`. `MenuResolveKeybinds`
(`game/menu_frame.cpp`) builds the keyboard list into a static buffer: the sixteen base
roles, *Secondary* only under *Separate*, the ten hotkeys, and the five cheat rows only
while *Cheats* is on; `specific/LoadSave.cpp` carries the capture. A block in
`S_UpdateInput` ORs the four arrow keys and Return into
`IN_FORWARD/IN_BACK/IN_LEFT/IN_RIGHT/IN_SELECT` under `tomb5.control_modern &&
ModernMenuReadsPad()`, reading `keymap[]` raw because those five are the menu's own fixed
keys. One measured collision is left as it is and written down beside the row: Modern's
walk key is Left Alt, and the title screen (`game/gameflow.cpp`), load/save
(`specific/LoadSave.cpp`) and the outfit changer suppress confirm while Left Alt is down,
which is the guard that keeps Alt+Enter from choosing a row while it toggles fullscreen;
Escape still leaves and nothing locks. The look-key bypass lives in `specific/input.cpp`:
the latch, the bypass condition moved up to where the stick is read so the sector and the
classic assembly answer the same question once (`modern_tank`), `modern_tank_aim` gating
the sector call alone, the sector call with its one-tick static, and the tank log line;
`ModernTankSector` and its two constants — `MODERN_TANK_TURN_SECTOR` 9102 and
`MODERN_TANK_SECTOR_HYST` 1456 (8 degrees), which keeps a thumb resting on the boundary
from alternating at 30 Hz — are in `game/modern_move.h` / `.cpp`, `ModernLookTankActive()`
is the predicate the seam and the log share, and `specific/input.h` with
`specific/dxshell.cpp` carry the stick reading it sits behind. The bypass costs no extra
tick on release: it is one tick behind at both ends, the same latency the plain `input &
IN_LOOK` gate had. Tests: `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/ModernTest.cpp` has `look_tank` (ten
held ticks against ten bypassed ones) and `tank_sector`, whose boundary walk checks the
two constants themselves and asks the two edges strictly against the plain boundary,
because every other assertion in the group derives its expectation from the constant; both
groups state in writing that they mirror `specific/input.cpp` and `game/camera.cpp` rather
than linking them. `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/MenuTest.cpp` with `bmenu.bat` covers the
role tables, `TOMB5 Code/tomb5.vcxproj` lists the new header, and `docs/Engine-Manual.md`
carries the layouts.

### The mouse: the modern camera's second input, five bindable buttons and two rows
2026-09-27

**What.** Under *Control type: Modern* the mouse turns the orbit camera beside the right
stick, and a camera turned with the mouse takes her held course with it exactly as the
stick's does. The five mouse buttons - left, right, middle and the two side buttons - are
bindable on the keyboard's *Key bindings* list in either scheme and named *Mouse L*,
*Mouse R*, *Mouse M*, *Mouse 4* and *Mouse 5* (*Maus L* and so on in German). The Modern
default row draws on the right button, looks on the middle one and takes the secondary
action on the left one; Q, R and Numpad 0 leave the row. Two *Controls* rows follow *Dead
zone*: *Mouse sensitivity*, 0 to 100 with 50 as the default, and *Invert mouse*, off by
default. The cursor is hidden and held inside the client area while the window is active,
Modern is on and no FMV plays. The files: `specific/winmain.cpp` (`WinMouseInput`,
`WinMouseTake`, `WinMouseCapture`, `WinMouseWant`), `specific/input.cpp` (`S_UpdateInput`,
`Key()`), `game/modern_camera.cpp/.h`, `game/camera.cpp`, `game/key_scheme.h`,
`game/menu_frame.cpp`, `game/gameflow.cpp`, `global/types.h`, `tomb5/tomb5.cpp`.

**Why.** The modern camera wants a second input beside the right stick for a player at the
keyboard, and the three roles the camera hand rests on - draw, look and the secondary
action - want buttons of their own. The engine read no mouse at all: the `WM_MOUSEMOVE`
case of `WinMainWndProc` stored `mouseX`, `mouseY` and `mouseB` into statics that nothing
read, and `Key()` read `keymap` alone, which is why `game/key_scheme.h` called Q, R and
Numpad 0 placeholders for the three roles.

**How.** Raw Input: `WinCreateWindow` registers usage page 1, usage 2, no flags, the game
window as target, so the mouse arrives as `WM_INPUT` while the window is in the
foreground. `WinMouseInput` folds the button flags - button n down on bit 2n, up on bit 2n
+ 1 - into a five-bit mask of the buttons held and one of the buttons pressed since the
last take, whether captured or not, and adds the move to two counters with
`InterlockedExchangeAdd` only while captured; an absolute report (a tablet, a remote
desktop) is turned into pixels and differenced against the previous position, the first
one after a capture only seeding it. The dead `WM_MOUSEMOVE` stores are gone. The window
procedure runs on the main thread inside `WinProcMsg`'s `GetMessage` loop, which does
nothing else once `GameMain` runs on its own thread, so `WM_INPUT` is handled at the
mouse's report rate whatever the frame rate. The game thread takes what gathered with
`WinMouseTake`, an `InterlockedExchange` of both counters to 0 and the pressed mask ORed
with the held one, once per `S_UpdateInput` - once per logic tick in play - so the counts
of every drawn frame between two ticks reach the one tick at 30, 60 and the display's own
rate alike, and a click shorter than a tick still counts for one. No lock: everything the
two threads share is a `LONG` changed through the Interlocked functions, and a lock would
be a hazard of its own, because `WM_ACTIVATE` suspends the game thread with
`SuspendThread` and a suspended holder would never let go.

The capture, `WinMouseCapture`, runs on the main thread only, because `ShowCursor`'s
counter belongs to the thread that owns the window: captured is (window active) and
(Modern) and not (FMV) and not (closing). Catching the cursor calls `ShowCursor(FALSE)`
until the counter is below 0 and counts the calls; letting it go calls `ShowCursor(TRUE)`
exactly that many times and `ClipCursor(0)`, so the counter ends where it was found and a
full screen that kept it at -1 stays hidden. While captured the clip rectangle is set
again on every call, which `WM_MOVE` and `WM_SIZE` make. The game thread's two terms come
from `WinMouseWant`, called at the top of every `S_UpdateInput` with
`tomb5.control_modern` and `App.fmv` and posting `WM_APP_MOUSE` only on a change, so the
*Control type* row, the start of a video (`specific/fmv.cpp`, then the player's own
`S_UpdateInput`) and its end reach the window thread at once. The window's term comes from
`WM_ACTIVATE` as its first statement, ahead of the FMV guard, from `WM_SETFOCUS` and
`WM_KILLFOCUS`, and from `WM_SIZE`, which takes it afresh as "the foreground window and
not minimised": a window restored from the taskbar gets its `WM_ACTIVATE` while still
minimised, which reads as inactive, and a later `WM_SETFOCUS` is not certain, so the
restore itself seats the term again. Losing the term also clears both button masks,
because the up messages go to another window. The cursor is released when the window goes
inactive or is minimised, the focus leaves, *Tank* is chosen, a video starts, and on
`WM_CLOSE` and `WinClose`, since a clip holds for the whole system. While the cursor is
not captured the counts are dropped where they arrive and the buttons still count, as a
keyboard key does; under *Tank* the cursor is never caught and no step is handed to any
camera.

The orbit term is pure arithmetic in `game/modern_camera.cpp`. `ModernCameraMouseGain` is
the gain in 512ths of a unit per count, 16384 * 2^((s - 50) / 25) for a sensitivity s of 0
to 100: a table `pow25` of round(4096 * 2^(r / 25)) for r = s mod 25, shifted left by s /
25 (0 to 4), so the gain is 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 units a count at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 -
8192, 4096, 2048, 1024 and 512 counts a full turn of 65536 - and every step of the slider
is the same 2.8 per cent. 512ths and not 256ths because the bottom end is a quarter of the
middle and a quarter of every table value has to stay whole for the doubling to be exact.
`ModernCameraMouseSteps` makes yaw = dx * gain / 512 and pitch = -dy * gain / 512, the
invert flipping the pitch alone, so a mouse pushed away looks up as the stick pushed
forward does. The numbers are this engine's own: 2048 counts is about 13 cm of desk at 400
counts per inch and 3.3 cm at 1600.

A step is bounded at 2048 units each way a tick (`MODERN_CAMERA_MOUSE_STEP_MAX`,
`game/modern_camera.h`), 11.25 degrees, 337.5 degrees a second at 30 ticks, because the 60
fps interpolator calls a tick a camera cut, and draws it without interpolation, when the
eye moves more than `INTERP_CAM_SNAP` (1024 Manhattan) or the aim does
(`InterpCamAimCut`). ModernTest's camera cut sweep holds the bound on both axes at once at
the three target distances the engine sets, 1024, 1536 and 2048: the eye moves at most
967, with no aim cut, while 2176 on both axes already moves it 1027 at 2048 and cuts the
aim. The stick's own top, 2184 a tick at *Camera speed* 100, is about the same. The counts
beyond the bound are not dropped: `ModernCameraMouseSpend` spends at most the counts of
one bounded step a tick - 64 at sensitivity 50, 16 at 100, 256 at 0 - and owes the rest to
the next tick, so a brisk sweep turns the camera as far as the hand went, spread over a
few more ticks. What is owed is bounded at half a turn of steps
(`MODERN_CAMERA_MOUSE_OWED_MAX`, 1024 counts at 50), sixteen ticks of the largest step, so
the camera goes on turning for at most about half a second after the hand stops; the
counts past that are dropped. `S_UpdateInput` keeps the two owed counts, forgets them
while the cursor is not captured, spends, and hands the two steps to `ModernCameraMouse`
(`game/camera.cpp`) inside the Modern block that also hands over the stick;
`ModernCameraOrbit` moves them into `MODERN_CAMERA_STATE::mouse_yaw` and `mouse_pitch`
before `ModernCameraUpdate` and clears its own copy. The update counts a nonzero mouse
step as steering, so it stands the return still and cancels a carried swing as the stick
does; takes `stick_step = ModernWrap(rate(rs_x) + mouse_yaw)`; adds `mouse_pitch` after
the stick's pitch term, before the clamp; and clears both steps. Nothing else in the
camera changes: `ModernCameraPlayerStep` (`game/modern_state.cpp`) hands `stick_step` to
her held course, and the eye's lead takes the world yaw's step, the mouse's included. The
first person view does not take the orbit's input: `FirstPersonCamera` looks along
`lara.head_x_rot` and `head_y_rot` plus her own rotation, `ModernCameraActive` refuses the
orbit under it and the modern seam excludes it, so the mouse does not turn it.

The buttons are key codes above every scan code: `KEY_MOUSE_FIRST` 0x100 to `KEY_MOUSE_X2`
0x104 in Raw Input's order left, right, middle, X1, X2 (`game/key_scheme.h`), with
`KeySchemeIsMouse`, `KeySchemeMouseBit` and `KeySchemeMouseName`, which has the key
tables' two columns, German and every other language. `Key()` reads the button mask this
`S_UpdateInput` took for a code at or above 0x100 and `keymap` below it, both for a
binding and for the default row's fallback; a code above 0x104 answers 0 instead of
reading past `keymap`. `static_assert`s say the Modern row's slots 9, 11 and 18 are the
right, the middle and the left button and that the codes start above `keymap` and fit a
short. `KeySchemeConflicts` compares codes, so a button claims and is claimed as a key is.
The bindings page names a button before it indexes the key table (`game/menu_frame.cpp`),
whose entries past 0xFF are Core's old joystick names and would call the right button "Joy
2". `MenuSelectBinding` notes the buttons already down and `MenuCaptureBinding` takes a
button newly pressed during the wait: the press and not the release, one role per press, a
key in the same frame first, the lowest button on a tie, on the keyboard page only. Tank's
row has no button. The registry keeps `Key*` and `MKey*` as longs, so a code is stored as
it is (`specific/registry.cpp`); a registry that already holds `MKey9`, `MKey11` and
`MKey18` keeps the player's keys there, the buttons answering beside them through
`Key()`'s default-row fallback, and *Reset to defaults* seats the new row. A set saved by
this build is not safe for an engine that predates the mouse codes: that one indexes its
256-entry `keymap` with the code and reads past the end, and its bindings page names the
buttons with Core's joystick names; *Reset to defaults* in that engine puts its own row
back. *Combat mode* at *Hold* needs nothing new: its seam reads `IN_DRAW` as `Key(9)` left
it, a level read of the mask, so a held right button keeps the weapons out (read from the
code).

The rows: `MenuStepMouseSensitivity` (`game/menu_frame.cpp`) steps through
`MenuSliderStep` (`game/menu_nav.h`), the rule Camera speed and Dead zone write out by
hand, and `MenuStepInvertMouse` flips the bit; the rows are a `MENU_SLIDER` and a
`MENU_VALUE_IF`, both `MENU_SAVE_TOMB5` and `MenuEnabledModern`, which makes *Controls*
twelve rows, its `MENU_MAX_ROWS`, still one page. Labels in the string table
(`game/gameflow.cpp`, German *Mausempfindlichkeit* and *Maus invertieren*, the values the
table's own *on* and *off*); fields `tomb5.mouse_sensitivity` and `tomb5.mouse_invert`
(`global/types.h`); registry values `mouse_sens` and `mouse_invert`, written on a first
run, read with 50 and off for a missing value and 50 for one over 100, and saved
(`tomb5/tomb5.cpp`). The seams behind `-log`: `MOUSELOG f=<tick> dx=<counts> dy=<counts>
buttons=0x<mask> yaw=<units> pitch=<units> sens=<0..100> captured=<0/1> owed_x=<counts>
owed_y=<counts>` once per `S_UpdateInput` on which the mouse moved, a step was handed over
(owed counts paid out with `dx=0 dy=0`) or the mask changed, and `MOUSELOG
capture=<on|off> active=<0/1> modern=<0/1> fmv=<0/1>` on every change of the capture. The
tests: ModernTest's `camera_mouse` (with `mouse_course_step`) and `camera_camcut` groups,
and MenuTest's `key_mouse` and `controls_mouse_rows` groups.

**Decisions.** Raw Input (`WM_INPUT`) carries the counts and the buttons, not
DirectInput's mouse device. The mouse turns the camera under *Modern* only; *Tank* keeps
its classic look. Moving the mouse does nothing in the menus or the inventory; a button
bound to a role works there as that role's key does. The three Modern defaults are this
project's choice for the three buttons the camera hand rests on: draw on the right button,
look on the middle one, the secondary action on the left one. The message of commit
`59ca9b7` names another product's page of default keys for this row and cannot be changed;
the row's three defaults are this project's choice, as said here. A full circle takes 2048
counts at the middle of the slider, and the slider spans a quarter to four times that; the
yaw and the pitch share one gain, and the mouse's pitch invert is a setting of its own.
The camera turns no faster than 2048 units a tick with the mouse, so that the 60 fps
interpolator never takes a mouse turn for a camera cut; a faster hand is paid out over the
following ticks, at most half a turn behind, rather than drawn at 30 Hz. The step bound
holds at `fps_mode` 0 as well, where no in-between frame is drawn; it stays so. The
capture has no term for the F4 outfit window: that window is drawn with `PrintString` and
driven by `dbinput` (`specific/hd/hd_outfitmenu.cpp`), not an ImGui window, and wants
nothing of the mouse, so it is a menu like the pause menu and the cursor stays caught
under it.

**Commits.** `59ca9b7`, `31d3a43`, `4cca46c`, `db228d5`, `38358ae`

### The movement keys as the modern stick
2026-09-27

**What.** Under *Control type: Modern* the four movement keys are the modern control's
left stick: forward, back, left and right each push one axis to full deflection, so the
forward key runs Lara where the camera looks and the other three move her as the stick
pushed that way does, on the keyboard page and on the pad page alike. The function is
`ModernKeyStick` (`game/modern_move.cpp/.h`), called from the modern seam of
`specific/input.cpp`; the tick line of `MODERNLOG` ends in `feed=pad`, `feed=keys` or
`feed=none`. Under *Tank* nothing of this runs: `tomb5.control_modern` is the first term
of both blocks named below.

**Why.** The scheme translated only the pad's left stick. Its seam was closed on the
keyboard page, where `ControlMethod == 1` was a term of `modern_seam`, and on the pad page
a stick at rest left the keys' classic bits standing. So a keyboard player under Modern
moved as at Tank - the forward key ran her along her own heading, left and right turned
her - while the mouse turned the camera round her.

**How.** `ModernKeyStick` is pure. With the pad's pair off centre it hands that pair on
unchanged and answers `MODERN_FEED_PAD`; otherwise it makes x = (right ? 128 : 0) minus
(left ? 128 : 0) and y = (back ? 128 : 0) minus (forward ? 128 : 0), 128 being
`MODERN_STICK_FULL`, and answers `MODERN_FEED_KEYS`, or `MODERN_FEED_NONE` for 0/0. The
sign is the pad's: a stick pushed forward reads y negative on both paths
(`specific/dxshell.cpp` on DirectInput, `-ly / 256` on XInput, the d-pad's up -20), the
classic assembly reads `tank_y < -8` as `IN_FORWARD` and `ModernTranslate` takes the
stick's angle from (x, -y). The call stands in the seam itself, inside `if (modern_seam &&
!modern_tank)`, reads the same four `Key(0..3)` as the classic bits above it and writes a
local pair, `seam_x`/`seam_y`, so `move_x`/`move_y`, `tank_x`/`tank_y` and the classic
assembly keep the pad's own reading. `ControlMethod == 1` leaves `modern_seam`; the pad's
pair is kept out on the keyboard page instead: the block that zeroes it asks
`tomb5.control_modern && !ModernMenuReadsPad()` and applies the stick's dead zone only
under `ControlMethod == 1`, so a controller resting on the desk, or a d-pad press that
reads +-20 in `joy_x`/`joy_y`, cannot steer a keyboard player. The seam's action and jump
reads carry the term themselves: `JoyRole(4)`, `JoyRole(JOY_ROLE_SECOND)` and `JoyRole(3)`
count only under `ControlMethod == 1`, as at every other `JoyRole` call site, so a
connected pad's button cannot put a keyboard player into aiming or a directional jump. The
keys' classic bits stay in the word: when the translation takes the vector, the one write
in `ModernUpdateInput` (`game/modern_state.cpp`) replaces `MODERN_MOVE_MASK` as it does
for the pad, and when it steps aside - a classic state, a ladder, a push block - they
stand. The look key's bypass is the same code as before: `modern_tank` stands the seam
aside and the keys' classic bits turn her on the spot. The walk key is still read after
the seam. `ModernUpdateInput` takes the source as a sixth argument
(`game/modern_state.h`), and its tick line ends in `feed=%s` through `ModernFeedName`. The
field is not called `src`: the line's `src=` already says whether the translation wrote
the word (`pad`) or stood aside (`keys`), and keeps saying it. The seam still refuses the
inventory, the pause menu, the load and save screens, the outfit window, the title and the
first person view.

The keyboard page now runs the whole seam, and with it two things the pad page already
had: with no weapon ready the look key is taken out of the word, so held it steers her as
described above instead of turning the classic look camera, and `ModernHeadingAfterInput`
answers on the keyboard page too, so the orbit swings after a roll or a jump's twist as it
does for a pad player. The tests: ModernTest's `key_stick` group and `key_seam_model`, a
model of the guard chain read against `input.cpp`.

**Decisions.** The four keys are a full-deflection stick, fed to the seam's one call and
nowhere else. The pad wins: its stick off centre is taken and the keys are not added. A
diagonal of two keys is exactly 45 degrees, the magnitude clamp making it full. The look
key still bypasses the translation, so the keys turn her on the spot as at Tank. The keys
give no half deflection; the walk key walks. The keys still write their classic bits, so
every state where the scheme steps aside behaves as before. Opposite keys cancel to
nothing, so the forward-and-back roll chord fires only while no side key is held.

**Commits.** `be3c38a`, `5bcc669`, `9a91a90`, `30e6a37`

### Two action keys: the interaction bit and the Secondary role
2026-09-20 - 2026-09-20

**What.** A *Controls* setting **Action**, **One key** by default (the engine's own
behaviour: one button both interacts with the world and fires) or **Separate**. Under
*Separate* the *Action* role interacts with the world — switches, pickups, doors, pushable
blocks, the pulley, use-item triggers — and a new *Secondary* role does the climbing,
grabbing, hanging, monkey swinging and firing, so a player can hold one button to bring
the weapons up and press the other to fire. *Secondary* has a keyboard role (slot 18, Tank
default Home, Modern default Numpad 0, registry `Key18`/`MKey18`) and a pad slot
(`jLayout[15]`, registry `JSec`, default -1 = unbound); under *One key* the role produces
no bit, is not offered on the *Key bindings* page and claims no key in the conflict table.

**Why.** The unused bit was there: `IN_A = 0x4000` was declared and read nowhere in the
tree, so it is retired and `IN_INTERACT` takes its place at the same value. Under *One
key* the one action key raises both bits in a single statement, so the engine is
byte-identical at the default by construction rather than by argument. Two state routines
had to change with it: `LaraAboveWater`'s `input &= ~IN_ACTION` is followed by
`TestTriggers()`, whose `TO_CUTSCENE` case reaches five interaction sites, and left as it
was it would have let those five triggers fire where the base engine cannot; and
`lara_col_poledown` substituted the new bit inside a composite equality, which is sound
while the right-hand side is one bit and wrong when it is two — under *Separate* only ever
one of the two arrives, so the test was true on every tick and sliding down a pole was
reachable by no key at all.

**How.** `global/types.h`: `IN_A` retired, `IN_INTERACT = 0x4000`, `IN_ACTION_ANY =
IN_ACTION | IN_INTERACT`, `bool action_split`, with `specific/registry.cpp` storing it.
The two producers in `specific/input.cpp` / `.h` set `IN_SELECT | IN_ACTION | IN_INTERACT`
at one word under *One key*, and `IN_SELECT | IN_INTERACT` for *Action* with `IN_ACTION`
alone for *Secondary* under *Separate*. The `IN_ACTION` reads in nineteen files are split
three ways: 35 read `IN_INTERACT` alone (`game/switch.cpp` 13 — every switch but
`JumpSwitchCollision` — `game/pickup.cpp` 6, `game/control.cpp` 5 in
`NeatAndTidyTriggerCutscene`, `game/door.cpp` 4, `game/moveblok.cpp` 3, `game/traps.cpp`
`FloorTrapDoorCollision`, `game/flmtorch.cpp` `FireCollision`, and the two state routines
`lara_as_ppready` and `lara_as_pulley`); 20 read `IN_ACTION_ANY`, so neither key is ever
the wrong one — `game/objects.cpp` (`PoleCollision` twice, `TightRopeCollision`,
`ParallelBarsCollision`), `game/rope.cpp` `RopeCollision`, `game/deathsld.cpp`,
`game/switch.cpp` `JumpSwitchCollision`, `game/traps.cpp` `CeilingTrapDoorCollision`, and
every state routine in `game/lara.cpp` and `game/rope.cpp` that holds her on a pole, a
rope, the parallel bars or a death slide, since a state entered by an either-key collision
routine but held by `IN_ACTION` alone would throw her off the moment *Secondary* let go;
and the rest stay `IN_ACTION`, which under *Separate* is the *Secondary* key's — her
grab/climb/hang/monkey/swim automaton, the sixteen weapon reads, the binocular and
laser-sight reads and the swim cheat. `LaraAboveWater`'s mask clears `IN_ACTION_ANY` under
*One key* and `IN_ACTION` alone under *Separate*; `lara_col_poledown` is two mask tests
now, the shape `lara_col_poleup` already had. The inventory ring's confirm
(`game/newinv2.cpp`) reads `IN_SELECT`, with Core's `IN_ACTION` term kept behind
`!tomb5.action_split`. `MenuResolveKeybinds` (`game/menu_frame.cpp`) drops the *Secondary*
row of either list under *One key*, `KeySchemeConflicts` (`game/key_scheme.h`) takes an
argument saying whether the role is live, `game/pad_scheme.h` pins `JOY_ROLE_SECOND` to
15, and `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/MenuTest.cpp` and `docs/Engine-Manual.md` carry the
rule.

**Commits.** `0edeefa`, `4a55808`, `e817294`, `816d9d7`, `80837a7`, `a12de8b`

### Combat, Sprint, Duck and Grab: hold or toggle
2026-09-20 - 2026-09-21

**What.** Four settings on a *Modes* sub-page of *Controls* (German *Modi*), each
defaulting to 0 = the engine's own behaviour, each read on both control types and for
keyboard and pad alike. **Combat mode** defaults to *Toggle*, the engine's own, where the
draw key draws and holsters in turn; at *Hold* the weapons stay out while the key is held
and are holstered when it is released. **Sprint mode** and **Duck mode** default to
*Hold*; at *Toggle* a press latches the bit and the next press releases it. **Grab mode**
defaults to *Hold*; at *Toggle* she keeps hold without the button — a ledge, both shimmies
and the corner turns, the monkey swing, the climb and ladder states, the pole, the rope,
the zip line and the parallel bars — and a fresh press lets go. Registry names
`combat_hold`, `sprint_toggle`, `duck_toggle`, `grab_toggle`.

**Why.** Nothing in the base engine debounces the draw key: `IN_DRAW` has two producers
and no consumer reads its edge, so what limits it is Lara's own animation and a key held
down really does draw and holster without end. A latch must not manufacture behaviour the
held key does not have: the sprint latch drops when she stops or when the dash timer ends
the sprint, and the duck latch must survive a crawl, since `ANIM_DUCK_TO_ALL4S` sets
`lara.gun_status = LG_HANDS_BUSY` and that would otherwise drop it the instant she goes
down. The grab latch may not ask about `bUseSpotCam`: `InitialiseSpotCam` leaves that flag
standing through an ordinary flyby, and `game/control.cpp` holds `bDisableLaraControl` at
1 for as long as a `GF_OFFICE` level's flipmap is above 10 — in both windows the player
still has control, and a *Toggle* player would have lost `IN_ACTION` and fallen where a
*Hold* player hangs on. The let-go press needs a mask of its own: thirteen of the family's
thirty-five states test `IN_ACTION_ANY`, and under *One key* both bits leave the producer
together, so clearing `IN_ACTION` alone left them reading "still holding on" — on a rope
or in an `AS_PBSPIN` there is no other way out, so she swung or spun until a reload.

**How.** The arithmetic is pure and lives in `game/modern_move.cpp` / `.h`:
`ModernWeaponBits` (one request per tick on which the weapon state and the key disagree,
none while the animation runs, self-correcting on the next tick), `ModernModeLatch` /
`ModernModeLatchDrop` with `modern_latch_bits` keeping `MODERN_LATCH_ON` and
`MODERN_LATCH_KEY` apart, `ModernGrabLatch(..., bit, release, bits)` and
`ModernStateIsGrab`. All of it is applied at two seams at the end of `S_UpdateInput`
(`specific/input.cpp`): the mode latches immediately before the weapon seam and after the
walk-sidestep rewrite, so a sidestepping player is not read as pushing nothing; the weapon
seam after the `IN_RIGHT | IN_LEFT` cancel, so it sees `linput` as every other consumer
does. The weapon seam's guard is `!App.fmv` (a bit held through the outro video would have
saturated `specific/fmv.cpp`'s rising-edge skip on `IN_OPTION|IN_DRAW|IN_SELECT` and made
the video unskippable) plus `lara_item`, `GLOBAL_playing_cutseq`, `bUseSpotCam`,
`bDisableLaraControl`, `InventoryActive`, `gfLevelId != LVL5_TITLE` and `lara.gun_type !=
WEAPON_TORCH`, so a burning torch passes through untouched and can still be thrown by
`game/flmtorch.cpp`; the sprint and duck latches drop on those eight terms, the grab latch
asks the seven without `bUseSpotCam`. The grab family is 35 of Lara's 140 animation states
— fifteen read plain `IN_ACTION` (hang, both shimmies, both hang turns, the overhead hang,
the four monkey-swing states, five of the six ladder states), thirteen read
`IN_ACTION_ANY` (pole 99-103, rope 90/91/111/114/115, `AS_SLIDEROPE` 113, the zip line 70,
the parallel bars 128), six read no input and are in the family only so the bit cannot
blink off mid-transition (`AS_CLIMBEND` 59, `AS_CLIMBROPE` 112, the four corner shimmies
107-110), read out of `game/lara.cpp` and `game/rope.cpp`; the thirty-fifth is
`AS_LEDGEHANG` 139, the *Ledge hang* move's turn and lowering (its own entry below), a
transition into `AS_HANG` that begins with the key held and is a grab from there on.
Delivery is `IN_ACTION` alone; the let-go mask is composed at the seam as `IN_ACTION_ANY`
under *One key* and `IN_ACTION` under *Separate*, and `IN_SELECT` is never in either;
while a let-go press lasts the whole mask stays clear wherever she is, so under *One key*
that press also picks nothing up and operates nothing until the button has been up once.
The duck-and-crawl family is twelve states — duck, its roll, both duck turns, all fours,
crawl forward and back, both crawl turns and the three pickup states reachable from a duck
or a crawl — and the latch holds through all of them; a low ceiling still keeps her down
through `lara.keep_ducked` exactly as a held key does. All three latches drop through
`InputModeLatchReset()` at a level's priming tick (`game/gameflow.cpp`), so a savegame
load gets it too, and through the menu rows' own step functions; a key held across a level
change is not a fresh press, because `ModernModeLatchDrop` clears `MODERN_LATCH_ON` and
leaves `MODERN_LATCH_KEY` standing. With both toggles off the whole mode seam is skipped
by one `if (tomb5.sprint_toggle || tomb5.duck_toggle)`, and `if (tomb5.combat_hold)`
guards the weapon seam the same way, so the binocular and laser-sight zoom, which read
`inputBusy & IN_SPRINT`/`IN_DUCK` on a held tick, are unaffected. The four settings live
in `global/types.h` and `tomb5/tomb5.cpp`; the rows sit on `MENU_PAGE_MODES`
(`game/menu_frame.cpp` / `.h`), opened by a centred tab on *Controls* after *View*, and
kept their callbacks, save class and `MENULOG` row names when they moved there. Seams
`COMBATLOG` and `MODELOG` behind `-log`. Tests in
`Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/ModernTest.cpp` and `Preparation/Tools/Diagnose/MenuTest.cpp`;
`docs/Engine-Manual.md` carries the four rows.

### Ledge hang: an automatic turn and lowering at an edge
2026-09-24

**What.** A fifth row, *Ledge hang*, on the *Modes* sub-page alongside Combat, Sprint,
Duck and Grab mode (`game/menu_frame.cpp`, `MENU_VALUE_IF`, a new macro beside
`MENU_VALUE`/`MENU_SLIDER` that puts a predicate in a value row's `enabled` slot),
registry name `ledge_hang`, default Off, read and written at the same three sites
`grab_toggle` is (`tomb5/tomb5.cpp`), greyed under Tank controls by the same
`MenuEnabledModern` predicate the Controls-page camera sliders use. With it on and Modern
controls active, running, walking, or standing and pushing toward an edge with the grab
key held (`IN_ACTION` — the action key under *One key*, the Secondary key under
*Separate*) stops her on the sector's standing line, turns her half round on the spot, and
lowers her into the settled hang by playing Tomb Raider 5's own pull-up animation (97)
backwards, instead of letting her run off. With the option on, holding the grab key while
running off an edge the move accepts no longer reaches for a ledge below the way
`lara_as_forwardjump` does (the action key sets `goal_anim_state = AS_REACH` once she is
already falling); a sprint and a refused edge still reach below. Under the Modern orbit
the camera swings round with her turn, ending behind her back over the drop where the
walls allow it, and keeps looking at her all the way down: its look-at point follows her
out over the edge and down the lowering in even steps, never standing still and never
jumping. Under *Grab mode* *Toggle* the grab is carried through the move: from the tick it
fires she keeps hold whatever the key does; a fresh press while she turns stands her back
up, a fresh press still down on the tick of the hand-over lets go of the ledge there, and
a short press during the lowering that is up again before the hand-over changes nothing.
Under *Hold* the lowering runs to the hand-over whatever the key does, and the hang then
needs the key as every hang does. The files: `game/lara.cpp/.h`, `game/lara_states.h`,
`game/modern_move.cpp/.h`, `game/laramisc.cpp`, `game/camera.cpp`,
`game/interpolate_math.h`, `game/interpolate.cpp`, `game/draw.cpp`, `game/savegame.cpp`,
`specific/gamemain.cpp`, `specific/input.cpp`, `global/types.h`.

**Why.** The design is this project's own and plays Tomb Raider 5's own pull-up, animation
97, backwards. The pull-up can be played backwards because during it `item->pos` never
moves — only the root offsets do, and the whole climb resolves in the one `TranslateItem`
at the animation's wrap — so counting the frame down and undoing that one translate at the
start reconstructs it exactly, which is why the state's own guard in `game/laramisc.cpp`'s
`AnimateLara` is enough. The option defaults off because it changes what holding the grab
key while running off an edge already does — the `AS_REACH` catch below — and a player who
relies on that should not have it silently replaced. It is Modern-controls only because
the turn leans on the Modern camera swinging behind her (`ModernCameraCarryHalfTurn`,
called once on the turn's first tick and gated on `ModernCameraActive()` so a swing is
never seated while nothing pays it out); Tank stays byte-identical by not being asked at
all. An aborted turn drops the camera's remaining swing (`ModernCameraDropSwing`, called
on a stand after the turn's first tick), as the right stick drops it, so the camera never
ends in front of her. The look-at point needs a rule of its own because the lowering's
first tick moves her 200 units out over the drop and 726 down (`LaraLedgeToHang`), and
`UpdateLaraRoom` puts her into the room below the ledge. `CalculateCamera` builds the
point in her room and moves it only a quarter of the way after her each tick, which leaves
it above the ledge; in her new room that sector can be closed above, and `ChaseCamera`'s
in-room test then finds the point above the ceiling and puts the previous one back, tick
after tick, until `TargetSnaps` passes 8 and the raw point is taken unsmoothed. In play,
at a walkway edge of Andrea1 whose sector in the room below is closed at the walkway's
underside, the point stood still while she lowered and then jumped about 200 units across
and 300 down in one tick, a 12-degree tilt of the view; the swing itself was even (its
3u^2 - 2u^3 profile, 13.5 degrees a tick at the peak) and is not changed. The lowering is
drawn at the full frame rate: the interpolator's neighbour rule (`curFrame != prevFrame +
1`, `game/interpolate_math.h`) refuses every backwards-stepped frame, so `InterpPoseBack`,
asked by `GetFramesAt` only while `LaraLedgeReversing`, walks the animation's own path
between the two tick poses instead - the previous tick's pose at the start of the tween,
the current tick's at its end, their midpoint at a half. The tween after each animation
change, into the pull-up and out of it into the hang, stays a tick frame, as everywhere.

**How.** The constants (`game/modern_move.h`): the turn is her own turn-on-the-spot
animation at the direct turn's rate, `MODERN_LEDGE_HALF_TURN` (0x8000) over
`MODERN_LEDGE_TURN_TICKS` (6) ticks, 5461 or 5462 units a tick, `MODERN_TURN_RATE` (5461,
30 degrees) to within a unit, so the half turn takes 0.2 s, to the side
`MODERN_LEDGE_TURN_SIDE` (1, right) names; the lowering steps the pull-up down
`MODERN_LEDGE_FRAME_STEP` (3) frames a tick; the standing line sits
`MODERN_LEDGE_STAND_IN` (99) units inside the sector's edge and the hang
`MODERN_LEDGE_HANG_OUT` (100) units past it, the engine's own catch-snap distances;
`MODERN_LEDGE_RESIDUAL` (15) is the most a walk or a stand may lie off the line and still
start the move; `MODERN_LEDGE_SNAP` (0x18E2) is the catch's own 35-degree cardinal window;
`MODERN_LEDGE_NEAR` (512) is how close an edge has to be before `LEDGELOG` reports the
refusal set.

The nine refusals, each one engine test asked the way its own site asks it
(`LaraLedgeRefusals`, `game/lara.cpp`, the bit values in `game/lara.h`): `SHALLOW` the
drop is 768 units or less; `SLOPE` the ledge floor's two front corners differ by 120 or
more; `SLIDE` the floor there would start `TestLaraSlide`; `OBJECT` an item, static, or
the catch's own `hit_static` is in the way; `CLIMB` a climbable wall sits under the edge;
`CEILING` the hang position's ceiling is too low or would catch her into the monkey hang
instead; `CATCH` the heading is outside the cardinal window, there is no floor, or the
engine's own edge catch itself fails; `WATER` water, lava, or a death floor lies below;
`LARA` her weapons are drawn, she is dead, a creature hit her this tick, or a cutscene
holds her. The triggers in the floor data of the sector she hangs in are not asked: the
engine's own catch hangs her in that same sector, and `LaraAboveWater` hands its
`coll->trigger` to `TestTriggers` every tick of the hang, so a camera, music, door or
flipmap trigger there fires after the move exactly as after a catch made by hand.

The trigger (`LaraLedgeTrigger`) is asked from `lara_col_run`, `lara_col_walk`, and
`lara_col_stop`, right after each routine's own ceiling test and after
`GetLaraCollisionInfo` has measured this tick's movement, so a state change and a position
write there land inside the tick order between `AnimateLara` and `TestTriggers`/`LaraGun`
exactly once. A run needs no forward input (so braking with the key held is still caught)
and is put on the standing line by a shift that is always forward and at most one ordinary
step; a standing state that became a run or a walk this tick is judged at `coll->old`,
where she actually stood, so the start of a run's own 23-unit hop never counts.
`ModernLedgeDecide` (`game/modern_move.cpp`) is the pure decision for one tick of the move
— the turn's ramp, signed by the side, and its abort tests, the lowering's frame step and
its hand-over — read by `lara_as_ledgehang`, the routine for the new state `AS_LEDGEHANG =
139` (`game/lara_states.h`); its collision row stays `lara_default_col`, since the state
itself fills `coll` for `TestTriggers` and `LaraGun` and never moves her by walking. The
turn runs in Tomb Raider 5's own turn on the spot, animation 12 (`ANIM_TURN_RIGHT`, the
animation of `AS_TURN_R`) or 13 (`ANIM_TURN_LEFT`, of `AS_TURN_L`): the trigger starts the
one for `MODERN_LEDGE_TURN_SIDE` at its `frame_base`, `AnimateLara` plays it forward as
any other animation (its footstep included; none of its state changes leads out of
`AS_LEDGEHANG`), the frame counts the turn's ticks, and the side is read back off it, so a
restored savegame goes on turning the way it started; a save that holds the idle,
`ANIM_BREATH`, in the turn phase is settled into the hang or a fall like any other that
cannot go on. One guard at the head of `AnimateLara` (`LaraLedgeReversing`) holds the
frame and skips every animation command while the lowering plays backwards, for
`AS_LEDGEHANG` only. The lowering steps the pull-up (74 frames at rate 4) from its last
frame down by three, 73, 70, ..., 4, 1, and cuts the last step short to land on 0: 25
backwards steps. The hand-over is exactly the engine's own settled hang — `ANIM_GRABLEDGE`
at `frame_base + 21`, `AS_HANG`, `LG_HANDS_BUSY` (`LaraLedgeHang`) — so `lara_col_hang`
and `LaraHangTest` take over from there exactly as they do from any other catch.

The hand-over happens inside the control routine, and the collision routine of the same
tick is dispatched on the state it wrote, so `lara_col_hang` → `LaraHangTest` reads a word
`S_UpdateInput` built for 139: the word is composed with the state the last tick ended in,
and without `IN_ACTION` `LaraHangTest` drops her at once. So `AS_LEDGEHANG` is in the grab
family (`ModernStateIsGrab`), and under *Toggle* `ModernGrabLatch` delivers the bit from
the turn's first tick on. The key memory the run set makes that first tick no fresh press
(`MODERN_LATCH_KEY`); a savegame restored in the move goes on under *Toggle* without a
key, as one restored in any hang does, since `InputModeLatchReset` (`game/gameflow.cpp`)
clears the let-go and keeps the key memory. `MODELOG`'s `grab=` field reads 1 from the
turn's first tick on. Under *Hold*, Tank controls and with the option off the family
changes nothing: *Hold* hands the word back untouched, and nothing enters 139 without the
option and Modern controls.

The savegame: the phase (`modern_ledge_phase`) and the heading she hangs with are appended
to `tomb5_save_info` as `ledge_phase` and `ledge_heading` (`global/types.h`). Every save
of this build carries them: `LaraLedgeSave` (`game/savegame.cpp`) writes the phase and
heading in the hang and `MODERN_LEDGE_NONE` and 0 otherwise, so the block written after
`SAVEGAME_INFO` (`specific/gamemain.cpp`) has grown from 4 to 7 bytes under `#pragma
pack(push, 1)`. The read is length-checked: `LaraLedgeLoad` takes each field only when the
byte count `ReadFile` returned reaches past its offset, and uses them only while she is in
the hang. An older build reads its own 4 bytes of the block and leaves the 3 after them
unread. A save that cannot go on this way is settled once by the same refusal test into
the hang or a fall.

The tweens of the lowering: `InterpPoseBack` (`game/interpolate_math.h`), a pure function
beside `InterpPoseAt`, which it leaves untouched, places both tick poses in key units
exactly as vanilla does (`InterpKeyAlpha` over `InterpKeyRate`), puts the drawn frame at
`pp + (pc - pp) * t` on that path and hands out the key interval it lies in - the upper
pair `kc + 1` when a step passes over a key and the midpoint still lies above it (70 down
to 67: 17.125, pair 17 at 0.125); it refuses a forward or standing frame, no rate, a frame
outside the animation and two frames more than one key interval apart. `GetFramesAt`
(`game/draw.cpp`) asks it only when `InterpPoseAt` has refused, and only for `lara_item`
while `LaraLedgeReversing`, so with the option off, under Tank controls and at `fps_mode
0` nothing reaches it; the pose and its root offset then come from the same key pair and
factor, and `item->pos` does not move during the lowering, so there is nothing for the
root rule to pay. `INTERPLOG` gains `pose_back=` at the end of its once-a-second line
(`game/interpolate.cpp`, noted by `InterpNotePoseBack`): the tween frames the rule
blended, one per drawn in-between frame, so a lowering's 25 ticks times the tween frames
per tick, and 0 everywhere else.

The camera's look-at rule holds while `ModernCameraActive()` and `LaraLedgeCamera`
(`game/lara.cpp`, its `lara_ledge_camera` phases in `game/lara.h`) names a phase:
`AS_LEDGEHANG` throughout, turn or lower as `LedgePhase` stands after the tick's control,
and a tail of `LEDGE_CAMERA_TAIL_TICKS` (10) ticks, the hand-over's own included.
`LaraLedgeHang` stamps the tail with `GlobalCounter`, so it runs out on time whatever runs
in between; `LaraLedgeStand` and `LaraLedgeFall` end it, and so does every level start
(`LaraLedgeCameraReset`, called from `InitialiseCamera`). `CalculateCamera` decides the
rule once a pass, off for the sniper camera and for a camera built round an item. Under it
the smoothed point's room walk starts in the room the point was in last tick,
`last_target.room_number`, instead of hers — only the walk's starting room changes, never
the point, and `ConfirmCameraTargetPos` still tests her own column from her own room — and
`ChaseCamera` asks a point that walk finds in no room once more from her room, as the
vanilla lookup asks it, and takes that room when the point lies inside it; only a point
both refuse counts as a snap and is put back, by the vanilla lines. A point accepted
either way lies inside the open volume of the room the walk found — `GetFloor` clamps a
point outside a room onto the room's edge sectors, which are walls or doors, and a wall
sector fails the test — so a point inside rock is still refused, and the eye, built from
the point by `mgLOS` as before, is not sent into geometry. At the Andrea1 edge the point
goes a quarter of the remaining 200 units across each tick, is over the pit by the third
tick while still some 650 units above the walkway's top, and never lies in the slab. Under
Tank and in first person the rule never holds, nor with the option off, where nothing
enters 139 (a move under way when the option is switched off from the pause menu ends in
an immediate hand-over and tail from the lowering, and in a stand from the turn); the
smoothing and the rule that takes the raw point after eight snaps stay vanilla's, and only
what counts as a snap changes, during the move and its tail. `last_target` is not in the
savegame: `InitialiseCamera` seats it at her own position in her own room before its first
pass, so in a savegame restored in the move the first walk starts from her room, exactly
as without the rule, and from the point's own room after that.

`LEDGELOG` behind `-log` prints one line per phase change, a line when the refusal set
changes while the key is held near an edge, and one fire line when the move starts, and,
under the Modern orbit, one `LEDGELOG cam` line per tick of the move and on the ten ticks
from the hand-over on (`ModernCameraLedgeLog`, printed at the end of `CalculateCamera`):
`f=` `GlobalCounter`, `phase=` turn, lower, hang (the hand-over's tick) or tail, the eye
and the look-at point as the pass left them and the point before the quarter smoothing
(`raw=`), each with its room, `item_room=`, `snaps=` `TargetSnaps`, `rejected=` 1 when the
in-room test put the previous point back, `head_fallback=` 1 when `ConfirmCameraTargetPos`
took the head position, `angle=` and `elev=` the actual angle and elevation, `world=` the
orbit's world yaw, `carry=` the swing still owed / its ticks paid, `lead=` the yaw step
asked of `ModernCameraLeadEye` / the step it gave after its distance scaling, `clip=` the
dialled eye's `mgLOS` clip, `pull=` the step of eight at which `ModernCameraRayBounds`
found clearance (0 none), `mc_pull=` 1 when `MoveCamera`'s own `mgLOS` pulled an eye in,
and `csnaps=` `CameraSnaps`. The values are collected in `ledge_log`, cleared at the top
of every pass and written where each is computed: stores to a static nothing else reads,
so they change nothing in any mode. The tests: ModernTest's `ledge_hang()` and
`ledge_trigger()` blocks (every turn step within a unit of `MODERN_TURN_RATE` among them)
and InterpTest's `pose_back()` block (rates 1, 2, 4 and 5, steps 1 to 3, the real lowering
at `frame_base` 0 and 3000, its refusals and a clamped last interval).

**Decisions.** A known limit stays as built: `tomb5.ledge_hang` switched off in the middle
of the automatic turn stands Lara up without dropping the camera's swing
(`lara_as_ledgehang`'s default case).
